chapters.title: Chapter 651: The Sentinel Beneath the Glass
paragraphs: The Nascent Soul sentinel crossed twenty paces in a single step.

Leon shifted half a pace aside and folded the space through its chest. The construct’s upper body separated from its legs before its fist completed the strike. Both halves crashed across the black stone.
The four Golden Core constructs lasted no longer.

Seraphine’s sword passed through the first two in a line of violet-white light, leaving their bodies divided into clean sections. Ira met the third with one direct thrust and shattered everything between its chest and spine. Vyra closed her hand, and the flames surrounding the fourth compressed until the stormglass softened, collapsed inward, and poured across the ground in a glowing heap.
Loriel did not need to intervene.
Five bodies lay broken within three breaths.
"That was disappointing," Ira said.
Pale light raced through the veins beneath their feet.

The pieces of the sentinel moved first. Broken stormglass liquefied, ran toward the nearest junction, and rose into a new pair of legs. Its torso rebuilt above them. The four smaller bodies followed, drawing replacement material directly out of the ground.
In less time than it had taken to destroy them, all five constructs stood again without a mark.
"That is less disappointing," Ira said.
They attacked a second time.

Seraphine removed the two Golden Core constructs from her path before they reached sword range. Ira smashed hers into fragments. Vyra burned the fourth down again, this time keeping the molten stormglass suspended so it could not immediately return to the ground.
The sentinel ignored Leon and appeared beside Loriel when the distance between them changed without warning.
Loriel turned and caught its descending wrist in one hand.
The stone beneath her feet cracked. She did not move.

Green light travelled from her palm into the sentinel’s arm. The construct had no life of its own, but its formation core imitated circulation closely enough for Loriel to seize the false rhythm. She drove a pulse through it in the wrong direction.
The sentinel’s chest burst outward. Its arm came away in Loriel’s hand, and the rest of it collapsed at her feet.
"There is a core behind the lower chest," she said. "Destroying it stops the body. It does not stop the formation from making another one."
The ground confirmed her conclusion. New columns of stormglass were already rising at five different points.

The formation briefly abandoned the smaller bodies and poured their charge into the sentinel. It rebuilt beside Seraphine with both arms raised. She met it head-on. Lightning accelerated one clean sword stroke through its neck, chest, and false core before its hands descended.

The next sentinel rose in front of Ira. She planted her rear foot and drove her lance through it with enough force to carry the entire body into the shelf behind it. The core shattered on impact. Neither woman had needed help or given up ground.

Five new columns began forming immediately afterward. The defense was not finding opponents strong enough to defeat them. It was replacing disposable bodies faster than ordinary cultivators could have destroyed them.

Leon watched the energy move beneath them. The constructs were not dangerous because of their cultivation ranks. Even the sentinel could not threaten anyone in the group by itself. The problem was the amount of stormglass available to rebuild them and a formation capable of changing where the next bodies appeared.
If they kept destroying each wave, the defense could continue until the corridor failed or the entire basin ran out of material.
"Stop attacking the bodies," Leon said. "We need the network beneath them."

Seraphine drove the point of her sword into the stone and released a controlled lightning pulse. Pale veins answered across fifty paces, briefly exposing five separate routes feeding the new constructs.
Vyra spread her fire over the revealed paths. The flames did not merely burn. They followed the external energy, marking every turn and junction as the current shifted underground.

"It’s the same forty-one-second cycle as the roads," she said. "The power moves between five junctions. When we sever one, the current diverts through the other four and rebuilds the damaged route from behind."
"Can you stop the diversion?" Leon asked.
"For a moment. Not while the current is spread through all five."
"Then make it choose one."
The next wave finished forming.

Seraphine and Ira moved first. Seraphine cut through two Golden Core bodies and struck the ground connections beneath them in the same motion. Ira destroyed the third and drove her lance through its junction deep enough to split the vein below the surface.
The formation redirected everything toward Vyra’s side.
She allowed it.

Her fire contracted around the fourth construct and the branching network beneath it. Every displaced current entered the space she controlled. Crownfire closed over the junction in concentric layers, suppressing the stormglass charge without consuming it.
"Now," she said.
For the first time, the full underground network had nowhere to send its power.

The sentinel formed beside Leon with every pale vein burning at once. It carried the combined charge of all five bodies, enough to distort the ground around it and bend the apparent distance to the others.
Leon met its first strike with his bare hand.
The impact stopped against his palm.
He had faced Mid Void Immortal power in Jade Moon Palace’s arena. A Nascent Soul formation construct, even one overfilled with borrowed energy, was not an opponent he needed to avoid.
He tightened his grip and tore the sentinel’s arm free. His spatial perception followed the power spilling from the wound, down through its false core and into the junction beneath its feet.
"Loriel."
"Low behind the chest," she said. "The false pulse turns just before the cycle resets."
Seraphine’s lightning illuminated the buried route. Vyra held every diverted branch inside her Crownfire. Ira stood over the three broken junctions and shattered each attempt to reopen them.
Leon waited for the false pulse to turn.
Then he folded the four inches between the sentinel and the ground.
The connection did not merely break. It led back into itself, trapping the charge in a path that no longer reached any of the five junctions.
Loriel placed her palm against the sentinel’s chest and released a second reversed pulse.
The formation core ruptured.
This time, no replacement body rose.

The four Golden Core constructs collapsed with it. Vyra released her fire gradually, watching for any current attempting to escape into a new channel. The trapped charge dispersed through inactive stormglass instead of returning to the defense.
Ordinary distance settled across the basin.
Leon took two steps toward the others. Both covered exactly two steps.
"Everyone intact?" he asked.
"Entirely," Seraphine said.
Ira rested her lance against one shoulder. "Can the next defenders be stronger?"
"No," Loriel and Vyra answered together.
A human voice carried across the quiet basin. Someone was discussing the angle of a marker line.
Two hundred paces away, beside the mineral pool, a man in a deacon’s grey robe turned toward the sound of collapsing stormglass.
For the first time since the disappearance, Deacon Yu looked directly at them.
Deacon Yu’s hand went to his sword before he called a warning.
The two Golden Core disciples moved in front of the six surveyors, who withdrew behind a shelf with their formation tools. Surprise lasted only a moment before training took over.
"Stop there," Yu called. "Identify yourselves."
Leon halted forty paces away and raised his authority token.
"Leon. Direct disciple of the Palace Mistress. Peak Golden Core. These four are members of my household, and Jade Moon Palace sent us to find your team."

Yu approached far enough to examine the token without placing his people within easy striking range. His attention moved from the Palace mark to the four Peak Foundation Establishment women, none of whom looked as though they had just fought above their recorded realms, and finally to the remains of the constructs behind them.
"The token is genuine," he said. "Since when does the Palace Mistress have a direct disciple?"

chapters.title: Chapter 652: Fourteen People, No Door
paragraphs: "Since roughly two months ago."
Yu frowned. "We’ve been in the field for nine days."
"Deacon, your final transmission reached the Palace nearly a month ago."
For the first time, Yu’s control slipped.
One of the younger disciples laughed once, apparently expecting someone else to recognize the joke. Nobody did.
"Prove it," Yu said.
Vyra opened her record plaque.
"Young Master’s mission order, our departure record, and every communication acknowledged by Han Suwen since then," she said. "The seals and timestamps are intact."
Yu read the records in order. Mo Rui joined him for the second examination, checking the Palace seals before comparing their last transmitted entry against Vyra’s calendar.
Neither found an error.
"How long have we been here?" Yu asked.
"How long do you believe has passed?" Leon asked.

"Less than an hour." Yu looked back at his team. "We activated the three tracking formations around our camp. All three needles changed direction together and pointed toward empty ground. Mo Rui thought the calibration had slipped."
"It had not," Mo Rui said quietly.

"Then the rain began rising," Yu continued. "The wet basin and a dry one appeared over each other. There was a flash strong enough that I felt it in my teeth, and we found ourselves here. The camp was gone."
"What did you do afterward?"
"Stopped moving until we understood whether the terrain was stable. When the distances began changing, we measured them. It was the only useful thing available to us."
He looked down at Vyra’s plaque again.
"Nearly a month?"
"Outside," Leon said. "Inside, your bodies appear to agree with your estimate."
Nobody among the surveyors was hungry, exhausted, or short of spiritual energy. None had needed sleep. Loriel examined them while Yu spoke and found no wasting or hidden depletion.
"All nine are healthy, Young Master," she reported. "This is not merely altered perception. Physically, they have experienced less than an hour."
Yu accepted that with visible difficulty, but he recovered quickly.

"Then there is something else you need to know. About two kilometres northeast, near the centre of this version of the basin, we observed a buried stormglass platform. The exposed section is terraced and roughly forty paces across. It does not exist in the basin we surveyed before the transfer."
"You reached it?" Leon asked.

"No. The changing distance kept moving it, but we observed it clearly from a high shelf. It emits a pulse every eleven minutes, near enough. After the second pulse, Mo Rui compared the signal against our formation logs."
Mo Rui opened his own plaque and displayed the traces.
"It is the same signal our tracking needles followed at the camp," he said. "Whatever they detected came from that platform. We had begun working out a route toward it when your battle drew us back."
The platform was their best lead, but it could wait until they had exhausted the safer option.
"Gather every portable record and formation tool," Leon said. "Leave the samples. We still have an open corridor to the real basin, and we return before anything else in this realm recovers."
Yu did not argue. The surveyors packed with the efficiency of people accustomed to abandoning a field site in bad weather.

As they worked, Yu confirmed that their communication plaques and distress devices had failed immediately after the transfer. They had attempted both before resuming their measurements. None had found a connection beyond the secret realm.

Seraphine cleaned stormglass dust from her sword while Ira checked the edge of her lance. The constructs had delayed them and forced them to use more of their retained power than they would have preferred, but none of the five had been injured.
Fourteen people started back toward the paired anchors.
They had covered two hundred paces when Leon felt the energy beneath the corridor change.

The closed circuit between the anchors had remained stable throughout their advance and battle. Now the current vanished from the outer branches and poured into deeper channels under the secret realm.
"Young Master," Seraphine said. "The corridor is thinning."
Leon reached for the alignment at once.
The two anchors were still intact, but the formation controlling the realm had redirected the stormglass charge sustaining them. Without that power, the paired plates could preserve nothing.

Leon circulated Space and Lightning through the Formless Myriad Scripture and used the Primordial Void Heart to take the returning pressure. For several seconds, he held the edges together by his own strength.
It was not enough. The original correspondence was disappearing beneath his grip.
He could attempt to force both spaces into contact. He had crossed worlds before and rebuilt a road the Upper Ones destroyed. This opening was smaller.
There were also fourteen people within thirty paces of it. If the two structures tore instead of joining, the collapse would pass through every one of them.
Not like this.
Leon released the alignment before his cultivation route began to strain.
The corridor narrowed until only a line of doubled ground remained. Then that line closed, leaving dry black stone between the two anchors.
Vyra opened her communication plaque. It searched and found nothing. Yu’s plaque did the same, as did every distress device carried by the survey team.
"Return talismans," Leon said.
The five members of his household tore theirs one after another.
Not one activated. The paper remained cold, and the jade threads carried no response from the receiving formation in Jade Moon Palace.
The four women looked toward him. The nine surveyors waited behind them, still absorbing the fact that nearly a month had passed without them.

"Our next communication window is tomorrow at the third mark," Leon said. "When we miss it, the Palace’s response team leaves within the hour. My records, the three tracking formations, and the outer anchor are waiting in the abandoned camp."
"How long before they arrive?" Yu asked.
"Eight days at best speed."
"And when they reach the basin?"
"They will know how we entered. Whether they can reproduce it without the right storm is another question."
Behind them, pale light began returning to the broken lines beneath the construct remains. The defensive formation was rebuilding its network, even if it could not yet produce another sentinel.
Far to the northeast, the buried platform released its next pulse.
Leon looked toward it.
They had found all nine missing cultivators alive. Now fourteen people were trapped inside the secret realm, and the only remaining lead lay at its centre.

chapters.title: Chapter 653: Fourteen Against the Road
paragraphs: The pulse came again eleven minutes after the last one, and Ira turned toward it before it finished.
"We should go now."
"We should go in forty minutes," Leon said.

He said it without heat and loudly enough that all thirteen of the others heard him, because half of them were already looking northeast with the particular expression of people who wanted very badly to be doing something.

"We have one lead and no retreat. Every mistake we make from here is permanent." He turned to the deacon. "Deacon Yu. Consolidate. All nine of your people’s records, every measuring tool, every marker, all the medicine and every portion of food anyone is carrying. Counted and distributed."
Yu did not argue, which Leon appreciated. "The samples?"
"Leave them. Everything heavy stays."
"Some of that material is—"
"Worth a great deal, and none of it is worth a step." Leon met his eyes. "If we get out, the Palace can come back for it with a proper expedition. If we don’t, it stays here either way."
Yu inclined his head and started giving orders.
Loriel used the time to build something the group did not yet know it needed.

She went through all fourteen again — pulse, colour, breathing, the rate at which spiritual energy returned to a channel after being spent — and wrote each result down twice, once in Vyra’s record and once on a scrap she folded into her sleeve.
Then she planted a seed.

"Windwort," she said, tamping soil into a shallow clay dish from her medicine kit. "Germinates in about six hours under this much ambient energy, and I’ve grown it often enough to know every stage. If it develops too quickly or too slowly, local time and living time have separated."
She set a marked flask of water beside it, filled to a scored line, with a second line scratched an inch below.
"And that gives me evaporation. Slow, boring, honest." She sat back. "Young Master, if any of those three disagree with each other, I want to be told to stop everything."
"You’ll be the one telling me," Leon said.
Vyra spent the forty minutes with Mo Rui and the surveyors’ logs.

"They watched the platform for most of what they thought was an hour," she reported. "Eleven-minute pulse, consistent, no drift they could measure. Mo Rui logged five of them." She turned the plaque. "But their notes record no change in the ambient light across the entire sequence. Five pulses, no shadow movement, no temperature drift."
"Meaning?"
"Meaning either this place has no sun and never did, or their hour and the pulse count are measuring two different things." She closed the plaque. "I would like to know which."
Behind them, Seraphine and Ira came back from the rear inspection.

"It’s rebuilding," Seraphine said quietly. "The wreckage from the fight. The pieces haven’t moved, but the veins in them are lighting again — not brightly, and not all at once. Something is putting charge back into that network."
"How long before it stands up?"
"Hours at that rate. Possibly a day." She glanced back the way they had come. "We should not be here when it does."
They left on the next pulse rather than in the gap between two.
Leon had thought about it for most of the forty minutes and could not prove it, so he said so.

"Every time that platform pulses, the routes here line up better. I’ve felt it three times and the correspondence tightens for about four seconds. That’s a theory built on three observations and it might be wrong. But if the geography is least unreliable during a pulse, leaving on one gives us the best starting alignment we’re going to get."
Nobody had a better idea. Yu made it clear that he regarded the theory as unproven, and then they went.
They travelled in a shape Vyra designed in twenty minutes and improved twice on the move.

Leon walked point on the route, reading correspondence ahead and calling every change of direction. Vyra held the column together — fourteen people at one pace, counted aloud, the pulse count called at every interval so nobody drifted. Seraphine took front guard and tested anything resembling a boundary with a thread of lightning too fine to charge anything badly. Ira held the rear and destroyed any of their own markers that began to move.
Loriel walked in the middle, checking faces, circulation, and pulse whenever the route forced them to stop.
The survey team turned out to be worth a great deal.

Mo Rui laid a measured marker line behind them, spacing every stake by chain rather than eye, which meant that when the ground lied they could prove it. Xie Lan kept a running comparison against the terrain notes from the team’s apparent hour. Yu ran his six surveyors the way men run a thing they have done ten thousand times: quietly, in order, without being told twice.
"Ridge bearing three-one," Mo Rui called at one point. "Two hundred paces."
Five hundred steps later he called it again, and it was still two hundred paces.
An hour after that, a stake Ira had driven behind them appeared forty paces ahead of Seraphine without passing anybody.
At a later pulse, three separate people said "now" at noticeably different moments.
The separation happened without any warning.
Leon felt the correspondence slip and turned around, and eleven of the fourteen were where they had been and three were not.
Ira. Xie Lan. One of Yu’s surveyors, a broad-shouldered man named Deng.

All three were still visible. That was the disturbing part. Ira stood four feet from Seraphine, close enough to touch, and when Seraphine reached for her arm her hand went through and closed on nothing.
Ira said something. It arrived thin and about a second late, as though she were shouting across a valley.

He put his perception on the three of them and made himself watch instead of act.

Vyra stepped where all fourteen could see her and began marking the count with her arm, a slow deliberate sweep, over and over.
On the far side, Ira picked it up in three beats and matched it. Xie Lan followed her. Deng took longer and got there.
"Seraphine. I need one event that happens in both layers at the same instant. Small. Precise."
Seraphine did not ask why. She put a single point of lightning into the stone between the two halves, no larger than a coin, on Vyra’s count — and it appeared in both.
"Again. Every count."
She repeated it eight times.
Leon used each spark as a fixed instant shared by both layers. Every time it appeared, he caught the correspondence and pulled the offset a little closer.
On the ninth, Seraphine’s hand closed on Ira’s arm.
Nobody cheered. Yu had Deng by the shoulder and was talking to him quietly. Ira stood very still with Seraphine’s grip on her forearm and did not shake it off for a while.

"That took four minutes," Leon said, to all of them. "Understand what nearly happened. Nobody was attacked and nobody was hurt. If we had walked on another hundred paces, we would have lost three people who were standing in front of us."

Three marks appeared across the disk’s face, each broken, each flashing.
Spatial alignment: severed.
Temporal regulation: severed.
Defensive governance: severed.
—restore all three anchors before requesting exit. Restore all three anchors before requesting exit. Restore all—

"We should go in forty minutes," Leon said.

He said it without heat and loudly enough that all thirteen of the others heard him, because half of them were already looking northeast with the particular expression of people who wanted very badly to be doing something.

Consolidate.

Counted and distributed."

"The samples?"
"Leave them.

"Some of that material is—"

chapters.title: Chapter 654: Where the World Was Cut
paragraphs: "It thinks we work here," said Ira.

"It thinkssomebodyworks here." Vyra had already climbed to the first terrace and was walking its edge with a hand out, testing where the authorization ended. "It has been waiting a very long time for them, and something is broken badly enough that we look close enough."
They spent an hour finding out how much that was worth.

The answer was limited: access to the outer terraces, several fragmentary diagrams, and nothing else. Vyra could raise parts of a schematic by touching certain channel junctions, but it used conventions neither she nor Mo Rui had seen. Broad commands did nothing. When Yu asked directly for an exit, the nexus repeated the line about the three anchors twice and then fell silent for four minutes.

"It isn’t a guardian and it isn’t intelligent," Mo Rui said eventually. He had spent the hour studying every fragment Vyra could raise. "It’s an administrative system. It has been running maintenance procedures with nobody to perform them, and half of what it says refers to functions that no longer answer."

"Four functions," said Vyra, tracing the schematic. "Space — where things are relative to each other. Time — the local flow. Defence. And exits." She tapped the fourth. "Exits are sealedbecausethe other three report catastrophic faults. It won’t open a door while it believes the room behind the door is broken."
"So we fix its three faults."
"We fix its three faults, or we spend eight days waiting for a Palace force that has no idea how to get in."
The nexus opened the first route twenty minutes later without being asked — a channel of light running off the western terrace and down into ground that had not previously had anything in it.

Leon and Seraphine took the front of the shortened formation. Vyra kept the remaining twelve close behind them, with Ira at the rear and Loriel in the centre. After what had happened on the road, nobody suggested sending two people alone into another divided route.
The route to the spatial anchor did not stay one route.
It divided within sixty paces — the same terrace, ahead of them, in four slightly different versions, all equally solid. Seraphine put light down each and got four identical answers.
"Lightning," Leon said.
She used it carefully, a fine discharge along the boundary between two versions, and for half a second the boundary showed as a seam in the air.

Then she used slightly more on the next division and made it worse. The charge went into the wrong version, and instead of one seam showing, the division doubled — eight terraces where there had been four.
"Understood," Seraphine said. "Too much charge and I’m feeding the split."
"How fine can you go?"
"Finer than that."
After that they used the pulse.

Leon had noticed it on the way in and it turned out to be the whole answer: when the nexus pulsed, every false version stayed dead and exactly one carried the pulse through. That one still had a genuine connection to the platform. The rest were geometry with nothing behind it.
They crossed division after division that way. Wait for the pulse. Watch which version lit. Take it.
Near the end, Leon and Seraphine slipped into an adjacent layer while the remaining twelve stayed on the last stable terrace.

Leon looked back and found the twelve people less than thirty paces away. Vyra’s arm was still moving in the count, but the space between them no longer corresponded to the visible distance. He could see them clearly and could not have reached them by walking.
"They’re fine," he said.
"I know," said Seraphine. "Young Master, the terrace divides again in forty paces and I’d like to know whether to prepare the fine discharge or the coarse one."
She did not ask him to explain the offset or suggest retreating. She had watched him solve the same kind of separation earlier and trusted him to tell her if this one was different.
"Fine," Leon said. "Then a coarse one along the left seam once I’ve picked the live version."
"Yes, Young Master."

They found the anchor beyond the final division, in a chamber that sat on no terrace at all. The other twelve remained visible through the boundary, close enough to exchange signals even though only Leon and Seraphine could cross the last correspondence.
It was a column of stormglass rising three paces out of the floor, with a dozen channels running into it from directions Leon’s eyes could not follow. Nine were dark. Three ran faintly.
And driven through the thickest channel at its base was a spike.
Leon crouched beside it and did not touch it.
Black metal, a foot long, square-sectioned, with a spiral of cut characters running down two faces. The stormglass around it had gone dead grey for a hand’s width in every direction.
"That isn’t part of this," Seraphine said.
"No."
"It isn’t even close. Look at the finish." She crouched opposite him. "Everything here was cut in a curve. That was hammered flat and cold by somebody in a hurry."

Leon put his perception on it and found a residual formation signature sitting in the metal. Faint as it was, the structure was familiar. He had felt the same method in Moonfall when the Shen estate raiders used a flat disc to silence the household wards.
"This is connected to the Shen estate attack," he said.
Seraphine studied the cut characters. "The same people?"
"The same formation-breaking method and the same construction style. That proves a common source. It doesn’t tell us who gave the orders."
Removing it took another forty minutes, most of it preparation.

Leon mapped the severed channel first — where it had run, where the spike had cut it, how far the ends had drifted apart in however long the thing had been sitting there. They had recoiled, which was the danger: pull the obstruction and they would spring further apart before anything could catch them.
"When it comes out, that channel has about a heartbeat where it’s open and unpowered," he said. "If there’s nothing in it, the ends go and I don’t get them back."

"Then there will be something in it." Seraphine studied the three channels and chose one point from which her lightning could divide cleanly among them. "I feed all three the instant you pull. How much?"
"Enough to hold a load. Not enough to jump the gap. Overfeed it and you’ll charge the wrong side of the break, and I’ll be pulling two live ends apart instead of two dead ones."
"Give me a number."
"I can’t. You’ll have to feel it."
Seraphine considered that, said, "All right," and went to her mark.

She fed the three intact branches on Leon’s count. He took hold of the spike, drew it out clean in one motion, and had both severed ends in a fold of space before the metal was fully clear of the stone.
For a second and a half the channel fought him.
Then Seraphine’s charge arrived from three directions at once, the dead grey stormglass lit pale from the inside, and Leon folded the ends into correspondence and let go.
The column came on.

The boundary between the chamber and the final terrace collapsed. Vyra led the remaining twelve across within moments, confirming that the repaired anchor had brought both layers back into correspondence.
The change was noticeable within seconds and was not spectacular.

The route stopped multiplying into separate versions. On the walk back, the terraces divided twice more, but both false paths collapsed within a few paces. When Leon looked away from a ridge and looked back, the ridge had not moved.
All fourteen returned to the platform in under twenty minutes along a route that had consumed nearly two hours going out.
"It’s better," Vyra said before he could report. "We watched the correction from the last terrace. Most of Mo Rui’s marker line shifted back into proper spacing."
"It’s better," Leon agreed. "It isn’t fixed. There are still directions where the platform is much further away than it looks."

He put the spike down on the terrace where everyone could see it and explained what it was, along with everything he could support about its connection to the Shen estate attack. Thirteen other people would have to make decisions inside the realm, and none could do that on partial information.
Yu picked it up and examined the cut characters.
"The attack on the Shen estate and this sabotage used tools from the same source," he said. "That reaches far beyond a merchant household."
"It appears so," Leon said. "I won’t claim more until we have evidence for it."
Then the nexus spoke again, fractionally clearer than before.
Spatial alignment: restored. Partial. Partial.A pause.Second route unsealed. Temporal regulation—

The projection flickered and produced something new: a fragment of record. Two figures, indistinct, human, standing in the chamber Leon had just left. One of them crouched at the base of the column with something in his hand.
The timestamp, when Mo Rui converted it, fell four days before the survey team’s last transmission.
—temporal regulation reports interval failure,the nexus said.Cycle repeated. Cycle repeated. Cycle count: sixty-eight thousand four hundred and—
The number cut out.
"Sixty-eight thousand," Xie Lan said. "We were in here for less than an hour."
[Author: If you have bought privilege, thank you so much; if you haven’t, please do that would help me a lot]

chapters.title: Chapter 655: The Minute That Would Not Die
paragraphs: The second route ran east and downward, and for twenty minutes it was the easiest walking any of them had done since the corridor closed.

The spatial anchor held. The path stayed a path. Mo Rui’s stakes measured what they should measure, and Vyra’s count agreed with the nexus through one full pulse interval. Ira said aloud that she was starting to enjoy herself.
Then a chip of stormglass fell off the terrace wall ahead of them and struck the stone with a small clear sound.
Forty seconds later it fell again.
Leon stopped the column.
"Mo Rui. Did you see that?"
"See what, Senior Brother?"
"The chip."
"What chip?"
Xie Lan had seen it. So had Loriel and Seraphine. Nobody else had, and the chip was lying on the terrace where it had fallen, and there was only one of it.
Forty seconds later it fell a third time, from a wall it was already lying beneath.
"Nobody move," said Leon.
The loop ran about forty seconds and it took six cycles to establish that.
The chip was the readable part. It fell at the start of every cycle, and Vyra timed it, and it was consistent.
The second readable part arrived on the third cycle, when one of Yu’s surveyors — a thin woman named Fen — opened her mouth and said, "Deacon, the wall on the left is—"
The chamber reset before she finished. Fen returned to her original position with her mouth opening around the same first word, but her expression changed.
"I remember that," she said. "My body went back. I didn’t."
Everyone else remembered as well. Their positions and unfinished actions returned to the beginning of the interval, while their minds continued through it.
Not everything reset.
Loriel worked that out on the fifth cycle and it changed the situation entirely.
"Ira. Your pulse."
"What about it?"

"It’s up. It was seventy-one when we stopped and it’s eighty-four now." Loriel had two fingers on Ira’s wrist and her eyes shut. "Yours too, Young Master. Everyone’s is climbing. The chamber puts our positions back, but our bodies still spend the effort."

She went to her kit and took out the clay dish. The windwort had germinated during the journey, and Loriel had measured the shoot before they entered the second route. It had lengthened since then. The soil and dish returned to the same position with every reset; the living stem continued to grow.
"The growth matches the time our bodies have actually experienced," she said. "It isn’t being accelerated, but it isn’t being returned either."
Leon looked at the shoot.
Terrain resets. Formations reset. Bodies don’t.
"Say it plainly," he said.

"Plainly: this chamber is being put back to its starting state every forty seconds. Stone, formation energy, and our positions return. Living processes continue. Every attempt costs strength, but the distance we cross disappears." Loriel returned the dish to her kit. "We could exhaust ourselves here while remaining eighty paces from the anchor."
Yu said something under his breath that Leon did not catch.
"Then we break it," said Ira. "Where’s the anchor?"
The anchor was eighty paces farther in. They failed to reach it through nine cycles because the loop kept returning them to where they had started.
Leon solved that by refusing to be reset with everyone else.
He could not touch time. He said so out loud, to the whole column, because the last thing he needed was thirteen people expecting him to stop a clock.

"I have Space and I have Lightning. I have nothing that touches time and I’m not going to pretend otherwise." He crouched and put his palm flat on the terrace. "But this is doing itthroughsomewhere. There’s a fold — the chamber goes out through it at the end of a cycle and comes back through it at the start. I can feel the shape of that."
"And?" said Vyra.
"And I can stand outside it."
It cost more than he wanted it to.

He found the fold, took a position in the correspondence outside the resetting volume, and anchored himself there with Space and Lightning running together through the neutral centre of the Scripture. Every forty seconds the reset came through and tried to take him with it, and every forty seconds he refused, and the Primordial Void Heart took the returning pressure off his channels before it could reach the junctions that had spent nine days healing.
The first few resets nearly dragged him back into the chamber. By the seventh, his position held.
"I’m holding," he said. "Vyra, I’m your fixed point. Anything you write while touching me stays written."

That was what made progress possible. Everyone retained their memories, but ordinary markings, displaced stones, and changes to the formation vanished with each reset. Leon extended a narrow strip of stable space from his position. Ira marked its furthest edge before every reset, and the strip preserved that distance instead of returning with the rest of the chamber. Vyra kept her record against the same fold, where written measurements survived into the next cycle.
Loriel found the continuous channel after several more cycles.

"Not everything in that anchor resets either," she said. "Most of it does. There’s one circulation running through it that keeps going. I can feel it the way I feel a pulse, and it hasn’t returned to its starting state."
"Which one?"
"Second from the left, low, running clockwise." She pointed at the column without approaching it. "It’s the only part of that thing that remembers."
Ira had spent those cycles studying the anchor instead of striking it.
"I’ve been watching the feed," she said. "Lightning-fed, same as everything else here, and the charge arrives nine seconds after the chip falls. Every time. Never varies."
"And?"

"And my flame doesn’t reset." She said it flatly. "I burned the wall three cycles ago to test it. The wall came back. The calamity heat I put into it was still in the air on the next cycle. It’s mine. It doesn’t belong to this place and this place can’t take it back."
Leon looked at her, then at Loriel, and the shape of it assembled.
"Loriel’s channel doesn’t reset. Ira’s damage doesn’t reset. If Ira puts damage into Loriel’s channel, at the same instant, over enough cycles—"
"It accumulates," said Vyra, already writing. "In the one place the realm isn’t cleaning up."
It took eight more cycles.
Seraphine gave the timing — a single point of lightning on the stone, nine seconds after the chip fell, every cycle, so Ira had a signal she did not have to count for.

Vyra held the fourteen of them to the same positions and timing. Everyone remembered, but a single person moving too early could alter the chamber’s starting arrangement and ruin Ira’s accumulated damage.
Leon held the fold and read Vyra her own notes.
Ira drove her lance into the second channel from the left, nine seconds after the chip fell, eight times in the same place.
On the eighth, something in the anchor gave.

Leon felt the false circulation stagger and did not wait. He came off the fold and got both hands into the severed spatial channel — displaced like the first one, drifted apart in the direction the loop had been folding through — and closed it while the cycle was still stumbling.
The second spike came out with the break. It was identical to the first.
The chip did not fall again.
Forty seconds passed. Then a minute. Fen walked to the wall and placed her palm against the discoloured section she had been trying to report.
"The wall on the left is a different colour than it was," she said. "I have been trying to finish that sentence for far too long."
Temporal regulation: restored. Partial.The projection flickered.Local interval advancing. Cycle count closed at sixty-eight thousand four hundred and twelve.
"Our bodies," said Yu. "The month—"

"Nothing’s changed," Loriel said, already moving between them. "Nobody’s aged. Nobody’s lost anything. It has stopped the loop, that’s all. It hasn’t tried to correct the difference with outside and I would very much rather it didn’t try."
Then the nexus produced a record, and this one was legible. Mo Rui read it aloud in a voice that got flatter as he went.

Unauthorized access, central layer. Extraction attempt: spatial-temporal core. Anchor severance detected — spatial. Anchor severance detected — temporal. Structural instability: critical. Emergency correspondence pulse initiated. External tracking correspondence detected: three aligned signals. Emergency transfer executed. Personnel transferred: nine—

"That’s it," said Vyra. "They came in to take the core out of this place. They cut the space and time anchors to reach it, and the realm destabilized. The nexus sent an emergency correspondence pulse."
"And our formations answered it," said Yu quietly.

"Three of them running together, close enough to the pattern this nexus recognized." Vyra looked up. "Your formations answered its distress call, Deacon. The nexus used that correspondence to pull all nine of you through."
Yu was silent for a while. "Where are they now? The people who did it."
The nexus answered before anyone else could.
Third route unsealed. Defensive governance—The projection flickered hard.—defensive network reports competing administrative authority. Competing authority. Competing—

chapters.title: Chapter 656: The Fire Between Layers
paragraphs: Vyra understood the structure before the first wave fully formed, which kept the surveyors from being caught inside it.
"It’s not the same as the ones outside," she said at the entrance. "Those were a branch. This is the trunk."

The chamber was enormous and roughly circular, with the anchor column at its centre. What ran through the floor and walls was a network of channels wider than anything they had seen — and Leon’s perception told him the same channels ran through at least four overlapping layers, occupying the same physical space, feeding each other across boundaries nothing physical could cross.

"Reserve routes," Vyra said. "Dozens. We kill a construct here and the charge to rebuild it doesn’t come from the floor under our feet. It comes from a channel in another layer entirely and pops back out wherever it likes." She was already laying the first thin line of Crownfire along the floor. "Which means killing them faster is not a plan."

The stormglass began coming up before she finished. Twelve bodies at Foundation Establishment scale, four at Golden Core, and one sentinel that stood half again as tall as Ira and carried Nascent Soul pressure.
Ira put her lance through the first Golden Core construct’s chest before it finished forming.
"That’s one," she said. "How long before it’s back?"
"Thirteen seconds," said Vyra.
It was back in thirteen seconds.
For the first time, Leon properly watched Vyra fight.
She never touched a construct. For the entire engagement she did not attack one of them, and she decided the whole battle anyway.

Her flame spread across the floor in thin, precise lines laid along the channels themselves rather than at the enemy. Wherever Crownfire crossed a channel, the current slowed and bent toward the routes Vyra allowed it to use.
"Two feeds shut on the east arc," she called. "Sera, they’ll form on the west now."
They formed on the west. Seraphine was already there.

Seraphine destroyed only the constructs that threatened Vyra’s controlled ground. Two Golden Core bodies rose inside the suppressed zone, and she cut both apart before either achieved a complete shape. Nothing reached the anchor column.

Ira did the demolition. Whenever Vyra forced a current into a narrower route, the junction carrying it lit — and Ira put the lance through that junction while it carried a load it had not been built for. Each one she broke closed a door for good.
Loriel handled the sentinel by not fighting it. She read it from thirty paces and called it.
"Its core is borrowed," she said. "There’s a circulation in it that isn’t its own — connected to something deeper, and the connection isn’t constant. It opens." A pause. "Now.Now it’s shut."
"How long open?" Ira shouted.
"About a second and a half. Every nineteen seconds."
Across four openings, they destroyed the sentinel four times. It rebuilt after each destruction, and every return exposed another route for Vyra to close.
Leon handled the one part of the network none of them could reach.

The feeder routes ran through separate layers. Vyra could suppress a channel she could reach; she could not reach a channel occupying the same ground in a space beside this one, and there were four of those, and they were why her containment kept leaking.
So he folded them.

He found the correspondence between layers — much easier with the spatial anchor live — and took a feeder route from each of three separate layers and put all three in the same physical place at the mouth of Vyra’s containment. Three currents that had never been able to touch each other, arriving in one channel she had already surrounded with fire.
"Oh," Vyra said when the first arrived. "Oh.Do that again."
He did it again.
By the sixth minute she had stopped reacting to the reserve routes and started arriving before them.

"North-northeast, second ring," she said, laying fire across a channel that was still dark. A moment later the channel lit and found itself already contained. "He’s working a rotation. Whoever it is has four favourite feeds and cycles them in the same order. He’s done it three times now."
"You’re guessing," said Ira, breaking a junction.
"I’m predicting from a repeated pattern." Vyra shut a fifth route without looking at it. "East arc next. Sera, be there."
Seraphine was there.

Behind them, Yu ran the survey team as a support element and did it well. His people kept the marker lines intact so Vyra could see her own containment, logged every redirection with a time and a bearing, and moved the formation tools clear of the fighting twice without being asked.
Mo Rui spotted the pattern.
"Steward Vyra — the reserve routes aren’t opening randomly. Every one in the last four minutes has come from below. Not from the layers. Fromunderneaththe chamber."
Vyra’s head came up.
"Somebody’s doing it," she said.
They reached the anchor column ten minutes later, with the chamber’s defensive current squeezed into two routes and both inside Vyra’s fire.
The third spike was in the column’s base, identical to the others.
It was also, unmistakably, live.

Leon crouched over it and felt the difference at once. The first two had been inert once the damage was done — hammered in, left, forgotten. This one had a thread running out of it, downward, toward the sealed centre of the nexus, and something at the far end of that thread was awake.
"It’s a relay," he said. "Whoever put it in is still using it. That’s how they’re reaching the reserve routes."
"Then take it out," said Ira.

"Not yet." Leon did not move his hand. "Pull this while it’s live and the backlash goes down the relay and comes back into whatever’s nearest — and the nearest thing is four hundred paces of Vyra’s fire with every defensive current in this chamber trapped inside it."
Vyra did not look away from her containment. "How long do you need?"
"To do it properly, four or five minutes."
"Then take five." Her flame tightened another notch across the floor. "I can hold this."
Leon put his palm flat against the damaged anchor and began to map it.
And something on the other end of the relay noticed him.
It was not an attack. It was apressure— a second will arriving through the thread, taking hold of the defensive network from underneath, and pulling.
Every route Vyra had spent twenty minutes closing tried to open at once.
"He’s here," Vyra said. Interest sharpened her voice. "Young Master, he’s forcing every reserve route at once. He knows enough to overload the network if we let him."

chapters.title: Chapter 657: The Thief Behind the Glass
paragraphs: Whoever held the other end of the relay possessed more charge than Vyra, but she understood the network better.

He hit her containment across nine routes at once, attempting to overload the entire structure. Vyra had spent twenty minutes learning how much pressure each route could carry. She shifted her fire instead of meeting his strength directly.
"Every one of those routes draws from the same reserve," she reported. "He can force them open, but each attempt costs him. Sera, west arc again."
The sentinel came back for the fifth time and Seraphine took it apart in nine seconds. It came back a sixth time and Ira had that one.
"Each return costs him," Vyra said. "That reserve cannot sustain this indefinitely."
Leon stayed on the anchor and let them handle it.

He had the spike mapped now, and it was uglier than expected. The thing was doing two jobs. Its original function was straightforward butchery — driven through the principal channel to sever it. But somebody had come back afterward and threaded a control line through the shaft, turning a saboteur’s wedge into a crude relay, and the relay had roots in six directions.
Pull it and everything on those six branches comes home at once.
"Ira. Six branches. I’m going to mark them, and I want them gone in order from the outside in, and I want the last one still standing when I start."
"Why the last one?"
"Because if I take all six, he’ll know. I want him holding a line he thinks still works."
"That," said Ira, "is a genuinely unpleasant idea. I like it."
They executed it together and it took less than a minute.

Vyra forced every active defensive charge in the chamber into one contained route and sealed the rest, which meant that for about six seconds there was exactly one path the hostile will could push through, and it was surrounded by Crownfire.
Seraphine flooded the anchor’s three uncut channels with clean lightning, so the instant the obstruction left, the column would have power waiting rather than an empty second to fall through.
Ira destroyed five of the six relay branches in the order Leon marked and left the sixth.

Loriel watched the sentinel’s borrowed circulation, and when the hidden controller reached for it again to rebuild the construct a seventh time, she reversed the false circulation at the exact instant the connection opened. The command went out and did not arrive. The sentinel did not re-form.
In the gap that made, Leon separated the control path from the anchor.

It was fine work and it was fast. He took the hostile line where it entered the spike, folded four inches of space around it, and displaced it — not cut, moved, so that the far end was still pushing into somewhere and the somewhere was no longer connected to anything. Then he drew the spike out clean and closed the severed channel while Seraphine’s lightning was still standing in it.
The column came on, and every other light in the chamber came on with it.

Sixteen stormglass constructs collapsed at once. They did not rebuild. The pieces lay on the floor and stayed pieces, and the enormous distributed network running through four layers went quiet and orderly and stopped being a weapon.
Vyra let her fire out, sat down on the terrace step, and said, "Well."

Restoring the defensive anchor opened a direct maintenance route back to the nexus. Leon tested the correspondence before allowing anyone through. The passage held without shifting, and all fourteen returned together. They carried the three formation-breaking spikes and laid them across the outer terrace. Vyra took the nearest step while the nexus processed the restored network.
The nexus spoke, and this time it spoke almost like something that knew what it was saying.
Defensive governance: restored. Spatial alignment: restored. Temporal regulation: restored.A pause.Exit authorization: withheld. Central layer compromised. Central layer occupied.
Log recovered. Unauthorized access, central layer. Extraction attempt: spatial-temporal core. Method: anchor severance, three instances. Implement signature—
The projection produced an image of a spike, rotating, the cut characters visible along two faces.
—signature unrecognized. Origin external. Extraction incomplete. Personnel present.
"It doesn’t know who they are," said Mo Rui.
"It doesn’t need to," Leon said. "I do."

The three spikes lay in front of him. Their metal, cut characters, and formation signature matched the construction method of the ward-breaking disc used during the Shen estate attack. The connection was real, even if the identity of the people behind both operations remained unknown.
Then the platform changed.

It happened all at once. Sections of the black stormglass disk lost their colour — not shattering, not opening, simply becoming transparent, so that fourteen people found themselves standing on a floor they could suddenly see through.
Beneath it, occupying a space Leon’s perception insisted was both directly below and somehowinsidethe platform, was a chamber.

Circular, roughly forty paces across, its walls lined with the same channels as everything else. At its centre stood a dais, and the dais was damaged — a section of its surface cut away and the housing beneath forced open, with the tools that had done it still lying on the floor.
Seven people stood in that chamber.

Six were arranged around the walls in a defensive spread. Leon read all six at once: Golden Core, three early and three middle. They appeared competent, but none posed a personal danger to him or the four women.
The seventh stood at the dais with one hand on it.

He was perhaps sixty in appearance and very still, dressed in dark travelling clothes with the sleeves bound, and the pressure off him was Nascent Soul. A small notched iron ring was worked into the collar of his robe.
He had looked up at the exact moment the floor turned clear, and he was looking at Leon.
For three full seconds his face showed nothing but astonishment.
Leon watched the astonishment disappear. The man made a quick assessment of the fourteen people above him, then focused with the alert calculation of someone revising a plan under pressure.
Beside Leon, Ira cracked her neck.
"That’s him?" she asked. "The one who’s been fighting Vyra?"
"Apparently."
"He’s been here longer than we have, and she still took the network away from him."
Loriel had gone up on her toes to look. "Six Golden Core and one Nascent Soul. Young Master, do you want me to keep the surveyors back, or—"
"Back. All nine of them, behind the second terrace."

Yu was already moving his people, and moving them fast, and he did not ask why a Peak Foundation Establishment medicinal attendant had assessed a Nascent Soul cultivator in the tone of somebody reading a supply list.
Behind Leon, Xie Lan said, very quietly, to Mo Rui: "Did she just—"
"Don’t," said Mo Rui. "Whatever it is, don’t."
The man at the dais did not shout, or threaten, or waste time on outrage.

He looked at the three spikes lying on the terrace above him. Then he looked at Vyra, sitting on the step with her hands loose, and something in his expression suggested he had spent the last twenty minutes forming an opinion about her.
Then he put his other hand on the damaged dais.
The nexus’s projection stuttered.
—competing maintenance authority. Two authorities registered. Central layer authority: active. Outer authority: active. Conflict—
Every light on the platform dimmed by a third and came back.
The man took his hand away, and Leon understood exactly what he had been shown.
He can’t defeat the five of us directly. He doesn’t have to.
He was standing inside the core chamber with a hand on the only control surface that mattered, and the exit had not opened, and the thing that opened it was under his palm.

Leon looked down through forty paces of transparent stormglass at a man looking back up at him. Neither moved. Above and below them, the nexus continued announcing that two competing maintenance authorities remained active.
Leon’s household could clear that chamber quickly once they reached it.
Getting to it was going to be the entire problem.

chapters.title: Chapter 658: The Men Beneath the Glass
paragraphs: The transparent floor began to flicker.

Leon felt what caused it before he saw it. The man at the dais had both hands on the surface now, and the chamber below was sliding — not away, exactly, but out of true, the correspondence between the two layers loosening at the edges like a joint working itself apart.
"Six points," the man called to his people, without looking up. "Hold them and do not move."
The six Golden Core cultivators broke from the walls and took positions around the chamber, one to each of six recessed control plates set into the floor. They moved like people who had drilled it.
Then the man raised his head.

"You’ve done extraordinary work," he said. His voice arrived thin and slightly delayed through the stormglass. "Three anchors in one day. I spent a month studying this nexus and never understood half of what you repaired today. Whoever you are, you are not an ordinary Palace disciple."
Leon said nothing.

"So I’ll be direct, because I don’t think either of us benefits from a performance." The man’s hands stayed flat. "My hand is on the core housing. It is already damaged — you can see the cut, you can see the tools. If you force entry, I will finish what I started, and whatever this place is protecting will be finished with it. I don’t want that. It’s worth more to me intact than to you."
"What do you want?"

"The three spikes. Outer authority returned to this dais. And a route out for seven people." He shrugged, very slightly. "Nobody follows us and nobody dies. You keep your nine and your ruin. I keep my life. I am aware that you can kill me. I am telling you that killing me is the expensive option."
He was intelligent, which Leon appreciated, and he had made exactly one mistake.
He thinks he’s moving that chamber.
Leon crouched at the edge of the clear section and put his perception into the slipping correspondence, and did not answer for a long time.

The three anchor repairs had taught him more about this place than the enemy had learned in a month, because Leon had been forced to understand how the layers held together in order to reconnect them. What he was watching now was not a man freely relocating a room. It was a man cycling a room through a handful of damaged maintenance positions — the same four, in the same order, because those four were the only ones the broken system would still accept.
And every eleven minutes, the nexus pulsed, and for a moment everything in this complex remembered where it belonged.
"Vyra."

She was already crouched beside him. "Two currents, Young Master. One’s his and one isn’t — the one holding the chamber steady is the nexus’s own and he’s borrowing it. He can’t move that room without it, and he doesn’t know that’s what he’s using."
"Seraphine. I need the alignment interval measured, not estimated."
Seraphine put a fine discharge into the floor and watched where it went. She did it four times, across two pulses.
"It aligns for a little under two seconds," she said. "Starts a quarter-beat after the pulse begins."
"Loriel."

"All seven are physically present, Young Master," Loriel said. "Every shift, all the way through. Nothing down there is a projection and nothing is being left behind when the room moves. If you go in, you’ll be going into a room with seven living people in it."
Ira had not said anything for four minutes, which was its own kind of effort.
"Young Master," she said, "are we doing this, or are we negotiating?"
"We’re waiting nine more minutes."

Behind them, on the second terrace, nine Jade Moon Palace surveyors stood where Deacon Yu had put them and watched four women in attendants’ clothing discuss a Nascent Soul cultivator the way a formation crew discusses a jammed gate.
The pulse came. Leon went into the correspondence a quarter-beat behind it and refused to let it slip.
Leon had spent the day learning how these layers aligned and how to hold them together when they began to separate. Now he took the two-second window and made it wide enough for five people to cross.
"Go."
They went down through the floor.
The six lackeys were coming before the five of them landed, and Leon let the women have it, because there was nothing here worth his attention except the man at the dais.

Seraphine took the two on the left. The first threw a water-and-metal construct at her that would have gone through a wall, and she cut it apart at the seam holding it together and put the flat of her blade across his temple before the pieces hit the ground. The second got as far as raising his hands.

Ira went straight through the middle. She hit the third man bodily, took him off his feet, and drove him into the chamber wall hard enough to leave him in it. The fourth had a defensive art up, a good one, layered and dense — and Ira put a needle of calamity flame through it at one point and it came apart like wet paper, and she hit him once and he stopped moving.

Vyra did not attack anyone. She took the heat Ira had released and the energy the two disabled men had already spent, gathered all of it, and put it up as three curving barriers that cut the chamber into pieces — so that the fifth and sixth cultivators, who had been moving to support their brothers, found themselves alone in separate boxes.

Loriel dealt with those two. She did not strike either of them. She put a hand out toward the fifth man and something in his circulation stopped agreeing with him, and he folded at the knees and stayed down, breathing, conscious, and entirely unable to stand. The sixth she took the same way, three seconds later.
Six Golden Core cultivators, and it took under nine seconds, and none of them died.
On the terrace above, Xie Lan made a small sound.
The Nascent Soul leader had used those nine seconds properly.
He tore one hand away from the dais and released a compressed column of grey force. It came at Leon fast enough to be worth respecting, carrying the weight of a full realm above him.
Leon caught it.

He did not block it or dodge it. He folded the space it was travelling through, took the column into a pocket four inches deep, and let it exhaust itself somewhere it could not reach anybody. Then he crossed the chamber.

The man’s other hand was still on the dais and still connected to the formation beneath it, and Leon did not cut it off, because a corpse’s hand and a living hand were worth different amounts and one of them could answer questions.

He separated the hand from the connection instead — a thin, precise displacement of the four inches of space between palm and surface, so that the hand stayed where it was and stopped touching anything at all.
The man felt his authority go and his face changed for the first time.
Leon took him by the collar and put him on the floor twelve paces from the dais, and that was the end of it.
Seals went on all seven, one at a time, with Seraphine checking the work.

Deacon Yu came down the temporary route with three of his people once Ira gave him the signal, and Leon watched him look at the room: two men unconscious against the wall, four sitting or lying under seals, six Golden Core cultivators taken by four women registered in the Palace’s own books as Peak Foundation Establishment attendants.
Yu did not ask. He looked at Mo Rui, who was staring, and said, "Surveyor. Formation tools. Now," and Mo Rui went and got the formation tools.
Leon crouched in front of the leader.

"The fighting’s finished," he said. "You should understand that clearly, because I don’t want you spending the next hour looking for an opening that isn’t there." He kept his voice level. "You’re not leaving this room until I understand why nine Jade Moon Palace disciples were made to disappear."
[if you have bought privilege, thank you so much; if you haven’t, please do that would help me a lot]

chapters.title: Chapter 659: What Pain Uncovered
paragraphs: Securing the chamber took twenty minutes and produced most of what Leon needed before anybody said a word.

Seraphine went over every control surface and every seam in the walls and found four hidden weapon caches and a talisman rig under the dais that would have taken the roof down. She disarmed it and left it visible, which Leon thought was a good decision.
Ira sat on the dais steps facing the prisoners with her lance across her knees and did not blink for twenty minutes.

Vyra emptied all seven storage rings onto the floor and catalogued the contents in front of everybody. Two months of field supplies. Good formation tools. Four cutting implements of the same flat hurried make as the spikes. Personal notes, sketches of the nexus, three separate attempts at mapping the terraces. And seven signal tokens, every one unused.
Loriel went through the prisoners one at a time.

"No suicide seals," she reported. "No concealed poison. Nothing in any of them that will burn a memory or stop a heart. Two have soul-defence arts good enough to resist a shallow probe, which is normal for their realm and not evidence of anything."
Leon nodded and sat down on the step opposite the leader.
"One chance," he said. "Tell me the whole of it, in order, and I won’t do anything else. That’s not a negotiation and I’m not going to repeat it."
The man tried to bargain.
"My clan knows where we are," he said. "Seven cultivators do not vanish without a report. If we don’t return—"
"Vyra. Show him."
Vyra held up the seven signal tokens, fanned out.

"Unused," she said. "All of them. Charge intact, seals unbroken, no discharge residue on any." She dropped them back into the pile. "And your written records stop at day four. There are no completed reports in any of these rings. If you sent something, you sent it by shouting."
The man’s expression did not change much, but he stopped using that argument.

His second attempt was better. He offered to explain the nexus — its pulse cycle, its control structure, the routes between the terraces — in exchange for release, and he offered it with the confidence of a man who believed he held the only copy.

"We repaired all three anchors this afternoon," Leon said. "Vyra could draw you the control structure from memory. You spent a month learning what we took apart in a day, and I want you to sit with that for a moment before you offer it to me again."
He questioned the six separately, which was where the real progress happened.

Leon took them one at a time to the far side of the chamber, out of earshot, with Vyra writing everything down. He asked each of them the same eleven dull questions in the same order: when did you arrive, who went in first, what was your mission, when did you first see the inner correspondence, who found it, whose idea was the first spike, what date, who put it in.
They had agreed on a broad story. They had not agreed on details, because nobody had expected to be questioned by a man holding their own notebooks.

The third man put the discovery of the inner realm at "about the second week." The fifth said it was after they had already tried the outward route twice. The fourth, who was frightened and talking fast, mentioned an argument — a long one, over two days — and then stopped and would not say what the argument had been about.
By the fourth interview, Vyra had a timeline with three holes in it, and every hole was in the same place.
"They’re lying about one week," she said quietly. "The one where they decided something."
Leon went back to the leader and gave him one more opportunity, and the man refused.
So Leon did the other thing.

He did not raise his voice or take off a finger. He knelt beside the man, put two fingers against the air an inch from his forearm, and placed a spatial distortion the size of a grain of rice beside the nerve junction under the skin.
He never touched the nerve. He made the space around it discontinuous.

The man’s whole body locked. His arm remained intact, his skin unbroken and his meridian undisturbed, but the pain bypassed the defences of his Nascent Soul cultivation because there was no force to resist.
Leon held it four seconds and took it away.
"Loriel."

"Heart rate high, nothing torn, no lasting damage, Young Master," Loriel said. She had one hand near the man’s chest and her face was carefully blank. "He can take that a number of times. I’ll tell you when he can’t."
"Thank you." Leon looked back down. "I can repeat that wherever I choose. I’d rather not. You’ve already lost. The only thing left to decide is how unpleasant the next hour becomes."
He placed the second one.
The leader broke on the third, later than Leon expected.
Once the leader began talking, the timeline came together quickly, and it was not what Leon had expected.

They had been sent to investigate an anomaly. That was all. Their clan had reports out of the basin going back years — strange lightning, impossible tracking bearings, rain that behaved wrongly — and seven cultivators were sent to find the cause. Nobody who dispatched them had any idea a realm was involved.
They had gone into it by accident. The correspondence was unstable then; one of them walked into a fold and the other six went after him, and by the time they understood, the way out was gone.
Then a month.

A month of studying pulses, terraces, broken logs, and layered passages, with one objective, which was escape. They had learned a great deal because they had nothing else to do. They had mapped four of the terraces and worked out the eleven-minute cycle and got as far as identifying which route led outward.
And somewhere in the third week they had understood what the complex was for.
"That’s the argument," Leon said. "Two days. That’s what you decided."
"Yes."
"Say it."

The man’s jaw worked. "We agreed not to report it. Any of it. We would get out, seal the entrance, tell the clan the anomaly was a dead formation field, and come back when we could take it properly." His voice was flat. "Seven of us. Not seven hundred, and not an elder standing over us taking first pick."
"And then the surveyors arrived."

"Then the surveyors arrived." He closed his eyes briefly. "Three tracking formations, running together. The nexus answered them — it thought they were a maintenance contingent, the way it thought you were. And there were nine of them from the Palace that owns this territory, standing on top of the thing we had spent a month deciding to steal."
"You couldn’t let them leave."

"They’d have reported an anomaly. The Palace would have sent a formation elder. A formation elder would have found what we found inside a week." He opened his eyes. "So we tried to take the nexus properly. Full authority. Turn the threshold into a containment and hold the nine of them in it until we were clear."
"The spikes."

"How close were you?" Leon asked. "To getting out. Before they came."
The man was quiet for a moment.
"Minutes," he said. "We had the route open and we were arguing about who carried the notes."

The evidence agreed. Seven unused tokens, no completed reports, notes that stopped at day four.
Leon sat with that for a while.
They kept it from their own people so successfully that nobody is coming to look for what they found.
He gave Vyra one final conclusion for the record.

"The tools match the Shen estate work," he said. "The finish, character-cutting, and formation-breaking method point to the same workshop. That connects the craftsmanship. It doesn’t identify whoever bought or ordered the tools."

She disarmed it and left it visible, which Leon thought was a good decision.
Ira sat on the dais steps facing the prisoners with her lance across her knees and did not blink for twenty minutes.
Vyra emptied all seven storage rings onto the floor and catalogued the contents in front of everybody.
Two months of field supplies.
Good formation tools.

He made the space around it discontinuous.

chapters.title: Chapter 660: A Heaven Not Yet Born
paragraphs: Giving the dais back took the rest of the afternoon, and the enemy’s notes turned out to be worth more than the enemy.

"He was good," Vyra admitted, working through the fourth notebook. "Not at formations — at being systematic. He wrote down everything he tried and everything that failed for a month, and about a third of it is useful."
Leon worked the dais itself while she read to him.

The damage was ugly but shallow. The housing had been cut open and the surface plate lifted, and the core beneath it had been probed at and not removed — the saboteurs had run out of understanding before they ran out of nerve. Leon closed the housing, reconnected the four control paths they had severed to reach it, and stepped back.
The nexus came the rest of the way awake in stages over about twenty minutes, and its voice stopped being a broken loop.
Working from different parts of the chamber, they began to understand where they were standing.
Leon found it first and did not immediately believe it.

He had put his perception into the core to check the reconnection and found it doing something that made no sense: regulating a correspondence with a place that had no fixed position. Not hidden, not shifting —unfixed, the way a thing is unfixed when it has not settled yet.
"Vyra. What’s the energy budget in here?"

She had been asking the same question for ten minutes. "That’s what I don’t like, Young Master. This complex uses about a fifth of what it draws. Everything else goes inward, through the core, into whatever’s on the other side." She looked up. "It isn’t a fortress running its own defences. It’s a pump."
Loriel had gone to the chamber’s inner wall and put both hands flat on it, and had not moved for several minutes.

"There’s something living beyond this," she said. Her voice had gone strange. "Not creatures. I can’t find anything I’d call an organism. It’s — there’s an enormous amount of vitality out there and none of it has finished deciding what it’s going to be." She turned around. "Young Master, it’s like putting your hand on soil that hasn’t become a field yet."
Seraphine’s contribution was the least mystical and the most useful.

"The stormglass," she said. "I’ve been assuming it was used to build this place. It wasn’t. Centuries of lightning have leaked through the threshold and fused the surrounding rock. The stormglass is a consequence of whatever lies beyond that wall."
And it was Mo Rui who put the name to it.

He had been on the second terrace with Yu, comparing the newly stable readings against the anomaly data that had brought his team here in the first place, and he came down the temporary route at a dead run holding a rubbing he had taken off the outer rim.

"Deacon. Senior Leon." He was breathing hard. "These markers on the outer ring. I’ve seen this convention in the Palace archives — it’s a classification band used by old sects to identify independent spaces." He held up the rubbing with a hand that was not steady. "This mark means Earth-Grade."
Yu took the rubbing off him and looked at it for a long moment.
"Say it properly, Surveyor."
"It’s a Grotto-Heaven marker," Mo Rui said. "Earth-Grade."
The nexus confirmed it four minutes later, in plain language, when Vyra asked it directly.
Threshold complex. Function: stabilisation and protection, developing independent realm. Classification: Grotto-Heaven, Earth-Grade. Formation status: incomplete.
The reaction on the terrace was the loudest thing that had happened all day.
Leon let it run for a minute, because the surveyors had earned it and because he wanted to hear what people who knew this world thought.
What they thought was that it changed everything.

"It isn’t a ruin," Xie Lan was saying, to nobody in particular. "A ruin has a bottom. You empty a ruin. A Grotto-Heaven has its own environment — itmakesthings, it goes on making them, a mature one produces for centuries—"
"Earth-Grade," said one of the six surveyors. "That’s — Deacon, the Palace doesn’t have one. Nobody in the eastern islands has one."

"The Palace has three lesser pocket spaces, and they are the foundation of four peaks," Yu said. He had not stopped looking at the rubbing. "None of them is an Earth-Grade Grotto-Heaven. And this one is inside our monitored territory, in a basin we survey twice a year."
And Leon understood, at last, why seven cultivators had decided to keep a secret from their own clan.
The nexus filled in the rest over the following hour, and what it gave them was classification and forecast rather than a map.

The forming realm’s dominant laws were storm, space, and time. That accounted for the basin above — the lightning that struck more here than anywhere on the continent, the stormglass, the rain that climbed, the tracking formations that gave impossible bearings. Centuries of a nascent Grotto-Heaven’s laws leaking through a wall.

It would likely produce varied regions once it settled: the nexus listed probable formations of storm-aligned minerals, thermal zones, and spatial materials, with a caution attached that any forecast of an unformed realm was a forecast and not an inventory.

Loriel could feel unfinished life through the wall and could not describe it. Leon could see, when he pushed his perception at the closed correspondence, distances that were still arguing with each other about how long they were.
Nobody saw anything. There was nothing yet to see.
And it could not be opened.

Inward route: sealed. Formation incomplete. Estimated remaining stabilisation: ninety to one hundred and eighty days.A pause.Premature access will destabilise the developing realm. Probability of total structural failure: high.
"Three to six months," said Vyra.
"Three to six months," Leon agreed.
Ira had come down at some point and was leaning against the wall with her arms folded.
"So we found the greatest thing anyone in this Palace has found in a century," she said, "and the answer is that we have to go away and come back later."
"Yes."
"I hate it."
"You’ll hate what happens if we don’t wait even more." Leon turned back to the dais. "Whoever holds this door in six months holds the realm. Not whoever finds it. Whoeverholdsit."
The nexus offered the second route a few minutes later — outward, to the physical basin, restored and usable.
Leon looked at it for a while.

"Deacon Yu," he said. "Prepare your highest emergency report. Everything you have, sealed, ready to send the instant we clear the isolation." He put his hand on the dais and began locking the inward route. "We aren’t opening this today. We’re making certain Jade Moon Palace owns the door on the day it opens."
