chapters.title: Chapter 661: The Highest Signal
paragraphs: Leon tested the outward route himself before he let anyone near it.

He sent a marked stone through on a line, then a second, then walked into the correspondence himself for four paces and came back out. It held every time, and it held without effort — with all three anchors live and the hostile authority stripped out of the dais, the route behaved like a corridor rather than a coincidence.
"It’s stable," he said. "Deacon, your people first, in order, no gaps."
The nine went through as an organised group, and Yu counted them out loud and then counted them again on the far side.

The seven prisoners went next with their cultivations sealed, Seraphine leading and Ira behind them, and Leon watched Ira position herself so that any one of them who broke would go through her before anything else.

Leon crossed last. Before he did, he locked the inward route at the dais and set the control surface to refuse every command that did not carry the outer maintenance authority — which was, for the moment, him.
Then he stepped through into rain.
The basin had gone on without them.

That was the thing nobody was prepared for. It was still raining, and the abandoned survey camp was fifty paces away with its shelter wards still burning thin, and somebody’s outer robe was still folded on a pack where it had been folded for twenty-four days. The cooking pot still had a hard grey crust in it.
Deng sat down on a rock and put his hands over his face for a while, and nobody said anything about it.

The layers had kept different clocks. Twenty-four days had passed outside. The nine surveyors had experienced less than an hour, while the seven men kneeling beneath Ira’s attention remembered roughly a month. Leon’s household had experienced its own journey and the three anchor repairs in an ordinary sequence. Standing together in the same clearing did nothing to reconcile those different spans.
Vyra’s communication plaque woke up eleven seconds after she cleared the threshold.
"We’re out, Young Master," she said. "Properly out. It’s found the Palace."
They sent everything at once on Leon’s order.

Yu submitted the formal missing-team recovery signal and attached a territorial emergency flag, which Leon gathered was a thing a deacon used perhaps once in a career. Four of the surveyors sent to their own assigned seniors on separate channels. Mo Rui sent the raw formation data.
And Leon’s direct-disciple token sent the core report to Ji Liansu.
"Why all of them?" Xie Lan asked. "One would reach the Palace."

"One should," Vyra said without looking up from her plaque. "If several independent channels report from the same stable location, the Palace can trust the coordinate quickly enough to risk emergency transit. Nothing could reach them from inside the threshold, and an array cannot lock onto a signal that never arrives."
"How long, then?"
"If they spend what the transit costs? Minutes."

The five emergency return talismans could have carried Leon’s household back to the Palace, but they could not transport nine surveyors, seven prisoners, and the evidence. Leaving the site unguarded was not an option.
Nobody stood around waiting.

Seraphine established a guarded boundary around the empty ground and set markers on it, because fourteen people had come out of it and she did not intend for anything to go back in unobserved. Vyra sorted the confiscated material into evidence and ordinary supplies and sealed the first category in three separate cases. Ira put the prisoners in a line where the whole clearing could see them and made escape look as impossible as it was.
Loriel went through the nine surveyors again, now that they were standing in ordinary time, and found nothing wrong with any of them.
And Leon walked the boundary of the flat ground and checked the threshold from outside.

It was still there. Still stable. And when he put his perception into it and reached past the closed inward route, he could feel the pulse — slow, enormous, and patient, coming through a wall from something that had not been born yet.
Ninety to a hundred and eighty days.
The surveyors had changed toward them, and they were careful about it, which Leon respected.

Nobody asked. Nobody said anything within his hearing about six Golden Core cultivators falling in nine seconds to four registered Peak Foundation Establishment attendants. But Mo Rui, who had been treating Vyra as a clever colleague for two days, now waited for her to speak first. Xie Lan had stopped looking at Loriel entirely, which was its own kind of statement.
Deacon Yu came over once, while Leon was checking the threshold.
"Senior Leon."
"Deacon."

Yu was quiet for a moment. "Twenty-four days ago I was verifying a resource region. I am going to submit a report describing an ancient realm nexus, three severed anchors, a Nascent Soul saboteur, and an Earth-Grade Grotto-Heaven." He looked out at the rain. "I have been asking myself what else I am going to have to describe, and I have decided that the answer is: the recovery of nine Palace cultivators, by a direct disciple and his household, under conditions I was not qualified to assess."
"That’s an accurate report."
"It is acompletereport," Yu said, "of what I am qualified to assess," and went back to his people.
Leon read the confiscated records one final time while they waited.
Nothing in them contradicted the confessions. No completed dispatch. No message log. Seven unused tokens and a month of notes that never once mentioned the thing the notes were about.
They almost certainly never told anyone.
He wrote that down in exactly those words, becausealmost certainlywas the honest version and he was not going to hand his master anything better than the truth.
The rain changed at the fourth mark.

It did not stop. What happened was that the cloud above the basin lit — moon-white lines spreading across it in the middle of an overcast afternoon, running out from a central point in an expanding lattice, locking down onto Leon’s token and onto Yu’s emergency plaque with a precision that made the hair on his arms rise.
"Formation," Seraphine said sharply. "Young Master — everyone back from the ground."
The lattice completed.
Three presences came down through it, and Leon felt the basin itself react — the rain bending around them before they had arrived, the stormglass in the shelves lighting and going dark.
Ji Liansu landed first, in pale green and silver-grey with the veil across the lower half of her face.

Before he did, he locked the inward route at the dais and set the control surface to refuse every command that did not carry the outer maintenance authority — which was, for the moment, him.
Then he stepped through into rain.
The basin had gone on without them.
That was the thing nobody was prepared for.

It was still raining, and the abandoned survey camp was fifty paces away with its shelter wards still burning thin, and somebody’s outer robe was still folded on a pack where it had been folded for twenty-four days.
The cooking pot still had a hard grey crust in it.
Deng sat down on a rock and put his hands over his face for a while, and nobody said anything about it.
The layers had kept different clocks.
Twenty-four days had passed outside.
The nine surveyors had experienced less than an hour, while the seven men kneeling beneath Ira’s attention remembered roughly a month.
Leon’s household had experienced its own journey and the three anchor repairs in an ordinary sequence.
Standing together in the same clearing did nothing to reconcile those different spans.
Vyra’s communication plaque woke up eleven seconds after she cleared the threshold.
"We’re out, Young Master," she said.
"Properly out.
It’s found the Palace."
They sent everything at once on Leon’s order.
Yu submitted the formal missing-team recovery signal and attached a territorial emergency flag, which Leon gathered was a thing a deacon used perhaps once in a career.
Four of the surveyors sent to their own assigned seniors on separate channels.
Mo Rui sent the raw formation data.
And Leon’s direct-disciple token sent the core report to Ji Liansu.
"Why all of them?" Xie Lan asked.
"One would reach the Palace."
"One should," Vyra said without looking up from her plaque.
"If several independent channels report from the same stable location, the Palace can trust the coordinate quickly enough to risk emergency transit.
Nothing could reach them from inside the threshold, and an array cannot lock onto a signal that never arrives."
"How long, then?"
"If they spend what the transit costs?
Minutes."
The five emergency return talismans could have carried Leon’s household back to the Palace, but they could not transport nine surveyors, seven prisoners, and the evidence.
Leaving the site unguarded was not an option.
Nobody stood around waiting.
Seraphine established a guarded boundary around the empty ground and set markers on it, because fourteen people had come out of it and she did not intend for anything to go back in unobserved.
Vyra sorted the confiscated material into evidence and ordinary supplies and sealed the first category in three separate cases.
Ira put the prisoners in a line where the whole clearing could see them and made escape look as impossible as it was.
Loriel went through the nine surveyors again, now that they were standing in ordinary time, and found nothing wrong with any of them.
And Leon walked the boundary of the flat ground and checked the threshold from outside.
It was still there.
Still stable.

And when he put his perception into it and reached past the closed inward route, he could feel the pulse — slow, enormous, and patient, coming through a wall from something that had not been born yet.
Ninety to a hundred and eighty days.
The surveyors had changed toward them, and they were careful about it, which Leon respected.
Nobody asked.
Nobody said anything within his hearing about six Golden Core cultivators falling in nine seconds to four registered Peak Foundation Establishment attendants.
But Mo Rui, who had been treating Vyra as a clever colleague for two days, now waited for her to speak first.
Xie Lan had stopped looking at Loriel entirely, which was its own kind of statement.
Deacon Yu came over once, while Leon was checking the threshold.
"Senior Leon."
"Deacon."
Yu was quiet for a moment.
"Twenty-four days ago I was verifying a resource region.
I am going to submit a report describing an ancient realm nexus, three severed anchors, a Nascent Soul saboteur, and an Earth-Grade Grotto-Heaven." He looked out at the rain.

"I have been asking myself what else I am going to have to describe, and I have decided that the answer is: the recovery of nine Palace cultivators, by a direct disciple and his household, under conditions I was not qualified to assess."
"That’s an accurate report."
"It is acompletereport," Yu said, "of what I am qualified to assess," and went back to his people.
Leon read the confiscated records one final time while they waited.
Nothing in them contradicted the confessions.
No completed dispatch.
No message log.
Seven unused tokens and a month of notes that never once mentioned the thing the notes were about.
They almost certainly never told anyone.
He wrote that down in exactly those words, becausealmost certainlywas the honest version and he was not going to hand his master anything better than the truth.
The rain changed at the fourth mark.
It did not stop.

What happened was that the cloud above the basin lit — moon-white lines spreading across it in the middle of an overcast afternoon, running out from a central point in an expanding lattice, locking down onto Leon’s token and onto Yu’s emergency plaque with a precision that made the hair on his arms rise.
"Formation," Seraphine said sharply.
"Young Master — everyone back from the ground."
The lattice completed.
Three presences came down through it, and Leon felt the basin itself react — the rain bending around them before they had arrived, the stormglass in the shelves lighting and going dark.
Ji Liansu landed first, in pale green and silver-grey with the veil across the lower half of her face.

chapters.title: Chapter 662: Ash Before Heaven
paragraphs: She did not look at the threshold, or the prisoners, or Leon.
"Deacon Yu. Nine?"
"Nine, Palace Mistress. All present, all alive." Yu was already on one knee with his report in both hands. "No injuries, no illness, no deaths."
Ji took the report, then went and looked at them herself, one at a time, all nine. It took several minutes and nobody hurried her.
"Loriel," she said, when she had finished.

"They’re intact, Palace Mistress." Loriel bowed properly. "They were held in a layer where local time barely advanced. Their bodies experienced under an hour of the twenty-four days. I’ve examined all nine three times, before and after we crossed out, and I can find no wasting, no depletion, and no lasting effect. They will need to be examined by the medicine court, but I don’t expect the court to find anything I missed."
"Good." Ji turned. "Elder Shan."

The enforcement elder had already begun. Broad and unhurried, he took the seven into custody without appearing to move. He laid a second suppression over Seraphine’s seals, then silenced every communication artifact within forty paces with a single gesture.
"Elder Ruan. The threshold."
The formation elder was a small woman with ink on three fingers. She went to the flat ground, crouched, and did not move again.
Leon reported to his master standing in the rain, and it took a long time, and Ji asked questions the whole way through.

She asked how the seven had held the central chamber and he told her — the damaged dais, the four maintenance positions, the borrowed nexus current the leader had not known he was borrowing. She asked how they had gone in and he told her about the two-second alignment window and how he had held it open.
"And the fighting?"
"Six Golden Core and one Nascent Soul. It took under a minute. All seven were taken alive and none of them was permanently injured." He did not embellish it and Ji did not ask him to.

She asked about the interrogation, and he gave her the whole history in order: an ordinary clan mission to investigate an anomaly, an accidental crossing, a month spent trying to escape, the discovery in the third week, the two-day argument, and the decision.
"They didn’t tell their own clan," Ji said.

"They agreed not to. They intended to escape, seal the entrance, report a dead formation field, and come back for it themselves." Leon paused. "Then the survey team arrived and they couldn’t allow nine Palace witnesses to leave. Everything after that — the spikes, the attempted core extraction, the anchor failures — was an attempt to build a prison and it broke the thing they were standing in."
"You are certain their clan does not know?"

"No," Leon said. "The evidence supports it. Seven unused signal tokens, no completed reports, a month of notes that never mention the discovery, and seven separate confessions that agree on this one point when they disagree on others. That’s strong. It isn’t certainty. I can’t prove a message never left."
Ji looked at him for a moment.
"Correct," she said. "Continue."
He finished with the tools, and he was careful about it.

"The formation-breakers match the craftsmanship from the Shen estate attack in Moonfall. The finish, character-cutting, and formation-breaking method point to the same workshop." He met her eyes. "That connects the maker. It does not identify the buyer or whoever gave the order."
Elder Ruan came back from the threshold twenty minutes later and did not waste words.

"It’s a stabilisation gate," she said. "Built around a developing independent space. The core regulates size, internal flow rate, and attachment — it’s holding the thing on a leash while it finishes. Classification band on the outer ring is Earth-Grade and I’d stake my seat on it." She wiped rain off her face. "Ninety to a hundred and eighty days, near enough. Opening it early would very likely kill it."
"And the repairs?" Ji asked.
Elder Ruan looked at Leon with an expression he could not read.

"Three anchors, one of them with a live hostile relay in it, reconnected by somebody working without the original schematics, without the maintenance tools, and without knowing what the complex was for." She shrugged. "I’ve spent forty years on formations and I would have wanted a team and a season. I’d like to know how he did the temporal one, when there’s time."

"There will be time." Ji turned. "Reinforce and conceal the entrance. Nobody enters. I want a permanent seal designed before the month is out. Elder Shan — the basin is closed. Palace authority, no exceptions, and every report about this place passes through you before it goes anywhere at all."
Both elders acknowledged it.
"The nine surveyors remain under my protection," Ji added for the whole clearing to hear. "They will be examined by the medicine court, debriefed, and compensated properly."
Then she addressed the reward, and she did it formally, in front of everyone.

"Leon. Your household recovered nine Palace cultivators from an isolated space, restored a threshold complex whose failure would have destroyed a developing realm, prevented the theft of its core, preserved the evidence, and secured this site before another faction could reach it." Her voice carried. "The Palace will grant your household priority placement in the first expedition when the Grotto-Heaven opens, and a fixed share of everything the Palace draws from it."
"Thank you, Master."
"Don’t. This is not generosity — it is what the Palace owes and it is cheaper than what you have earned." She paused. "We will discuss the size of the share when the elders have argued about it."
Only then did she look at the prisoners.
The leader had been watching the whole exchange from his knees, and he had clearly spent it thinking, and he began speaking as soon as her attention arrived.
"Palace Mistress. My clan does not know what is here — you have heard that confirmed by seven separate mouths. That makes us the only living evidence of who came, and if you—"
"Leon," said Ji, without looking away from the man. "Have you obtained everything useful from them?"
Leon thought about it properly, because she had asked properly. The confessions. The timeline. The tools. The notes, catalogued. Seven statements, cross-checked, recorded in Vyra’s hand and sealed.
"Yes," he said.
The seven of them turned to ash.

There was no light and almost no sound. One moment there were seven men kneeling in the mud under Elder Shan’s suppression, and the next there was fine grey ash where they had been, already going dark in the rain, along with everything that had still been bound to them.
Nobody had time to scream. The leader had been mid-sentence.
Leon stood very still.

He had tortured that man three hours ago and had never intended to let any of the seven walk free. Even so, Leon had been thinking in terms of custody, evidence, judgment, and an execution carried out later.
Ji had asked one question and erased them before the answer had finished leaving his mouth.
She’s more ruthless than I am.

For the first time since becoming her disciple, Leon was genuinely wary of her. He also understood. The seven had entered her territory, tried to steal a realm’s heart, and imprisoned nine Palace disciples. Whether their clan knew the secret no longer changed what Ji considered necessary.
The same woman who had personally checked all nine surveyors had eliminated their captors without hesitation. Leon could fear that decisiveness and still respect it.
"Master," he said.
"Yes."
"Nothing. I understand."

"I know you do." Ji turned toward the flat ground, where Elder Ruan had already begun laying the first line of a seal. "You had sound reasons to keep them alive this morning. None of them could be allowed to leave this basin knowing what lies beneath that stone."

The rain came down on the clearing. Seven small grey heaps darkened, spread, and went into the mud among the survey markers, and within a few minutes there was nothing on the ground that a person walking past would have recognised as anything at all.
Beneath it, patient and enormous, something not yet born went on pulsing every eleven minutes.

chapters.title: Chapter 663: The Story the Palace Told
paragraphs: The rain took the ash into the mud within a few minutes, and Ji Liansu turned away from it before it was finished.
"Elder Ruan. You stay."
The formation elder was already back at the flat ground with a stylus between her teeth. She took it out. "How many people?"

"As many as you need, chosen by you, vetted by Elder Shan. Reinforce what my disciple repaired. Conceal the pulse — I do not want a wandering cultivator with a tracking formation stumbling into this a second time. Layered seals over the entrance, and a permanent access formation designed and built before that realm matures." Ji paused. "Nobody enters. Including you."
"I’d like to enter."
"I am aware. Nobody enters."
Elder Ruan made a noise that was not quite agreement and went back to her lines.

"Elder Shan. The basin is closed. Palace authority, a perimeter you can hold quietly, and every record from beneath this ground through your hands before anyone else’s." Ji’s voice did not rise. "No disciple, merchant, allied clan, or elder outside this conversation gets the true report without my permission."
"And the reason we give?"
"An unstable ancient formation field. It trapped a survey team, damaged the regional tracking arrays, and remains dangerous until the Palace certifies it. All of which is true."
Then she went to the nine surveyors, and Leon watched her handle them differently.
"Deacon Yu. I am going to restrict you and your people, and I would rather you heard why from me than guessed at it."
Yu came to attention. "Palace Mistress."

"Medicine court first, all nine, tonight. Then you will each be questioned separately. Nobody suspects you of anything; nine separate accounts simply reconstruct an event more accurately than one agreed version. You will be compensated for the mission at the rate for a completed survey plus hazard, and I will sign it myself." She let that sit. "After that, everything you experienced beneath this basin is sealed. You do not discuss it with your peaks, your families, or each other."
"Understood."

"Nobody is touching your memories," Ji added. "Nobody is threatening you. You went where the Palace sent you and kept all nine members of your team alive through a spatial event that lasted more than three weeks outside. That earns protection, not suspicion."
Xie Lan spoke without meaning to. "Palace Mistress — the Palace will be told we walked into a broken formation. Nobody will ever know what’s actually down there."
"A great many people will know," said Ji. "In three to six months, in an order I choose. At this moment, seventeen people know what lies beneath this basin. That is already more than I would prefer."
Mo Rui looked at the flat ground a while and said, quietly, "Then it’s a good story. I’d believe it."
Ji asked for the spikes before they left.
Leon handed over all three, cased and sealed, and gave her the same account he had given her in the rain.

"The craftsmanship matches the ward-breaker used against the Shen estate. Same finish, same character-cutting, in my judgment the same workshop." He met her eyes. "That’s a maker, not a buyer. I still can’t prove who commissioned either set."
"Good," said Ji. "Keep saying it that way until it stops being true."

The transit formation came down an hour later, a moon-white lattice opening in the clouds above the basin. Leon felt its cost now that he was not distracted. Fifteen people crossed eleven days of ground in a breath, and the Palace had spent that power on his household today.
Elder Ruan did not look up as they went.
The story reached Jade Moon Palace ahead of them and was already growing by the time they arrived.
A survey team lost in an unstable ancient formation field. Three weeks. All nine recovered alive. The region closed pending certification.

Every visible fact supported it. Leon heard three versions inside two hours, none correct and none dangerous. In one, he had personally carried the deacon out. Nobody guessed at a realm because nobody had reason to.

And I’m not going to be credited with the thing I actually did,Leon thought, and found he preferred it that way. Public credit for finding an unborn Grotto-Heaven would have made his household the most closely watched people on the mountain.
Han Suwen met them at the gate of his peak with a ledger and no expression.

"Twenty-four days," she said. "You left on a survey escort with a two-week estimate. You have returned with nine recovered disciples, a sealed report, a closed territory, and the Palace Mistress personally directing the aftermath." She looked at Vyra. "I am not going to ask what is in the report."

"Good," said Vyra, "because I would have had to be unpleasant about it. Here’s what I can give you." She handed over three pages. "Approved version, supply reconciliation, and everything we lost or abandoned in the field. The last page is a purchasing request the Young Master needs moved quickly."
Han Suwen read all three, wrote something in her ledger, and said, "This is well organised. Whatever you did down there, you kept your accounts."
"I kept my accounts," Vyra agreed, "while a Nascent Soul cultivator was trying to kill us."
Han Suwen’s pen stopped for exactly one beat.
"I am not going to ask about that either," she said.
Inside the sealed residence, they spent most of an hour discussing what Ji had done.
Ira said it first. "She turned seven people into ash between one word and the next."
"She did."

"They were kneeling. They weresealed." Ira had not sat down. "I’ve killed people. I could have killed those men in that chamber, and I would have if you’d ordered it. But that was different, and I can’t work out why."

"Because there was nothing left to decide," Loriel said from the edge of the table. "It wasn’t rage or punishment. She asked a question, received the answer, and decided they had stopped being useful. I understand the reasoning. I still didn’t like watching seven lives end because a piece of information had run out."
Seraphine had been quiet the longest.
"None of that is what worries me," she said.
"Then what?"

"She made an irreversible decision before anyone else in that clearing had finished thinking." Seraphine turned to him. "Leon, she landed with the arithmetic already done. While she checked the surveyors and signed their compensation, she was waiting for you to sayyes. I’m not saying she was wrong. I’m saying your master reaches conclusions faster than the people around her can follow, and she has no obligation to slow down for us."
Vyra had been writing the entire time and put her pen down.

"And here’s the part I want recorded," she said. "The Palace put two specialist elders and an emergency transit formation into that basin within twenty minutes. It closed the territory and built a public story before we returned." She tapped the page. "That is how an institution responds to something worth more than a mountain. Ji Liansu understood its value before her boots touched the ground."
They all looked at Leon eventually.
"It frightened me," he said. "Ji ended seven people in less time than it takes to breathe out. For a moment afterward, I understood exactly what she could do to any of us."
"And?" said Ira.
"She was right. I’d have reached the same decision after a trial and a great deal of paperwork." He shook his head. "Both things are true. I’ve stopped trying to make one cancel the other."
Nobody argued with him for what he stated.
He waited until the residence was quiet, then went through the formations one more time out of habit rather than doubt, and sat down on the floor of the main hall.

In two months, Leon had fought a duel, repaired an ancient nexus, rescued nine cultivators, and discovered an unborn realm. The circulation he had spent thirty-one days building had been tested, damaged, healed, and tested again, but never used for its actual purpose.
Enough.
He opened the connection and went through.
The light on the other side was late afternoon, and the air smelled of turned earth, and somewhere down the slope a work bell was ringing.
"Xyra," he said. "I need you."

The transit formation came down an hour later, a moon-white lattice opening in the clouds above the basin.
Leon felt its cost now that he was not distracted.
Fifteen people crossed eleven days of ground in a breath, and the Palace had spent that power on his household today.
Elder Ruan did not look up as they went.
The story reached Jade Moon Palace ahead of them and was already growing by the time they arrived.
A survey team lost in an unstable ancient formation field.
Three weeks.
All nine recovered alive.
The region closed pending certification.
Every visible fact supported it.
Leon heard three versions inside two hours, none correct and none dangerous.
In one, he had personally carried the deacon out.
Nobody guessed at a realm because nobody had reason to.
And I’m not going to be credited with the thing I actually did,Leon thought, and found he preferred it that way.
Public credit for finding an unborn Grotto-Heaven would have made his household the most closely watched people on the mountain.
Han Suwen met them at the gate of his peak with a ledger and no expression.
"Twenty-four days," she said.
"You left on a survey escort with a two-week estimate.
You have returned with nine recovered disciples, a sealed report, a closed territory, and the Palace Mistress personally directing the aftermath." She looked at Vyra.
"I am not going to ask what is in the report."
"Good," said Vyra, "because I would have had to be unpleasant about it.
Here’s what I can give you." She handed over three pages.
"Approved version, supply reconciliation, and everything we lost or abandoned in the field.
The last page is a purchasing request the Young Master needs moved quickly."
Han Suwen read all three, wrote something in her ledger, and said, "This is well organised.
Whatever you did down there, you kept your accounts."
"I kept my accounts," Vyra agreed, "while a Nascent Soul cultivator was trying to kill us."
Han Suwen’s pen stopped for exactly one beat.
"I am not going to ask about that either," she said.
Inside the sealed residence, they spent most of an hour discussing what Ji had done.
Ira said it first.
"She turned seven people into ash between one word and the next."
"She did."
"They were kneeling.
They weresealed." Ira had not sat down.
"I’ve killed people.
I could have killed those men in that chamber, and I would have if you’d ordered it.
But that was different, and I can’t work out why."
"Because there was nothing left to decide," Loriel said from the edge of the table.
"It wasn’t rage or punishment.
She asked a question, received the answer, and decided they had stopped being useful.
I understand the reasoning.
I still didn’t like watching seven lives end because a piece of information had run out."
Seraphine had been quiet the longest.
"None of that is what worries me," she said.
"Then what?"
"She made an irreversible decision before anyone else in that clearing had finished thinking." Seraphine turned to him.
"Leon, she landed with the arithmetic already done.
While she checked the surveyors and signed their compensation, she was waiting for you to sayyes.
I’m not saying she was wrong.
I’m saying your master reaches conclusions faster than the people around her can follow, and she has no obligation to slow down for us."
Vyra had been writing the entire time and put her pen down.
"And here’s the part I want recorded," she said.
"The Palace put two specialist elders and an emergency transit formation into that basin within twenty minutes.
It closed the territory and built a public story before we returned." She tapped the page.
"That is how an institution responds to something worth more than a mountain.
Ji Liansu understood its value before her boots touched the ground."
They all looked at Leon eventually.
"It frightened me," he said.
"Ji ended seven people in less time than it takes to breathe out.
For a moment afterward, I understood exactly what she could do to any of us."
"And?" said Ira.
"She was right.
I’d have reached the same decision after a trial and a great deal of paperwork." He shook his head.
"Both things are true.
I’ve stopped trying to make one cancel the other."
Nobody argued with him for what he stated.
He waited until the residence was quiet, then went through the formations one more time out of habit rather than doubt, and sat down on the floor of the main hall.
In two months, Leon had fought a duel, repaired an ancient nexus, rescued nine cultivators, and discovered an unborn realm.
The circulation he had spent thirty-one days building had been tested, damaged, healed, and tested again, but never used for its actual purpose.
Enough.
He opened the connection and went through.
The light on the other side was late afternoon, and the air smelled of turned earth, and somewhere down the slope a work bell was ringing.
"Xyra," he said.
"I need you."

chapters.title: Chapter 664: Seven Immortal Cores for One Step
paragraphs: She came out of the mansion in her own time, the way she did everything.

Xyra had not changed since the crossing: small, dark-haired, apparently about nineteen, with eyes far older than the face around them. Grass leaned as she crossed the courtyard, and the air adjusted around her.
"You’ve been busy," she said. "Three weeks outside. Something old, from the taste of what came back through you."
"Very old."
"Are you going to tell me?"
"Later, and not in front of anyone." Vyra was already there with a record slate; Seraphine and Loriel had come through behind him. "First I need a favour, and I want the cost before you say yes."
Xyra tilted her head.
"I want a thousand-to-one field," he said. "Localised. Around the eastern flat only, not the settlement. I need months and I have hours."
There was a pause.
"Is that all?"
"Xyra."
"You asked so carefully." There was definite amusement in it. "Four sentences. I was waiting to find out what the difficult part was." She raised one hand, turned it over, and closed it.
The eastern flat changed.

There was no light and no sound. The boundary simply became visible as a line where the grass on one side moved differently from the grass on the other — faster, in a way that made Leon’s eye slide off it.

"There," said Xyra. "It will hold as long as you want it. It costs me approximately what breathing costs you, and if you ask me again in that tone I will make it two thousand and let you find out what that does to your sense of taste."
"Understood."

"Ordinary life continues everywhere else at the usual pace," she added, more seriously. "Your people can walk in and out. The long time belongs to whoever stays inside it, which I assume is you." She looked at him properly then. "What are you doing, Leon?"
"Starting."
He laid the seven cores out on the stone in a line, and Vyra stopped writing.

They had remained in his private storage since his first days in this world, taken from seven Void Immortal robbers who had been destroying a caravan outside Moonfall. Seven Ethereal Initiate cores, preserved and untouched because he had never found a use that justified consuming them.
"Those are—" Vyra began.
"Yes."
"All seven of them."
"All seven."
Seraphine had gone very still. "For what?"
"For a realm that this world calls the first one," said Leon.
He explained it once because they deserved to understand what he was attempting.
His body already exceeded everything Body Tempering existed to accomplish. Repeating a mortal preparatory course would achieve nothing but wasted months.

His old core was why every artifact in Jade Moon Palace read him as Peak Golden Core. That reading was honest — it measured the power he actually carried. It simply had nothing to do with the sequence local cultivators walked, because he had never walked it.

"Every circulation I’ve run through the Scripture was a test," he said. "Whether the route held, carried an affinity, or leaked at the junctions. It worked, but none of it was permanent." He nudged the first core with two fingers. "Tonight I establish the first native layer through conscious absorption, purification, and circulation. Qi Refinement. Everything after it will rest on what I build here."
"And your old foundation?" Loriel asked.

"Stays exactly where it is. The new layer goes beneath it, not through it." He looked at the cores. "Drawing qi is easy. Building a layer clean enough to balance nine affinities, coexist with two Hearts, and support everything that follows is not."
Xyra, who had settled onto the courtyard wall, said, "And you would rather spend a month getting it right than a century regretting it."
"Yes."
"Good," she said. "Almost nobody does."
He crossed the boundary and began. The first attempt lasted eleven days before he took it apart himself.

The mechanics were straightforward. He drew refined energy off the first core, divided it nine ways at the intake, and let the Scripture’s neutral centre strip the dead man’s imprint before anything reached his channels. The nine branches ran the full meridian circuit and returned into the structure forming beneath his old core — a Qi Sea, the local texts called it, and his was going to be a strange one.
The problem was balance.
On day nine he measured the returning branches and found the Lightning branch running a fraction over and the Earth branch a fraction under. The difference was under two percent.

Two percent would be invisible in a Qi Refinement cultivator. Two percent, compounded through Foundation Establishment and again through a Golden Core, would put a permanent lean into a structure that had to hold nine things in equilibrium for the rest of his life.
He took the whole layer apart on day eleven and started again.

The second attempt failed at the intake — the nine-way division worked and the Scripture’s stripping did not, and traces of the core’s original owner made it three junctions deep before Loriel, watching from outside the boundary, made him stop.
"There’s someone else’s rhythm in your left channel," she said flatly. "I don’t care how small. Take it out."
The third attempt ran forty-one days and came close enough that another cultivator might have accepted it. Leon dismantled it anyway.Almosthad no place in a foundation meant to carry nine affinities.
Seraphine came in for a day in the sixth week and watched the Lightning branch with her hand a foot from his shoulder.
"It’s smoother than mine," she said. "Mine stutters at the third junction. I’ve had it for years and never found it."
"Yours was built for a sword. Mine’s built to be interrupted eight times a second by something that isn’t lightning."
"Mm. How many cores?"
"Four."
She looked at the dark stones lined up beside him. "Four. For Qi Refinement."
"Four so far."

Vyra recorded everything, three times a week, in a hand that got steadily more disbelieving. Loriel came in whenever he changed something structural and put her hands on his channels and told him what his own body thought of it.
Xyra visited twice. She offered no advice about the Scripture, but she did explain how a thousand-to-one field interacted with a circulation timed to fractions of a second.

"Your body is living a thousand days for every one outside," she said. "Your qi does not know that. If you tune the rhythm to what feels natural in here, you will walk out of my field with a circulation that is out of step with the world."
Correcting the error cost him another week.

The fourth attempt became the one he kept. Leon rebuilt the intake, recalibrated every branch against the world’s natural rhythm, and refused to close the circulation until all nine returned without measurable deviation.
The layer stabilised in the seventh subjective month.

He knew before he opened his eyes. The nine branches returned to the Qi Sea in perfect proportion and remained stable, with no drift, imbalance, or overheated channel. The new structure rested beneath his old core without disturbing it.
[Cultivation: Early Qi Refinement]
[Formless Myriad Scripture — Stage One, Early Layer: Established]
[Nine-Affinity Balance: Stable]
Leon sat and looked at that for a long time.
Then he looked at the seven cores.
Every core was dark. None was empty, and a competent alchemist would still pay a fortune for the residue, but they could not support another cultivation attempt.
Seven Void Immortal cores.
He did the arithmetic he had been avoiding. Sold properly in Moonfall, those seven cores could have funded several talented mortal-born disciples from their first breath of qi into Golden Core.
He had heavily drained all seven to reach the realm this world gave to fourteen-year-olds.
And I’d do it again.
What he had built was not a fourteen-year-old’s Qi Refinement layer. It balanced nine affinities beneath a foundation from another world, and every later layer could build upon it.

He tested the practical difference before he left the field, and it was real and it was quiet. His affinity transitions cost less. The residual loss he had accepted for years as the price of switching from Ice to Lightning had dropped by a noticeable fraction. Mixed energy behaved.

His combat power had risen slightly. Externally, nothing about him had changed at all — his old core still dominated every reading anyone in this world could take, and would go on doing so for a long time.
He stepped back across the boundary into late afternoon.
"Six hours," said Vyra, from the courtyard wall. She was holding a sealed message. "This arrived four of them ago. The Palace Mistress. Elder Ruan has found something inside the spikes."

chapters.title: Chapter 665: The Mark Beneath the Cut
paragraphs: They met in a private chamber under Ji’s own peak rather than any hall with a door onto a corridor, and Leon understood the significance of that before anyone spoke.
Ji Liansu. Elder Ruan, back from the basin with ink on four fingers now instead of three. Han Suwen with a case of records. Nobody else.
"Sit," said Ji. "Elder Ruan, show him."
Ruan put a viewing plate on the table and brought up an image magnified past anything Leon’s eyes could have managed.
"That’s the interior of the second spike," she said. "I took it apart in eleven layers. This is between the sixth and the seventh, underneath the third carved character."
There was a mark in the metal. It was tiny — smaller than a grain of rice at true scale — and it was not a signature. It was four strokes and a number.

"A craftsman proud of his work signs the outside," Ruan said. "This is placed where the character above it burns through on first use. Ordinary employment destroys it. The only way to find it is to do what I did, which is to disassemble a functioning implement layer by layer, which nobody does to a tool that works." She sat back. "It’s a batch identifier. Internal. It exists so a workshop can track its own output without telling the customer, or anyone who finds the customer, who made it."
"And the alloy?" Leon asked.

"Better." Ruan brought up a second plate. "There’s a stabilising additive in it — about one part in four hundred. It stops the cutting edge losing shape under formation backlash, which is exactly what you want in a tool meant to sever an active channel. It is also expensive, it comes out of three mines that I know of, and it moves through perhaps six regional markets on the whole eastern seaboard." She tapped the plate. "Mark, alloy, cutting angle, and the order the characters are laid down. Four independent things. Together they point at one workshop, and that workshop sells through Moonfall’s hidden formation trade."
Han Suwen produced the last piece from her case: a rubbing, and beside it a Palace record with the Shen family’s seal on it.

"The ward-breaker from the estate attack," she said. "The Shens still hold the original. This is a full technical record taken at the time, including an interior cross-section that somebody had the sense to order."
Ruan put it beside her own image.
Same four strokes. Different number.
"Same workshop," she said. "Different batch. That is as certain as anything in my discipline gets."
Leon looked at the two marks side by side for a while.
"It’s a maker," he said. "Not a buyer."
"Correct," said Ji. "And you will keep saying so, because a workshop that sells to one clan sells to four."
"You’ll lead it," Ji went on. "I want to explain why, so that you don’t mistake it for a favour.

"If I send Elder Ruan to Moonfall, every person in that trade knows within a day that Jade Moon Palace is dismantling formation-breaking tools. The workshop closes, the ledgers burn, and whoever commissioned those spikes learns that we found something inside them." She folded her hands. "If I send a squad of enforcement disciples, the same thing happens more loudly.

"If I send my direct disciple to buy cultivation resources for his household, nothing happens at all, because that is exactly what a man in your position does, and everybody in that city already knows your face and your business relationships."
"The Shen family," Leon said.

"You have a genuine relationship with the house that was attacked. You have a legitimate reason to return. Your household covers combat, medicine, administration, detection, and formation analysis between four people, and you personally have seen what these tools did in both incidents, which nobody else alive has." Ji’s voice sharpened slightly. "Now hear the limits.

"You are authorised to find the workshop, preserve evidence, question people involved in its trade, and defend your household. You are not authorised to name a clan, accuse a clan, or provoke one. I do not have proof, and neither do you, and a direct disciple of mine starting a quarrel with a regional power on the strength of a metallurgical match would be a disaster I would have to clean up personally."
"Understood."
"Say it back."
"Find the workshop. Preserve what’s there. Don’t start a war on suspicion."
"Good."
The cover was the part Leon liked, because it was not a cover.

"I need resources," he said. "Genuinely. I established the Early Qi Refinement layer two days ago, and it consumed considerably more than I expected. Nine affinities in balance means nine supplies, and materials carrying another cultivator’s imprint force the Scripture to waste most of its effort stripping them clean."
Ji considered that. "How much did the first stage cost?"
"Enough that I’d rather not say it out loud in this room."

"Mm." She did not press. "You may use the Palace’s trusted purchasing channels, and you may draw an advance of one part against the share your household is owed from the future expedition. Not more. I am not opening the vault to you — the reward is a future entitlement and I will not have it spent before the realm exists."
"That’s fair."
"It’s also all you’re getting."
Qingyue was summoned afterward, alone, and Ji told Leon in advance exactly what he could say.
He said it in her presence, plainly.

"The tools recovered during the Ashen Rain mission were formation-breakers. Elder Ruan has matched their maker’s mark and alloy to the ward-breaker used against the Shen estate. Same workshop. The trail runs back to Moonfall’s hidden formation trade, and the Palace can’t investigate it openly without warning everyone connected to it."
Qingyue’s eyes did not leave his face.
"What were formation-breakers doing in Ashen Rain Basin?"
"That part is sealed," said Ji. "By me. Not by him."
Qingyue looked at her master’s master for a moment and then, sensibly, let it go.

"Then I’m coming," she said. "Not as a favour to the Palace. Those people attacked a house under my guarantee — I brought Leon through that gate, and the Shens gave him papers, and four Void Immortals walked into their garden because somebody sold the tools that got them past the wall." Her jaw set. "I know who trades in Moonfall and who only appears to. I know which repair shops take commissions they don’t write down. You’d spend a month finding what I can find in four days."
"Good," said Ji. "Then it’s settled. Qingyue, understand that this is not your Palace assignment and I am not putting it in your record."
"I understand."
They planned it that night in the inner residence.

Vyra built two lists, one public and one not. "Purchases in the open. Questions in private, and none of them phrased as a question if I can help it — I’d rather trace an alloy through a shipping ledger than ask a merchant who bought it."

Seraphine had the mark image and was studying it with an expression Leon recognised. "Any workshop precise enough to cut this has equipment worth more than the building. There aren’t many. That narrows where we look before we ask anybody anything."
Ira, who had been listening with visibly diminishing patience, said, "So the plan is shopping."
"The plan is shopping," Leon agreed.
"For how long?"
"As long as it takes."
"I could find the workshop in an evening."

"You could findaworkshop in an evening," said Loriel, without looking up from her seed cases. "And then everyone in the trade would know somebody is looking, and the people who actually know things would stop being findable." She fastened a case. "Frightened people tell you less than comfortable people do. Dead ones tell you nothing at all."
Ira opened her mouth, considered it, and closed it again.
They left the following morning on an ordinary travel authorisation, six of them, with a purchasing list and no escort.
To anyone watching from the terraces, the Palace Mistress’s famous disciple was going to Moonfall to buy resources for four unusually talented attendants.
Three people on the mountain knew he was following a mark hidden inside a weapon.
[If you have bought privilege, thank you so much; if you haven’t, please do; that would help me a lot]

"It’s a maker," he said.
"Not a buyer."
"Correct," said Ji.
"And you will keep saying so, because a workshop that sells to one clan sells to four."
"You’ll lead it," Ji went on.
"I want to explain why, so that you don’t mistake it for a favour.
"If I send Elder Ruan to Moonfall, every person in that trade knows within a day that Jade Moon Palace is dismantling formation-breaking tools.
The workshop closes, the ledgers burn, and whoever commissioned those spikes learns that we found something inside them." She folded her hands.
"If I send a squad of enforcement disciples, the same thing happens more loudly.

"If I send my direct disciple to buy cultivation resources for his household, nothing happens at all, because that is exactly what a man in your position does, and everybody in that city already knows your face and your business relationships."
"The Shen family," Leon said.
"You have a genuine relationship with the house that was attacked.
You have a legitimate reason to return.

Your household covers combat, medicine, administration, detection, and formation analysis between four people, and you personally have seen what these tools did in both incidents, which nobody else alive has." Ji’s voice sharpened slightly.
"Now hear the limits.
"You are authorised to find the workshop, preserve evidence, question people involved in its trade, and defend your household.
You are not authorised to name a clan, accuse a clan, or provoke one.

I do not have proof, and neither do you, and a direct disciple of mine starting a quarrel with a regional power on the strength of a metallurgical match would be a disaster I would have to clean up personally."
"Understood."
"Say it back."
"Find the workshop.
Preserve what’s there.
Don’t start a war on suspicion."
"Good."
The cover was the part Leon liked, because it was not a cover.
"I need resources," he said.
"Genuinely.
I established the Early Qi Refinement layer two days ago, and it consumed considerably more than I expected.
Nine affinities in balance means nine supplies, and materials carrying another cultivator’s imprint force the Scripture to waste most of its effort stripping them clean."
Ji considered that.
"How much did the first stage cost?"
"Enough that I’d rather not say it out loud in this room."
"Mm." She did not press.
"You may use the Palace’s trusted purchasing channels, and you may draw an advance of one part against the share your household is owed from the future expedition.
Not more.
I am not opening the vault to you — the reward is a future entitlement and I will not have it spent before the realm exists."
"That’s fair."
"It’s also all you’re getting."
Qingyue was summoned afterward, alone, and Ji told Leon in advance exactly what he could say.
He said it in her presence, plainly.
"The tools recovered during the Ashen Rain mission were formation-breakers.
Elder Ruan has matched their maker’s mark and alloy to the ward-breaker used against the Shen estate.
Same workshop.
The trail runs back to Moonfall’s hidden formation trade, and the Palace can’t investigate it openly without warning everyone connected to it."
Qingyue’s eyes did not leave his face.
"What were formation-breakers doing in Ashen Rain Basin?"
"That part is sealed," said Ji.
"By me.
Not by him."
Qingyue looked at her master’s master for a moment and then, sensibly, let it go.
"Then I’m coming," she said.
"Not as a favour to the Palace.

Those people attacked a house under my guarantee — I brought Leon through that gate, and the Shens gave him papers, and four Void Immortals walked into their garden because somebody sold the tools that got them past the wall." Her jaw set.
"I know who trades in Moonfall and who only appears to.
I know which repair shops take commissions they don’t write down.
You’d spend a month finding what I can find in four days."
"Good," said Ji.
"Then it’s settled.
Qingyue, understand that this is not your Palace assignment and I am not putting it in your record."
"I understand."
They planned it that night in the inner residence.
Vyra built two lists, one public and one not.
"Purchases in the open.
Questions in private, and none of them phrased as a question if I can help it — I’d rather trace an alloy through a shipping ledger than ask a merchant who bought it."
Seraphine had the mark image and was studying it with an expression Leon recognised.
"Any workshop precise enough to cut this has equipment worth more than the building.
There aren’t many.
That narrows where we look before we ask anybody anything."
Ira, who had been listening with visibly diminishing patience, said, "So the plan is shopping."
"The plan is shopping," Leon agreed.
"For how long?"
"As long as it takes."
"I could find the workshop in an evening."
"You could findaworkshop in an evening," said Loriel, without looking up from her seed cases.
"And then everyone in the trade would know somebody is looking, and the people who actually know things would stop being findable." She fastened a case.
"Frightened people tell you less than comfortable people do.
Dead ones tell you nothing at all."
Ira opened her mouth, considered it, and closed it again.
They left the following morning on an ordinary travel authorisation, six of them, with a purchasing list and no escort.
To anyone watching from the terraces, the Palace Mistress’s famous disciple was going to Moonfall to buy resources for four unusually talented attendants.
Three people on the mountain knew he was following a mark hidden inside a weapon.
[If you have bought privilege, thank you so much; if you haven’t, please do; that would help me a lot]

chapters.title: Chapter 666: Buying Stones, Hunting Ghosts
paragraphs: The journey took eleven days, and almost nothing happened.

They travelled openly — Palace transport to the coast, then the northern road with an authorisation that opened every waystation without a question. Two months ago Leon had come the other way with a temporary jade and a merchant’s borrowed clothes. Now a garrison captain recognised the household mark on Vyra’s token and had their horses changed before she finished asking.
Leon spent the safe nights inside the dimensional world and did not gain a thing, which he had expected.

Early Qi Refinement held perfectly. The layer did exactly what he had built it to do, but his early estimates suggested Mid Qi Refinement would demand at least as much energy, and the seven cores were dark.

He spent those nights revising the purchase list instead. Every session taught him something about what the Scripture actually ate: not raw quantity, butcleanquantity. A hundred low-grade fire stones from four different sources cost him more effort to strip than forty from one.
"Single-source lots," he told Vyra on the ninth night. "Even at a worse price. Add it to the list."
"Noted, Young Master." She was already writing. "It’ll cost about a fifth more and I’d rather pay it than have you spend a week scrubbing four strangers’ imprints out of the same crate."
Moonfall in the rain looked exactly as it had.

The walls, the lantern-lit ore lift over the northern quarter, the caravan queue at the eastern gate—Leon remembered all of it. He had once stood outside that gate as an unregistered stranger while an officer dismissed his story about a collapsed inheritance realm.
Six of them went through it this time without stopping. The gate officer took one look at Qingyue’s collar and the household tokens and waved the whole party past a queue half a kilometre long.
"That," said Ira, "is going to be very easy to get used to."
The merchants adjusted faster than the walls did.

Two months ago an alchemist had looked at Leon and asked which house he came from, and told him that everything above the counter had a buyer before it was made. This time three separate senior merchants sent invitations to their private rooms before the household had unpacked.
Vyra ran all of it and enjoyed herself enormously.

"Eleven percent," she told a spirit-stone factor on the second morning, in a tone of mild surprise. "You quoted the Palace’s purchasing office eight last quarter. I have the reconciliation." A pause. "I’d like eight."
She got eight and a half and considered it a defeat.

Each of them had a real list. Seraphine wanted lightning and light materials with their native charge intact and rejected four artificially treated lots. Ira returned from the fire markets complaining that most fire materials merely burned. "I don’t need it to burn. I need it to surviveme." Vyra chose slow, dense materials suited to sustaining a formation rather than powering a single strike.
Loriel spent the longest and bought the least, because everything she wanted had to survive being moved into soil that came from another world.

Leon’s own list was the strangest, and he never handed it over in person. It went to merchants in Vyra’s writing: balanced quantities across nine categories, single-source lots, unimprinted stock preferred, prices agreed for repeat supply.
Nobody in Moonfall learned that the Palace Mistress’s disciple had nine affinities. They learned that his household had an unusually broad shopping list and paid on time.
They went to the Shen estate on the third evening.

Shen Baoyuan met them in the front courtyard and did not know what to do with his hands. He looked less strained than he had two months earlier, which Leon took as a good sign for both the man and his household.
"Senior Leon," he said, and then stopped, because the last time he had said anything to Leon it had been in a garden full of bodies.
"Master Shen."

"I have — the guest wing is still yours. I said it and I meant it, though I confess I did not expect—" He gestured helplessly at Qingyue, at four registered attendants, at the general shape of what had walked through his gate.
"Father," said Yanning, arriving at a fast walk with a ledger still in her hand, "you’re standing in the rain. All of you, inside."
She had not changed. Within four minutes, she had six people, their horses, and their cases sorted and food on its way. Then she stopped in the doorway to look at Leon properly.
"Direct disciple."
"Apparently."
"We heard in the second week. My father cried, which I’m telling you because he’ll deny it." She held his eyes a moment. "You look better than the last time you left this house."
"I was bleeding the last time I left this house."
"You were. Come in."
Only Shen Yuanhe was told the rest, and only what was necessary.

The old ancestor heard Qingyue’s request without asking about Ashen Rain Basin. He retrieved the preserved ward-breaker from beneath the counting house, along with the estate’s full record of how the raiders had crossed the outer array.
"Take it," he said. "Take the rubbings, take the formation logs, take whatever you need. I have wanted somebody to ask me for these for two months."
Comparing the two sets of evidence took Seraphine and Vyra an evening and produced the first genuinely new thing.

"They’re built for different jobs by the same hand," Seraphine said, with the ward-breaker and a spike rubbing side by side. "This one is delicate. It’s meant to put an active array to sleep without the array noticing — the cutting is shallow and it’s all about the timing of the entry. The spikes are the opposite. They’re built to sever a major channel and thensit thereso the ends can’t find each other again."

"Which tells us the maker isn’t a specialist in one thing," said Vyra. "It tells us he’s competent enough to build to a brief. Somebody comes to him with a target and a requirement and he makes the tool for it." She set the rubbing down. "That’s not a criminal with a forge. That’s a supplier with clients."
The hidden trade was nothing like Ira had hoped.

There was no market. A legitimate repair shop accepted commissions absent from its books. A formation-components merchant kept a clean front room and referred certain customers upstairs. Four shell companies had held one warehouse lease for eleven years without filing a shipping manifest.
Qingyue got them through doors. She did not get them answers, and she knew it.

"Watch," she said quietly, after the second interview. "That man told me the truth about three things and stopped the moment the answers got useful. He isn’t protecting anyone. He’s frightened of me and frightened of somebody else, and I’m the one standing in front of him."
"Then we stop using you as the door, Young Master’s leave permitting," said Vyra. "I’d rather find the alloy in a customs book than in a man’s face."
So they changed methods.

Vyra traced the stabilising additive through customs reconciliations and bulk purchase records over four days, and found three importers who could legally have handled it and one who had received four consignments and sold on three.
Qingyue named the intermediaries who could move the fourth without a manifest.

Seraphine walked eleven workshops and eliminated eight of them on equipment alone. "The cutting on those spikes needs a stabilised bench and a fine-draw press. Four shops in this city have both. Three of them do Palace-certified work and would be insane to risk it."
And on the sixth day, a components merchant in the eastern industrial ward went pale before anyone asked him anything.
Loriel noticed it first. "Young Master, his pulse jumped when you said the wordcommission," she murmured. "Before you saidformation-breaker. He’s already been warned."
Leon narrowed the questions after that and stopped asking about tools at all. He asked about deliveries, and schedules, and who had cancelled recently.

The answer, when it came, arrived from three directions at once and pointed at the same place: an old workshop behind a legitimate metal-repair business in the fourth industrial ward, owned through four false names, receiving the rare alloy on a standing quarterly order.
The last contact told them the rest without being asked, because he wanted them to leave.
"They stopped taking messages this morning," he said. "Shutters down. Furnace cold since before dawn. I sent a runner about a bill and nobody answered the door."
Leon stood in the rain outside that shop for a moment, doing arithmetic he did not like.
Seven men have been missing their check-in for over three weeks.
"Seraphine," he said. "We approach it as a hostile scene. Nobody touches a door until I’ve looked at it."

chapters.title: Chapter 667: The Workshop That Died First
paragraphs: The fourth industrial ward continued working around them. A scrap cart passed the alley, a tinsmith hammered two doors down, and someone upstairs argued about rent. Nobody in the street knew what had happened.
"The outer ward was reset within the last day," Seraphine said, one palm extended. "Whoever did it used the shop’s own key sequence."
"The ventilation shut before the furnace," Vyra said after circling the building twice. "That let the shop cool without smoke. They knew its routine."
"Nobody alive inside, Young Master," Loriel said. "Not hiding or unconscious. No heartbeat anywhere."
Ira had her hand on her lance. "Then let me open it."
"No." Leon sent his perception through the door, its frame, and the floor beyond. "Two pressure triggers under the mat and a collapse rig in the front-room ceiling. Give me six minutes."
He took nine, and they went in through the side.
There were fourteen of them, dead within about a quarter of an hour of each other.

Leon had seen worse. The problem was howtidyit was — no fighting through rooms, no bodies in doorways, nobody caught halfway out a window. The craftspeople had died at their benches. The clerks had died at their desks. Somebody had been eating.
"They came in through the front with the workshop’s own authority, Young Master," Seraphine said from the entry hall. "The inner wards never triggered. Whoever they were, the building let them in."
Ira found the only resistance in the place: a scorched wall in the rear yard, a broken bench, and a big man who had managed perhaps four seconds of a fight.
"He reached the yard door," she said. "Already sealed from outside. They closed the exits before they started."
Vyra had gone straight to the ledgers and found none.
"They left eleven years of legitimate accounts and took everything from the last four months," she reported. "The finished tools are gone, but the raw stock remains. This wasn’t robbery."
Loriel worked through all fourteen and came back grim.
"Between eight and ten hours ago," she said. "Before dawn. And the killers’ residue is nothing like these people’s — cleaner, colder, and there were five of them at least."
Qingyue had been standing in the middle of the workshop floor with her arms folded for several minutes.

"Ten hours," she said. "We began asking questions in this ward yesterday afternoon. Someone could have heard and reacted overnight, but there’s a simpler explanation here." She turned. "Vyra. What triggered it?"
"I’m getting there."
She got there twenty minutes later, out of a wastebasket.
"Payment fragments, Young Master." She laid six burnt scraps on a bench. "They burned the ledger and missed the bin. This one is part of a standing-order instruction."
Leon read it over her shoulder. Half a line survived:...if no contact by the—
"There’s a check-in protocol," Vyra said. "A scheduled window. If a field team misses it, this workshop burns. Nobody was betrayed. Seven people stopped reporting and a rule engaged."
"Seven people," said Qingyue.

"The ones Ji killed had been out of contact since before the surveyors vanished," Leon said. "Three missed windows. The delay was built into the protocol. Once the third passed, the contingency triggered exactly as designed."
Ira looked around the room. "So these fourteen died because seven idiots got themselves trapped under a rock a thousand kilometres away."
"Yes."
Leon found the shard because he was the only person in the building who could.
He had been examining the workshop’s folded storage and spatial seams when he sensed something humming beneath the main control table, displaced two inches outside ordinary space.
"Ira. Lift this."
The table came up. There was nothing under it. Leon reached into the offset and brought out a formation-memory crystal the size of a thumb joint, cracked along one face and very warm.
"They destroyed the visible recorder," he said. "This backup sits inside a displaced pocket. Nobody without spatial perception would find it."
Vyra took it in both hands. "How much is left?"
"Not much. It’s badly damaged."
The projection came up crooked, silent for the first four seconds, and then found sound.

Five masked figures stood in the entry hall while the workshop’s inner wards admitted them without resistance. The second wore a small logistical seal on one shoulder, the kind courier networks used to authorise movement.
Qingyue made a sound.
"I know that," she said. "That’s from the Moonfall side of the Qiao network. We pulled two of them off couriers after the Shen attack and nobody could prove what they authorised."
The recording jumped. When it came back the masked leader was speaking to somebody offscreen, in the tone of a man reading an instruction.

—the field team has failed to report for the third window. That closes it. The site is erased under the standing contingency, the finished stock moves tonight, and the last four months of paper goes with me.
Another voice, further away:All of them?
Everyone who can name a buyer. That’s the contingency. I didn’t write it.A pause.The Steward wants no thread left in this city that leads back to Ninefold Ridge.
Vyra’s stylus stopped moving.
Who’s carrying the delivery?the second voice asked.

Not your business. It’s diverted — it isn’t coming here and it isn’t going to the ridge.The leader’s mask turned toward the recorder for a moment, and then away.White Reed Crossing. Seventh night. On the Hollow Steward’s authority, and if you repeat that name outside this room you’ll be on the floor with these people.
The projection froze on the five masked figures and collapsed into static.
Nobody said anything for a while.
"Qiao," Leon said at last. "Confirmed."

Leon had suspected the Qiao clan when he first recognised the matching craftsmanship beneath Ashen Rain Basin, but he had refused to put the suspicion into his report. At the time, he could not support it. Now he could.

"It confirms the workshop supplied them," he said carefully, because getting it right mattered. "Their own courier seal, their own name, in their own cleanup. It does not tell us who the Hollow Steward is. That could be a Qiao elder. It could be a specialist they hire. It could be somebody the Qiao clan answers to, and I’d like that possibility written down."
"Noted," said Vyra, writing it down.
Qingyue had not moved from the middle of the floor.

"They killed fourteen of their own suppliers," she said. "Not enemies. People who made their tools and took their money for eleven years." Her voice stayed even, which Leon had learned was how it went when she was furious. "I spent two months telling myself the Shen attack was one clan overreaching for one treasure. It wasn’t. It was a network doing something it has procedures for."
"White Reed Crossing," said Seraphine. "Where is it?"
"Four days from here on the eastern road. It’s a river ford with a customs post." Qingyue’s eyes came up. "Seventh night is six days away."
Leon did the arithmetic, and did not like that either.

Eleven days back to the Palace. Six days to the crossing. He could send a report by plaque within the hour, but a plaque carried words, not authority, and Ji had told him with considerable precision what he was and was not permitted to do.
Report and lose it, or follow it and exceed her.

"Vyra, preserve that shard — sealed case, and I want a second record made before we move it. Seraphine, sweep four streets out and make certain nobody is watching this building." He was already composing it in his head. "Loriel, I need cause of death and time for all fourteen in a form an elder will accept. I’m sending the Palace Mistress everything we have inside the hour."
He looked back at the cracked crystal in Vyra’s hands.
The damaged projection had begun to repeat, the way damaged records did, cycling through the last fragment it could still hold.
White Reed Crossing. Seventh night. On the Hollow Steward’s authority.
