And the killers’ residue is nothing like these people’s — cleaner, colder, and there were five of them at least."
Qingyue had been standing in the middle of the workshop floor with her arms folded for several minutes.
"Ten hours," she said.
"We began asking questions in this ward yesterday afternoon.
Someone could have heard and reacted overnight, but there’s a simpler explanation here." She turned.
"Vyra.
What triggered it?"
"I’m getting there."
She got there twenty minutes later, out of a wastebasket.
"Payment fragments, Young Master." She laid six burnt scraps on a bench.
"They burned the ledger and missed the bin.
This one is part of a standing-order instruction."
Leon read it over her shoulder.
Half a line survived:...if no contact by the—
"There’s a check-in protocol," Vyra said.
"A scheduled window.
If a field team misses it, this workshop burns.
Nobody was betrayed.
Seven people stopped reporting and a rule engaged."
"Seven people," said Qingyue.
"The ones Ji killed had been out of contact since before the surveyors vanished," Leon said.
"Three missed windows.
The delay was built into the protocol.
Once the third passed, the contingency triggered exactly as designed."
Ira looked around the room.
"So these fourteen died because seven idiots got themselves trapped under a rock a thousand kilometres away."
"Yes."
Leon found the shard because he was the only person in the building who could.
He had been examining the workshop’s folded storage and spatial seams when he sensed something humming beneath the main control table, displaced two inches outside ordinary space.
"Ira.
Lift this."
The table came up.
There was nothing under it.
Leon reached into the offset and brought out a formation-memory crystal the size of a thumb joint, cracked along one face and very warm.
"They destroyed the visible recorder," he said.
"This backup sits inside a displaced pocket.
Nobody without spatial perception would find it."
Vyra took it in both hands.
"How much is left?"
"Not much.
It’s badly damaged."
The projection came up crooked, silent for the first four seconds, and then found sound.
Five masked figures stood in the entry hall while the workshop’s inner wards admitted them without resistance.
The second wore a small logistical seal on one shoulder, the kind courier networks used to authorise movement.
Qingyue made a sound.
"I know that," she said.
"That’s from the Moonfall side of the Qiao network.
We pulled two of them off couriers after the Shen attack and nobody could prove what they authorised."
The recording jumped.
When it came back the masked leader was speaking to somebody offscreen, in the tone of a man reading an instruction.
—the field team has failed to report for the third window.
That closes it.
The site is erased under the standing contingency, the finished stock moves tonight, and the last four months of paper goes with me.
Another voice, further away:All of them?
Everyone who can name a buyer.
That’s the contingency.
I didn’t write it.A pause.The Steward wants no thread left in this city that leads back to Ninefold Ridge.
Vyra’s stylus stopped moving.
Who’s carrying the delivery?the second voice asked.
Not your business.
It’s diverted — it isn’t coming here and it isn’t going to the ridge.The leader’s mask turned toward the recorder for a moment, and then away.White Reed Crossing.
Seventh night.
On the Hollow Steward’s authority, and if you repeat that name outside this room you’ll be on the floor with these people.
The projection froze on the five masked figures and collapsed into static.
Nobody said anything for a while.
"Qiao," Leon said at last.
"Confirmed."
Leon had suspected the Qiao clan when he first recognised the matching craftsmanship beneath Ashen Rain Basin, but he had refused to put the suspicion into his report.
At the time, he could not support it.
Now he could.
"It confirms the workshop supplied them," he said carefully, because getting it right mattered.
"Their own courier seal, their own name, in their own cleanup.
It does not tell us who the Hollow Steward is.
That could be a Qiao elder.
It could be a specialist they hire.
It could be somebody the Qiao clan answers to, and I’d like that possibility written down."
"Noted," said Vyra, writing it down.
Qingyue had not moved from the middle of the floor.
"They killed fourteen of their own suppliers," she said.
"Not enemies.
People who made their tools and took their money for eleven years." Her voice stayed even, which Leon had learned was how it went when she was furious.
"I spent two months telling myself the Shen attack was one clan overreaching for one treasure.
It wasn’t.
It was a network doing something it has procedures for."
"White Reed Crossing," said Seraphine.
"Where is it?"
"Four days from here on the eastern road.
It’s a river ford with a customs post." Qingyue’s eyes came up.
"Seventh night is six days away."
Leon did the arithmetic, and did not like that either.
Eleven days back to the Palace.
Six days to the crossing.
He could send a report by plaque within the hour, but a plaque carried words, not authority, and Ji had told him with considerable precision what he was and was not permitted to do.
Report and lose it, or follow it and exceed her.
"Vyra, preserve that shard — sealed case, and I want a second record made before we move it.
Seraphine, sweep four streets out and make certain nobody is watching this building." He was already composing it in his head.
"Loriel, I need cause of death and time for all fourteen in a form an elder will accept.
I’m sending the Palace Mistress everything we have inside the hour."
He looked back at the cracked crystal in Vyra’s hands.
The damaged projection had begun to repeat, the way damaged records did, cycling through the last fragment it could still hold.
White Reed Crossing.
Seventh night.
On the Hollow Steward’s authority.

chapters.title: Chapter 668: The Seventh Night
paragraphs: The shard was still repeating when Vyra finished the second record.
"Copy’s clean, Young Master. Every frame the original still holds, including the seal on the second man’s shoulder." She secured both crystals in separate cases. "Which one goes to the Palace?"
"Both, once an elder takes custody. Until then, keep them apart."
Seraphine returned from the streets while Vyra was fastening the second clasp. "Nobody watching the building. I checked the surrounding roofs as well."
"Good. Help Loriel when she’s finished."

Loriel came out carrying her notes and a small case of sealed samples. She had recorded a cause of death for each of the fourteen victims, along with the residue left by their killers. At the bottom of the last page, she had drawn the position of a woman’s hand beside an overturned bowl.
Leon glanced at the drawing, then back at her.
"She was eating," Loriel said. "I wanted the person reading it to know."
He left the page where it was.

The report went out within the hour. He described the Qiao seal, the recorded reference to Ninefold Ridge, and the standing contingency that had killed the workshop’s staff. He included the diverted delivery, its location, and the six days remaining before the seventh night.
Then he made his request.
Authorisation to secure the shipment. Qingyue and my household can assist, but I need someone empowered to take custody and deal with any wider response. We do not know who will receive it.
He sent the message and went outside. The tinsmith two doors down was still working.
Ji answered four hours later.
"You followed the evidence properly," she said through the plaque. "Elder Shan will command the interception. He leaves within the hour."
Leon straightened. "He can reach the crossing in time?"
"Well before you. Take the eastern road and meet him there. He will contact you on arrival."
"And our part?"
"Help identify and secure the cargo. Shan will handle the escort and any reinforcements. Once the prisoners and records are in his custody, your assignment is finished."
That last sentence improved Leon’s evening considerably.
"I understand, Master."
"Tell Qingyue the arrangement. Her presence will be useful, if she wishes to continue."
"She will."
"I thought so," Ji said. "Keep the originals safe. I want to see what they tried so hard to remove."
They left at dawn, and the road east took four days.
There were two waystations, a ferry, and an inn where Ira lost a handful of silver at dice to a horse trader. She spent breakfast explaining why she would have won if he had stayed for another game.
"He stayed for six," Vyra reminded her.
"That was before I understood him."
Leon slid the last steamed bun onto Ira’s plate before she could propose following the man.
On the third evening, Qingyue found him outside the waystation, looking over the road map Shan had sent.
"Will you return straight to the Palace afterward?" she asked.
"Through Moonfall. I’d like to see the Shens before we leave."
"So would I." She rested her arms on the railing beside him. "Three raiders dead, their leader and observer still sealed, and the family still has to wonder who else is watching their gates."
"The prisoners gave us the Qiao name."
"They did. But the clan can deny a prisoner. I want the records of the person who ordered the tool. Something they can’t dismiss as a thief trying to save himself."
Leon folded the map.
"They helped me when they had plenty of reasons to turn a stranger away. I’d prefer to leave them with more than another warning."
Qingyue looked down the dark road. "Then let’s bring something back."
White Reed Crossing was a ford, a customs post, and a small collection of warehouses serving the eastern road.

The river ran shallow over pale gravel. Reeds crowded the near bank, with a worn track between them and the buildings. Two officers sat beneath the customs lantern, inspecting an axle while its owner complained about the delay.
Shan met them in a warehouse office wearing a clerk’s brown robe. There was grain dust on one sleeve.
"Tomorrow night," he said, once the door closed. "Nine wagons. The manifest lists refined ore and finished ironwork."
He put a sketch on the desk.
"Four of the wagons were loaded separately in Moonfall. My people followed them out. Those are the ones we secure first."
"Escort?" Leon asked.

"Six hired guards and four cultivators travelling behind them. Two Golden Core, one Nascent Soul, and another concealing his cultivation." Shan tapped the rear of the convoy. "Nothing observed so far should trouble us. The problem is preventing them from destroying what they carry."
Qingyue drew a finger across the ford. "I’ll take the far bank. Anyone trying to leave through the water comes to me."
"Thank you. I’ll contain the rear escort. Leon, wagons four through seven are yours. Take the people riding with them alive. My disciples will secure the ordinary carters and close the road."
Shan moved four small weights onto the sketch.

"We wait until the wagons reach the approach and the rear escort falls behind. That gives us space to act on both groups at once. If anyone looks ready to burn a case, don’t wait for a second signal."
Leon studied the marked positions, then passed the sketch to Seraphine.
The convoy arrived an hour after full dark.
Leon watched from the reeds as the first wagon rolled down toward the ford. Its wheels sank into the softer ground beside the approach, and the driver called back for the others to slow.
The four cultivators remained behind the last wagon, watching the road they had come down. One turned his horse to look toward the warehouses.
Shan stepped out before the man completed the turn.

Pressure closed around the rear escort. A blade came halfway free of its sheath and stopped. The concealed cultivator threw himself sideways, shedding his disguise in a burst of dense qi, but Shan caught him with the others before his feet touched the ground.
Leon was already moving.

Seraphine reached the front of wagon four first. A guard swung at her from horseback. She turned his sword with hers, struck him across the jaw with the hilt, and pulled him clear of the animal as he fell.
On the opposite side, Ira drove three guards away from the cargo. Her lance struck gravel between their feet, throwing up a line of heat that sent them stumbling into open ground.
"Stay there," she told them, and one dropped his weapon immediately.
Vyra climbed onto wagon five as its driver reached under his seat. She caught his wrist, removed a striker from his fingers, and pressed him facedown against the boards.
A narrow curtain of flame rose around the outside of the cargo bed, held clear of the covered cases.
"Wagon five is secure!"

Loriel guided a frightened young driver out of the roadway before his panicking horse could drag him beneath a wheel. She sent him toward the customs post, where Palace disciples were gathering the carters, then crouched beside Seraphine’s unconscious guard to check his breathing.
Across the water, Qingyue stopped a man running along the shallows. He saw her waiting and tried to turn back. The water rose around his knees and held him where he stood.
Most of the convoy surrendered within moments.
The courier in wagon seven did not.
He slipped over the far side carrying a sealed case, using the wagon to hide him from the road. Leon caught the movement through the gap beneath the cargo bed and followed.
The man went onto the open gravel. His free hand closed around a talisman.
Space stirred around his boots.
Leon sensed the transfer forming before its light appeared. The talisman was fixing its departure point, gathering the connection it needed to carry both the man and his case away.
He could reach the courier. Striking him would be easy. But the talisman was already active, and the man’s arm was clamped around the case’s fragile seal.
Stop the passage first.
Leon reached past the courier and caught the forming spatial connection.

chapters.title: Chapter 669: The Debt Brought Home
paragraphs: The talisman needed a stable departure point.
Leon gave it two.

He displaced a narrow strip of space beneath the courier’s boots, just enough to split the location the transfer was trying to fix. The talisman attempted to settle its connection, failed, and began drawing more energy from the man holding it.
The courier looked down.
Leon was beside him before he could make another choice. He caught the man’s wrist, cut off the flow feeding the talisman, and took the case from under his arm.
The transfer collapsed with a sharp crack.
Ice bound the courier’s hands before he hit the gravel. Leon lowered the case onto the wagon step and inspected its seals. One had bent beneath the man’s grip, but it remained intact.
Good.
Behind him, someone dropped a spear.
"On your knees," Ira said. "Hands where I can see them."

Twenty-three people were held for questioning by the time Shan’s disciples finished searching the wagons. The ordinary carters were seated near the customs post, separated from the guards and the convoy’s clerks.
Nobody had died.

Shan’s four prisoners knelt under suppression beside the warehouse. The concealed cultivator had proved to be a Nascent Soul body cultivator. His attempt to break free had accomplished nothing beyond tearing his own outer robe.
"Your case?" Shan asked Leon.
"Still sealed."
"Open it with the others."
They spread a tarpaulin over the gravel. Vyra and Qingyue began with the cargo from wagons four through seven.
Forty-one formation-breaking implements lay in fitted cases. Alongside them were three strongboxes of workshop records, including recent commission books and payment ledgers.
Vyra checked the dates before looking up.
"The four-month period from the recording. There are gaps, but enough survived."

The courier’s case held different papers: delivery acknowledgements, payment authorisations, and a seal used to approve commissions. A narrow register recorded who had signed the documents and which consignments they accompanied.
Qingyue found the Shen entry in a workshop book.
"Here. Silent entry through an active estate ward." She drew the lamp closer. "The same four-layer structure. Same dimensions, same vulnerable junction."
Leon leaned over her shoulder. The specification included the delay the ward-breaker required before suppressing the inner alarm. He remembered watching the raiders exploit it.
"That’s their wall," he said.
Vyra opened the payment ledger beside it. "And here’s the money."
The commission had been paid several weeks before the raid. Its authorisation mark appeared again in the courier’s register, linked to a named receiving clerk travelling with the convoy.
Shan sent a disciple to fetch him.
The man they brought was middle-aged, soft-handed, and thoroughly frightened. He had remained on a wagon step throughout the seizure, presenting himself as an ordinary accounts clerk.
"That seal is yours?" Shan asked.
The man looked at the papers on the ground.
"It belongs to the office."
"Were you authorised to use it?"
"Yes, Elder."
"And this signature?"
The clerk swallowed. "Mine."
Shan laid the Shen commission beside the acknowledgement bearing that signature.
"Then begin there."
His account matched the records.

He had received the requirement, commissioned the ward-breaker, approved the payment, and arranged delivery to the raid’s intermediaries. He had never entered the Shen estate or fought the men who defended it. He had handled the preparations from a desk.
He tried to describe each act as an ordinary part of his employment. That became harder when Shan asked him to read the target address aloud.
Leon listened until the clerk began discussing other commissions. Then he stepped away to let the elder finish.
Qingyue stood near the lantern, still holding the workshop book.
"The order is between a granary repair and a purchase of formation flags," she said. "I keep looking at that."
Leon could see the three entries from where he stood. Similar amounts of space had been given to each.
"We have the person who arranged it," he said. "And the records to support the prisoners’ accounts."
"Yes." Qingyue closed the book carefully. "I would like to be there when the Palace asks him who gave him the requirement."
"So would I. But Shan can do that."
She looked toward the clerk, then back at Leon.
"Shan can," she agreed.
By dawn, the prisoners and seized goods were under Palace seal. The carters whose identities had been verified were released after giving their accounts. The others remained with Shan’s disciples.
Vyra received certified copies of the records concerning the Shen estate and a receipt for the evidence they had handed over.

"The courier meant to take the authorisations out of our reach," Shan told Leon. "Without them, that clerk could have claimed to be copying someone else’s instructions. Preserving the case saved us considerable work."
"Will you need us back?"
"If I have questions, I’ll send them. The network is my assignment now, including this Hollow Steward." Shan glanced toward the prisoners. "You have given us enough to begin."
He clasped Leon’s forearm before returning to his disciples.
For the first time since they had entered the workshop, Leon had no next location to search.
Four days later, they returned to Moonfall.
Shen Baoyuan sat down halfway through the account, both hands resting on the table. Qingyue had placed the certified records in front of him. He had read the target address twice.
"The man who arranged it?" he asked.
"In Palace custody," she confirmed. "With the supporting books and authorisations."
Baoyuan drew a slow breath. "We kept discussing whether to move the grandchildren. Every time a messenger came late, I thought..." He stopped and pressed his lips together. "You’ll excuse me."
Shen Yuanhe continued reading. When he reached the payment entry, he asked two questions about its authentication and a third about the courier’s register.
Then he set the papers down.
"Our two prisoners’ accounts should be sent to Elder Shan. Proper copies, with their original seals."
"I’ll arrange it," Yanning said.
The ancestor nodded. "Good. He should have the whole case."

They discussed the practical arrangements briefly. Nobody promised that the Qiao clan had become harmless. But the Shens would no longer be trying to force a hearing with only their own influence behind them.
Nothing about the sealed discovery at Ashen Rain entered the conversation.
Yanning had dinner brought into the family court, and by the time the lamps were lit, Baoyuan was asking whether the fish had been cooked the way Leon remembered it.
It had. Ira confirmed that loudly enough for the kitchen to hear.
Later, Yanning found Leon beneath the courtyard roof.
"How long are you staying?" she asked.
"Two days. Then back to the Palace."
"Good. I can have the rest of your purchases packed by then." She leaned against a pillar. "We’ve reopened the Baihe warehouses."
"You mentioned moving vulnerable stock last time."

"We did. Now we’re moving some back." Yanning watched a servant carry an empty dish toward the kitchen. "The first shipment made me so nervous I checked the guards myself. Father pretended he hadn’t already done it."
Leon smiled. He could imagine both inspections.
"Was there trouble?"
"A broken wheel. I was almost grateful."
She laughed, and for a moment he remembered the young woman who had helped a stranger negotiate his way through Moonfall’s markets. She looked less tired tonight.
"Thank you for coming back," she said.
"Your family made it easy to want to."
Yanning lowered her gaze briefly, then pushed away from the pillar.
"Come inside. Ira’s asking whether anyone else wants the fish, which means she’s already reaching for it."

Two mornings later, the Shens saw them off from the gate. Baoyuan insisted on provisions for the journey. Yuanhe entrusted Qingyue with the sealed accounts of the old prisoners, and Yanning checked the labels on Loriel’s living stock one final time.
Leon looked back as their cart turned into the street.
Yanning raised a hand. He returned the gesture, then settled beside Vyra for the road home.

He had remained on a wagon step throughout the seizure, presenting himself as an ordinary accounts clerk.
"That seal is yours?" Shan asked.
The man looked at the papers on the ground.
"It belongs to the office."
"Were you authorised to use it?"
"Yes, Elder."
"And this signature?"
The clerk swallowed.
"Mine."
Shan laid the Shen commission beside the acknowledgement bearing that signature.
"Then begin there."
His account matched the records.
He had received the requirement, commissioned the ward-breaker, approved the payment, and arranged delivery to the raid’s intermediaries.
He had never entered the Shen estate or fought the men who defended it.
He had handled the preparations from a desk.
He tried to describe each act as an ordinary part of his employment.
That became harder when Shan asked him to read the target address aloud.
Leon listened until the clerk began discussing other commissions.
Then he stepped away to let the elder finish.
Qingyue stood near the lantern, still holding the workshop book.
"The order is between a granary repair and a purchase of formation flags," she said.
"I keep looking at that."
Leon could see the three entries from where he stood.
Similar amounts of space had been given to each.
"We have the person who arranged it," he said.
"And the records to support the prisoners’ accounts."
"Yes." Qingyue closed the book carefully.
"I would like to be there when the Palace asks him who gave him the requirement."
"So would I.
But Shan can do that."
She looked toward the clerk, then back at Leon.
"Shan can," she agreed.
By dawn, the prisoners and seized goods were under Palace seal.
The carters whose identities had been verified were released after giving their accounts.
The others remained with Shan’s disciples.
Vyra received certified copies of the records concerning the Shen estate and a receipt for the evidence they had handed over.
"The courier meant to take the authorisations out of our reach," Shan told Leon.
"Without them, that clerk could have claimed to be copying someone else’s instructions.
Preserving the case saved us considerable work."
"Will you need us back?"
"If I have questions, I’ll send them.
The network is my assignment now, including this Hollow Steward." Shan glanced toward the prisoners.
"You have given us enough to begin."
He clasped Leon’s forearm before returning to his disciples.
For the first time since they had entered the workshop, Leon had no next location to search.
Four days later, they returned to Moonfall.
Shen Baoyuan sat down halfway through the account, both hands resting on the table.
Qingyue had placed the certified records in front of him.
He had read the target address twice.
"The man who arranged it?" he asked.
"In Palace custody," she confirmed.
"With the supporting books and authorisations."
Baoyuan drew a slow breath.
"We kept discussing whether to move the grandchildren.
Every time a messenger came late, I thought..." He stopped and pressed his lips together.
"You’ll excuse me."
Shen Yuanhe continued reading.
When he reached the payment entry, he asked two questions about its authentication and a third about the courier’s register.
Then he set the papers down.
"Our two prisoners’ accounts should be sent to Elder Shan.
Proper copies, with their original seals."
"I’ll arrange it," Yanning said.
The ancestor nodded.
"Good.
He should have the whole case."
They discussed the practical arrangements briefly.
Nobody promised that the Qiao clan had become harmless.
But the Shens would no longer be trying to force a hearing with only their own influence behind them.
Nothing about the sealed discovery at Ashen Rain entered the conversation.
Yanning had dinner brought into the family court, and by the time the lamps were lit, Baoyuan was asking whether the fish had been cooked the way Leon remembered it.
It had.
Ira confirmed that loudly enough for the kitchen to hear.
Later, Yanning found Leon beneath the courtyard roof.
"How long are you staying?" she asked.
"Two days.
Then back to the Palace."
"Good.
I can have the rest of your purchases packed by then." She leaned against a pillar.
"We’ve reopened the Baihe warehouses."
"You mentioned moving vulnerable stock last time."
"We did.
Now we’re moving some back." Yanning watched a servant carry an empty dish toward the kitchen.
"The first shipment made me so nervous I checked the guards myself.
Father pretended he hadn’t already done it."
Leon smiled.
He could imagine both inspections.
"Was there trouble?"
"A broken wheel.
I was almost grateful."
She laughed, and for a moment he remembered the young woman who had helped a stranger negotiate his way through Moonfall’s markets.
She looked less tired tonight.
"Thank you for coming back," she said.
"Your family made it easy to want to."
Yanning lowered her gaze briefly, then pushed away from the pillar.
"Come inside.
Ira’s asking whether anyone else wants the fish, which means she’s already reaching for it."
Two mornings later, the Shens saw them off from the gate.
Baoyuan insisted on provisions for the journey.
Yuanhe entrusted Qingyue with the sealed accounts of the old prisoners, and Yanning checked the labels on Loriel’s living stock one final time.
Leon looked back as their cart turned into the street.
Yanning raised a hand.
He returned the gesture, then settled beside Vyra for the road home.

chapters.title: Chapter 670: What a Master Notices
paragraphs: The journey back took eleven days.

Leon checked his cultivation on the safe nights. Early Qi Refinement remained stable, but the dark cores offered the same difficulty as before. He could recover small amounts of energy from them. He could not make that irregular trickle support the circulation he needed for another attempt.
The Moonfall purchases gave him cleaner supplements. What he needed now was a better way to use the resources already in his hands.
Ji received him three days after their return.
"Shan has the two prisoners’ accounts from the Shen estate," she said. "They agree with the records you recovered."
"Then he has enough?"

"To proceed. He will handle the rest." She placed a requisition slip on the table. "Your reward has been approved. Purchasing credit and one cultivation treasure from the second vault. The four women receive separate material allocations."
Leon picked up the slip. The credit would cover the supplementary stock on his revised list, with room for the array supplies he had been considering.
"And the advance against our expedition share?"
"Remains an advance. This is earned payment for completed work."
"Vyra will be pleased."
"I expect you will all find a use for it." Ji leaned back. "Have you decided what treasure to request?"
"Not yet. I’d like your advice first."
She listened while he described the problem.
He kept the origin of the seven cores private. Ji needed to know how the material behaved, not where he had obtained it.
"It’s heavily drained," he said. "There is valuable residue left, but extracting it gives me an uneven supply. Then I have to remove the original imprint before I can use any of it."
"And you do that while cultivating?"

"I’ve had to. If the supply changes, I need to adjust it without disturbing the nine branches. During the first session I kept losing progress because I couldn’t give both tasks the attention they needed."
Ji rested a finger against the requisition slip.
"How much can you extract without cultivating at all?"
"Slowly? Enough to be worth doing."
"Then come with me."

The second vault contained weapons, sealed medicines, and objects Leon could not identify even after reading their labels. Ji led him to a wooden case holding a broad intake plate, a grey reservoir, and two control assemblies.
"A regulated cultivation array," she said. "You’ve probably seen diagrams of the smaller ones."
"I have. I wasn’t sure they could hold energy this dense without losing most of it."

"Most couldn’t." She indicated the fine inscription inside the reservoir’s rim. "This one was made for sustained work with high-grade materials. It retains the prepared charge and keeps the release steady as the reservoir empties. The tolerances are what you’re paying for."
Leon bent closer. The inscriptions continued beneath a transparent inner lining, packed more tightly than his eye first suggested.
Ji placed a clean spirit stone on the intake plate and opened its valve. A thin current entered the vessel. She let it run, then closed the valve and removed the stone.
The stored charge remained.
"Your supply doesn’t have to arrive while you’re using it," she said. "Prepare enough first."
She turned the release ring. A steady current emerged from the outlet, unchanged as she moved the now-empty intake plate aside.
Leon watched it for several breaths.
I could spend a week just extracting.

He could give the purification his full attention, accumulate the cleaned energy, and begin the circulation afterward. The residue would still take effort to recover. It simply would not need to support every task simultaneously.
"For your material, keep the inlet under your control," Ji continued. "This array regulates energy. It does not remove a dead cultivator’s imprint."
"I clean each portion before storing it."
"Yes. Then close the extraction line when you begin cultivation. Work from what you’ve prepared."
She handed him the release control.
"Start low. Find what your routes accept before increasing it. Change the feed setting separately from the circulation, or you won’t know which adjustment caused a problem."
Leon tried the second setting, then the third. The difference was small enough to feel useful.
"How long will the charge keep?" he asked.
"Long enough for this work, provided you maintain the seals. The operating materials are listed in the case."
He turned the ring back and shut the outlet.
"I want this one."
Ji wrote her approval on the slip. "Good. Bring me the result when you’ve used it."
The women spent most of the next day making their own selections.

Seraphine chose a naturally charged storm-heart shard and conductive plates for testing its light and lightning. Ira found a slab of ember-iron whose internal channels could withstand repeated exposure to her flame.
"The quartermaster thought I wanted it forged into a spearhead," she told Leon. "He started explaining how much that would cost."
"What do you want it for?"
"To train against something I won’t keep melting." She patted the wrapped slab. "Then we’ll discuss the spearhead."

Vyra selected slow-burning fire cores and replacement components for the formations she had been improvising since Ashen Rain. Loriel returned with three moonvine cuttings, a jade-root seedling, and a small jar held carefully in both hands.
Leon looked inside. A curled green shoot turned toward him.
"Coilvine," Loriel said. "It follows warmth. The nursery keeper let me have a cutting."
"Will it survive beside your other plants?"
"If Ira leaves it alone."
"I haven’t touched it," Ira said from the doorway.
Loriel carried it past her. "That’s why it still has leaves."
They celebrated that evening with the residence sealed and far too much food on the table.

Ira had arranged the meal without consulting anyone. There was river fish, a pot of fragrant soup, and dumplings arriving in quantities that suggested she had misunderstood how many people lived there.
"Did you order for tomorrow as well?" Leon asked.
"I ordered until the cook stopped looking worried."
Vyra inspected the spread. "You paid in advance?"
"Of course."
"That explains it."
Leon laughed and drew Ira down beside him before she could go back to the kitchen. He took her hand under the table, rubbing his thumb over the callus at the base of her fingers.
"You did well at the crossing," he said quietly.
Her expression softened. "The guards weren’t much."
"The cargo survived you. That’s what impressed everyone."
She pinched his hand, then leaned against him while reaching for a dumpling.

Across the table, Seraphine was telling Loriel how she intended to test the shard. Vyra listened until the conversation reached the likelihood of ruined equipment, then began asking what was replaceable.
Leon took the ledger she had brought and set it on the empty chair behind him.
"After dinner."
"I was only checking—"
"After dinner," he repeated, and placed a piece of fish in her bowl.
Vyra considered arguing. Instead, she picked up her chopsticks.
Loriel’s jar sat beside the tea. Its shoot turned when Ira reached across the table, following the warmth of her wrist.
Ira stopped.
"Why is it doing that?"
"It likes you," Leon said.
"It wants the heat," Loriel corrected, pleased. "Hold still."
"I am trying to eat."
Seraphine moved the jar closer. Ira watched the shoot uncoil, suspicious until its small leaf brushed her knuckle.
"Oh," she said.
Loriel smiled. "See?"

A little later, Leon found himself with Ira leaning against one side and Loriel tucked against the other, explaining where she would plant the moonvine. He listened, asked about the soil, and kissed her forehead when she finished.
The array case stood beside the wall. The new supplies were packed and ready. For once, he did not feel the need to get up and use them immediately.
He stayed until the tea went cold.

chapters.title: Chapter 671: What Remained in the Cores
paragraphs: Xyra made the field the following afternoon.
"Eastern flat," she said. "A thousand to one, as before."
The boundary appeared across the grass. She glanced at the wooden case under Leon’s arm.
"Something useful?"
"I think so. My master helped me choose it."
Xyra bent over the reservoir when he opened the lid, studying the inner inscription.
"Carefully made," she said. "Whoever cut that lining had patient hands."
"I’m hoping it means I can be a little less patient."
She smiled at him. "Let me know how that goes."

Leon placed the equipment, supplies, and all seven cores inside the field. He checked the timing against the rhythm he had established during his earlier session, remembering Xyra’s warning. Then he separated the extraction line from the reservoir and began.
The cores were dark and heavily drained. Their remaining energy had been valuable all along; recovering it in a usable form was the work ahead of him.
He set the first on the intake plate and opened the valve only a little.

A thin current emerged. He caught it before it reached the storage inlet, drew it through his established purification route, and examined it for the dead cultivator’s imprint. Only when it was clean did he let it enter the reservoir.
The next portion came more thickly. He reduced the intake and took his time.
Nothing in his cultivation depended on finishing that portion quickly.
By the end of the first subjective week, he had filled roughly a fifth of the vessel. He had also learned how easily his attention wandered when the work went well.
Twice, he closed the storage inlet because he had caught himself thinking about something else. A trace of foreign rhythm remained in the energy waiting between his hands.
That would have gone straight into the batch.
He cleaned it again before proceeding.
Three cores were genuinely spent by the end of the fourth week.

Leon set them apart from the others. There was satisfaction in knowing he had recovered something useful from material his previous method could no longer use, but he did not mistake that for an endless supply.

The reservoir was two-thirds full. He continued with a fourth core and supplemented the prepared energy with the clean stock from Moonfall. The materials suited to his individual affinities remained arranged beside him for the next stage of work.
Vyra came in while he was changing a seal on the reservoir.
"How much have you lost to the array?" she asked.
"Less than I expected. Most of the cost has been preparing the energy."
She examined the three spent cores without picking them up.
"And those?"
"Finished."
Vyra wrote that down. "I’ll move them to the separate case. Otherwise you’ll spend half a day checking them again before you admit it."
Leon handed her the case. He had been considering exactly that.
By the end of the sixth week, he had the supply he needed. He checked its purity, closed the storage seals, and physically disconnected the extraction line.
The remaining cores went back into their case.
Testing took another two subjective weeks.

At the second setting, his routes accepted the feed comfortably. The third remained stable through increasingly complete circulations. At the fourth, the Earth branch accumulated warmth during a rapid transition, and Leon stopped to examine it.
There was no contamination. The prepared energy was clean, and the idle circulation settled correctly. He returned to the third setting and recorded the response for Ji.

He also practised cutting off the release without disturbing what was already circulating. The reservoir held its remaining charge when he closed the outlet, allowing him to pause, inspect, and resume without chasing an unstable source.
At the end of the eighth week, he began cultivating the Mid layer.
The first full circulation took most of his attention. He widened the developing routes, guided the returning branches, and checked the new structure beneath his old core.
Beside him, the array fed at the rate he had chosen.
The extraction plate sat empty.
For several hours he worked without once having to turn away from his own channels. When he finally paused, he looked at the disconnected plate and laughed under his breath.
I should have asked her sooner.
The next six weeks still demanded work.

His first arrangement carried energy smoothly while idle, then distributed it poorly when he changed affinities. Leon dismantled the unsettled extension and rebuilt the widths according to what each branch actually carried.

The second problem appeared at the return junction. It was small enough that he noticed it through accumulated warmth rather than an obvious interruption. He stopped the feed, allowed the current to settle, and revised the junction before continuing.
Neither correction required him to throw away the stored supply or rebuild his established Early layer. He could work on the mistake itself.
Seraphine joined him in the tenth week, carrying her shard and two of the conductive plates.
She sat nearby and spent an afternoon drawing lightning along a chosen fault in the crystal. The first plate blackened at one edge. The second remained intact.
"That was different," Leon said when she lowered it.
"The return was cleaner." Seraphine turned her wrist, checking the sensation. "I’ve been losing a little there. I can feel where now."
She tried again. A narrow light ran down the plate, followed by lightning that left no scorch behind.
Leon smiled. "There."
Seraphine nodded, pleased, and repeated it before the feeling faded.

Ira brought the ember-iron into the field the next day. Her first strikes heated its surface unevenly. By the end of her practice, she could drive a controlled pulse through the lance and into the slab without the rebound climbing her arm.
She made Leon watch the final attempt.
"Again?" he asked.
"Of course again. The first one could have been luck."

Vyra tested a sustained flame around one of her new components, adjusting it until the heat held evenly around the entire ring. Loriel visited with news that the jade-root had accepted its new soil, then demonstrated the gentler life-force circulation she was using to encourage its finer roots.
All four remained at Peak Foundation Establishment. The progress was in what their foundations could carry and how reliably they could use it.
Leon liked seeing them pleased with their work. It made him eager to return to his own.
The Mid layer stabilised at the end of the fourteenth subjective week.

Leon let the nine branches complete another circulation, then another. The returns remained balanced. There was no foreign imprint, no drifting junction, and no pressure against the old foundation above the new layer.
He reduced the feed and tested the circulation again.
[Cultivation: Mid Qi Refinement]
[Formless Myriad Scripture — Stage One, Mid Layer: Consolidated]
[Nine-Affinity Balance: Stable]
For a while, he simply sat with the result.

Four of the seven cores were now fully spent. The other three retained energy he had not yet recovered, and the reservoir still held the remainder of his prepared charge. He sealed both carefully before standing.

Outside assessments would continue to find his old core and read Peak Golden Core. What he had built beneath it was his own progress along the native path, and he could feel the difference when he moved energy through it.
He crossed the boundary a little over two hours and twenty minutes after entering.
Xyra was sitting on the courtyard wall.
"Well?" she asked.
"Mid Qi Refinement."
She looked at the case in his hand. "Useful, then."
"Very."
Leon set the equipment down before he was tempted to begin planning the next session. He wanted a meal, some sleep, and a chance to see what the improved circulation would do in a fight.
For the moment, that was enough.

He stopped the feed, allowed the current to settle, and revised the junction before continuing.
Neither correction required him to throw away the stored supply or rebuild his established Early layer.
He could work on the mistake itself.
Seraphine joined him in the tenth week, carrying her shard and two of the conductive plates.
She sat nearby and spent an afternoon drawing lightning along a chosen fault in the crystal.
The first plate blackened at one edge.
The second remained intact.
"That was different," Leon said when she lowered it.
"The return was cleaner." Seraphine turned her wrist, checking the sensation.
"I’ve been losing a little there.
I can feel where now."
She tried again.
A narrow light ran down the plate, followed by lightning that left no scorch behind.
Leon smiled.
"There."
Seraphine nodded, pleased, and repeated it before the feeling faded.
Ira brought the ember-iron into the field the next day.
Her first strikes heated its surface unevenly.
By the end of her practice, she could drive a controlled pulse through the lance and into the slab without the rebound climbing her arm.
She made Leon watch the final attempt.
"Again?" he asked.
"Of course again.
The first one could have been luck."
Vyra tested a sustained flame around one of her new components, adjusting it until the heat held evenly around the entire ring.
Loriel visited with news that the jade-root had accepted its new soil, then demonstrated the gentler life-force circulation she was using to encourage its finer roots.
All four remained at Peak Foundation Establishment.
The progress was in what their foundations could carry and how reliably they could use it.
Leon liked seeing them pleased with their work.
It made him eager to return to his own.
The Mid layer stabilised at the end of the fourteenth subjective week.
Leon let the nine branches complete another circulation, then another.
The returns remained balanced.
There was no foreign imprint, no drifting junction, and no pressure against the old foundation above the new layer.
He reduced the feed and tested the circulation again.
[Cultivation: Mid Qi Refinement]
[Formless Myriad Scripture — Stage One, Mid Layer: Consolidated]
[Nine-Affinity Balance: Stable]
For a while, he simply sat with the result.
Four of the seven cores were now fully spent.
The other three retained energy he had not yet recovered, and the reservoir still held the remainder of his prepared charge.
He sealed both carefully before standing.
Outside assessments would continue to find his old core and read Peak Golden Core.
What he had built beneath it was his own progress along the native path, and he could feel the difference when he moved energy through it.
He crossed the boundary a little over two hours and twenty minutes after entering.
Xyra was sitting on the courtyard wall.
"Well?" she asked.
"Mid Qi Refinement."
She looked at the case in his hand.
"Useful, then."
"Very."
Leon set the equipment down before he was tempted to begin planning the next session.
He wanted a meal, some sleep, and a chance to see what the improved circulation would do in a fight.
For the moment, that was enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 672: The Opening She Expected
paragraphs: Ji gave him three days to rest before calling him to a practice chamber.
"Report first," she said. "Then show me."
"Fourteen subjective weeks in all. Six preparing the supply, two testing the feed, and six cultivating. I corrected the developing layer twice before it stabilised."
"And the stored energy?"
"Clean throughout. I disconnected the extraction line before beginning. The array only fed what I’d already prepared."
"Good." Ji moved to the centre of the chamber. "What did you notice during testing?"
"Heat in the Earth branch when I raised the feed and changed affinity quickly. It settled when I slowed down. I recorded the setting and the transition."
"Then we’ll look at that as well."

Leon left his outer robe on the bench. There was no audience, no elder waiting to judge his performance, and no rival with something to prove. Somehow, that made him more conscious of wanting to do well.
Ji stood with her hands loose at her sides.
"Begin."
Her first attack was a narrow line of pressure aimed at his shoulder.
Leon raised ice to meet it. The barrier split, and he moved behind the falling fragments before the pressure reached him.
A second strike came low. He turned it aside with a sloping sheet of ice and sent lightning toward Ji’s wrist. She dispersed it with a small movement of her hand.
"Again," she said.
He had expected to be outmatched. It was still irritating how little she needed to do.
For the next few exchanges, she let him choose the response. Whenever he repeated something out of convenience, she pressed the weakness in it until he changed.
Then she began setting the sequence.
"Ice. Hold it."
He built a barrier and maintained it against her pressure.
"Lightning."
Leon let the ice fall and sent the next current through the neutral centre. Lightning gathered along his hand before the last fragments struck the floor.
Ji’s answering pressure passed across his sleeve. It had been aimed at the short interval between his techniques, but his second attack was already complete.
She stopped.
"Repeat it."
He did. Ji used the same pressure and the same timing, watching the exchange rather than trying to defeat it. The lightning formed before her interruption arrived.
On the third attempt, she adjusted.
Her pressure caught his wrist during the transition and turned his attack into the floor beside him. Leon stepped to recover, and a second touch behind his knee put him down.
He lay there for a moment, looking at the ceiling.
There she is.
"Up," Ji said. "Do you know what changed?"
"The gap is smaller."
"Yes. Again, and pay attention to the return."
By the time she let him stop, Leon could feel the difference clearly.

The Early layer had already reduced the loss when he switched affinities. Mid Qi Refinement carried the change more smoothly through the whole circulation. He spent less effort clearing one current before directing the next, and the returning energy settled sooner.
Ji sat on the low bench while he worked the stiffness out of his shoulder.
"You were right to bring me this," she said. "The improvement is real."
Leon stopped rubbing his arm.
"It feels faster in practice. I wasn’t sure how much of that would survive pressure."
"Enough to matter. Someone accustomed to your previous timing will need to adjust. You should expect a capable opponent to do so."
"As you just demonstrated."
"Several times."
He laughed, despite himself.
Ji waited until he had caught his breath, then pointed to the space in front of her.
"Now Earth into Lightning. Slowly first."
The slow transition was clean.
When she made him repeat it under pressure, heat began gathering at the same point he had noted during testing.
"Stop there," Ji said.
Leon cut the next attack and allowed the current to settle.
"Your layer is holding," she told him. "But you’re still bracing the Earth technique after you’ve begun calling Lightning. Why?"
"To keep the defence from weakening during the change."
"An old habit. It made sense when the transition took longer. Now you’re maintaining the brace after you need it."
She had him repeat the movement without an incoming attack. At her direction, he released the last hold earlier.
The warmth diminished.
Leon tried again, this time with a little pressure against the defence. His instinct was to keep reinforcing it. He caught himself and let the current move on.
The transition completed cleanly.
"Oh," he said.
Ji watched him repeat it twice more.
"The array exposed the habit when you increased the feed. You were right to reduce the setting until you understood it."
"I was going to examine the branch again."
"You still should. But check what you’re asking a sound structure to do before rebuilding it."
That advice was going to be unpleasantly useful.
Leon looked down at his hands. "How long until the new timing feels natural?"
"Practice will tell you. Stop before fatigue makes you careless, and don’t compensate by forcing more energy through it."
He nodded. This time, he knew exactly what he would be practising.
"There is somewhere suitable for testing it," Ji said as he retrieved his robe.
Leon turned back.
"The Tempering Hall, on the northern face. Its formations produce opponents for staged combat trials. You may request an assessment and enter the course appropriate to your actual strength."
"How far does the course go?"
"Further than you’re ready to clear. The upper stages of the disciple course have not been completed by an eligible challenger in two hundred years."
"Eligible?"

"There are entry conditions. An elder cannot walk through and claim the disciples’ rewards." She took a small jade from her sleeve. "First clears earn contribution. Repeating a stage is useful practice, but earns no additional payment."
Leon accepted the jade.
"What can the contribution buy?"
"Cultivation materials, medicine court services, and access to approved vault stock. The hall steward will give you the current schedule."
He was already thinking about the remaining cores, the reservoir, and how much more convenient it would be to prepare the next session with suitable resources waiting beside him.
Ji noticed.

"You may read the reward schedule before you enter," she said. "You must also read the withdrawal conditions. The formation has safeguards, but you are expected to stop when you can no longer continue safely."
"I will."
"Your permission covers your assessment and entry. It does not admit your attendants as contestants."
"I’ll tell them."
Ji rose. "Rest today. Work on that Earth transition tomorrow, then arrange the assessment when you’re satisfied with it."
Leon bowed before leaving.
"Thank you, Master. For the array as well."
"You used it properly," she said. "That’s enough."
Ira was the first to react when he told them that evening.
"A hall full of things we can hit?"
"Things I can hit," Leon said. "The permission is for me."
Her disappointment was immediate. "That’s unfortunate."
"For the hall?" Seraphine asked.
"For me. The hall sounds well made."
Leon sat beside her and let her inspect the permission jade. Vyra asked for the reward schedule, and he promised to bring it back before spending any contribution.
"Bring the medicine list too," Loriel said. "There may be things I can grow more cheaply than we can keep buying."
"I haven’t earned anything yet."
"We’re giving you reasons," Ira told him, handing back the jade.
Seraphine waited until the others had finished asking questions.
"And the assessment with Ji?" she asked.
"She found the improvement immediately. Then she put me on the floor."
"Only once?"
"I’m not giving you a number."
Seraphine smiled. "Did she find the Earth problem?"
"An old defensive habit. I was holding the brace too long during the transition."
"I can help you practise that tomorrow."
Leon nodded. He would enjoy having an opponent whose smallest movement did not make him reconsider his life.
He turned the jade over in his palm once more, then put it away and drew Ira closer.

The next place he was going would have opponents he could fight openly, a result he could measure, and rewards he could use. After weeks spent looking for people who wanted to remain hidden, he was looking forward to it.
[If you have bought privilege, thank you so much; if you haven’t, please do that would help me a lot]

chapters.title: Chapter 673: What the Hall Keeps Secret
paragraphs: Seraphine waited until Leon had finished his breakfast before taking him into the residence’s training yard.
She had tied her hair back and exchanged her outer robe for something that would stay clear of her sword arm. Leon looked at the practice blade in her hand, then at the closed gate.
"How much did Ji tell you?" he asked.
"Nothing. You told me enough last night." Seraphine moved to the opposite side of the yard. "Raise the Earth defense. Keep the pressure low until we know what we’re correcting."

Leon formed a layered barrier across his left side. She approached with a measured thrust, letting light gather along the edge of her blade. It pressed into the overlap between two layers without breaking either.
He reinforced the seam automatically.
Seraphine shifted toward his exposed side, and he called Lightning. Heat gathered briefly in the Earth branch before the new current cleared it.
Her blade stopped against his sleeve.
"Still holding it?" she asked.
"A little."
"Then do it again. I’ll use the same approach."
On the next attempt, he released too early. The barrier weakened while her sword was still pressing against it, and she stepped through before his answer formed.
Leon looked down at the wooden blade resting against his chest.
"That was worse."
"It was different," Seraphine said. "You can correct different."
She withdrew and gave him room to reset.

The difficulty was trusting how quickly the next current would arrive. His old timing had kept the defense intact while he prepared an answer. Now the answer was ready sooner, and he kept spending effort on a brace he no longer needed.
Ji had made it seem simple. Leon suspected she had forgotten what it felt like to possess hands that occasionally failed to obey.

They repeated the exchange until he stopped rushing the release. On one attempt, Seraphine committed to the outside and Lightning gathered along his fingers before her blade cleared the falling barrier.
She stepped back, smiling.
"There. Did you feel it?"
He had. The return settled cleanly, with none of the lingering warmth.
"Again," Leon said.
This time she changed her approach.
He caught the first variation and missed the second. By the end of the session, he was watching her shoulder and sword instead of waiting for a particular moment in a familiar sequence.
Seraphine lowered her blade when his attention began drifting.
"That’s enough. You’re going to undo good practice if you keep trying while tired."
"I was about to get that one."

"You can get it tomorrow." She came closer and straightened the collar he had pulled loose. "Try it against something manageable first. You don’t need to test every improvement against the strongest thing in the building."
Leon caught her hand before she withdrew it and kissed her knuckles.
"I’ll bring back the reward list."
"Bring yourself back with it." Her fingers closed around his briefly. "The others will want both."
The Tempering Hall stood against the northern face of the mountain, its broad entrance worn smooth by generations of visitors.
Inside, a steward examined Ji’s permission jade and opened a register.
"Assessment and disciple-course entry," he said. "Your attendants may wait in the public hall, but this permission does not admit them as contestants."
"They know."
"Good. Before we begin, read these."
He gave Leon two thin booklets. One contained the course rules; the other listed rewards and requisitions. Leon set the second aside long enough to read the withdrawal conditions properly.

A challenger could end a trial by speaking the withdrawal command or pressing the token. Between stages, leaving preserved all completed clears. Emergency termination counted as failure of the active stage.
"What does the safety formation monitor?" Leon asked.
"Whether the challenger remains conscious and able to sustain the trial. It also intervenes when an injury passes its emergency threshold."
"So someone can be badly hurt before it stops the opponent."

"Yes." The steward rested a finger beside the relevant passage. "Do not treat intervention as a substitute for withdrawing. The formation can end an attack. It cannot promise that everything preceding it is easily repaired."
Leon nodded and turned the page.
"What leaves the chamber?"
"Stage results and safety signals. Nothing else."
"No image?"
"No image, technique record, or transmitted energy signature. Combat methods are neither sent outside nor retained for later examination."
The answer was clear enough that Leon looked up from the booklet.
"Even for the elders?"

"The restriction is part of the Hall’s construction. The hall elder receives the same results I do." The steward pointed toward the passage behind him. "An assessment can be witnessed with your agreement. The trial itself is private."
Leon read the provision again. He had become accustomed to choosing what other people were allowed to see. The prospect of putting that concern aside was almost as attractive as the rewards.
Almost.
Unaspected Spirit Marrow appeared halfway through the requisition booklet.
Nine measures cost five thousand four hundred contribution. Ordinary purchasing credit could not be used for that allocation.
Leon placed a finger beside the entry.
"How clean?"
The steward leaned over to see what he meant.
"Neutral qi, densely condensed. No elemental alignment or residual cultivator imprint. The vault tests each allocation before release."
"Why restrict it to contribution?"
"Supply. The Palace has a limited stock, and money alone would empty it."

Leon thought of the weeks spent drawing usable residue from the Ethereal Initiate cores. Even with the array, every portion had required examination before he could let it reach the reservoir. Twice he had caught his attention wandering and closed the inlet until he had cleaned the waiting energy again.
He would still need to prepare this material and regulate the feed. But he would not have to spend weeks separating his supply from someone else’s lingering imprint.
That would be nice.
He checked the course payments against the price.

A full set of array consumables and preparation materials would cost another nine hundred. He copied the medicine entries Loriel had requested and several supplement prices for Vyra, then wrote six thousand three hundred beside the marrow allocation.
"That’s your target?" the steward asked.
"At least that much."
"First clears only. Repeating a stage will not earn another payment."
"I read it." Leon tucked the copied lists into his robe. "Let’s see where I can start."
The assessment room held a construct, several measurement plates, and a woman whose hall-elder insignia was the only ornament on her plain robe.
Leon agreed to have the assessment witnessed. He used familiar abilities drawn from the affinities already recorded by the Palace, keeping his concealed methods to himself.

The construct tested his reactions before increasing its force. Ice turned its first serious attack. Lightning caught its recovery. When it tried to pin him against the room’s boundary, Leon folded the last few paces of his retreat and appeared beyond its reach.
The elder stopped the assessment shortly afterward.
"Senior course," she told the steward.
Then she turned to Leon.
"The early stages should let you settle into the chamber. Beyond those, the benchmarks rise sharply. They remain fixed regardless of who enters."
"How many stages?" Leon asked.
"Twelve. Eleven is the highest recorded clear among eligible disciples. Two challengers reached it within the last sixty years. The twelfth has remained uncleared for more than two hundred."
Ji had warned him the course went further than he was ready to finish. He believed her. He was still curious about what waited at the end.
The elder handed him a trial token.
"You may examine each benchmark before accepting the stage. Completing one does not oblige you to attempt the next."
Leon thanked her and followed the steward to the chamber entrance.
When the stone door closed, the room beyond was empty and comfortably lit. His token showed the first challenge, its reward, and the withdrawal command.
He drew his sword and tested the movement of his shoulders.
No one was watching for an affinity that did not belong on his record. No one would examine the fight afterward.
Leon accepted the first stage with a grin.
All right. Let’s earn something.

The vault tests each allocation before release."
"Why restrict it to contribution?"
"Supply.
The Palace has a limited stock, and money alone would empty it."
Leon thought of the weeks spent drawing usable residue from the Ethereal Initiate cores.
Even with the array, every portion had required examination before he could let it reach the reservoir.
Twice he had caught his attention wandering and closed the inlet until he had cleaned the waiting energy again.
He would still need to prepare this material and regulate the feed.
But he would not have to spend weeks separating his supply from someone else’s lingering imprint.
That would be nice.
He checked the course payments against the price.
A full set of array consumables and preparation materials would cost another nine hundred.
He copied the medicine entries Loriel had requested and several supplement prices for Vyra, then wrote six thousand three hundred beside the marrow allocation.
"That’s your target?" the steward asked.
"At least that much."
"First clears only.
Repeating a stage will not earn another payment."
"I read it." Leon tucked the copied lists into his robe.
"Let’s see where I can start."
The assessment room held a construct, several measurement plates, and a woman whose hall-elder insignia was the only ornament on her plain robe.
Leon agreed to have the assessment witnessed.
He used familiar abilities drawn from the affinities already recorded by the Palace, keeping his concealed methods to himself.
The construct tested his reactions before increasing its force.
Ice turned its first serious attack.
Lightning caught its recovery.
When it tried to pin him against the room’s boundary, Leon folded the last few paces of his retreat and appeared beyond its reach.
The elder stopped the assessment shortly afterward.
"Senior course," she told the steward.
Then she turned to Leon.
"The early stages should let you settle into the chamber.
Beyond those, the benchmarks rise sharply.
They remain fixed regardless of who enters."
"How many stages?" Leon asked.
"Twelve.
Eleven is the highest recorded clear among eligible disciples.
Two challengers reached it within the last sixty years.
The twelfth has remained uncleared for more than two hundred."
Ji had warned him the course went further than he was ready to finish.
He believed her.
He was still curious about what waited at the end.
The elder handed him a trial token.
"You may examine each benchmark before accepting the stage.
Completing one does not oblige you to attempt the next."
Leon thanked her and followed the steward to the chamber entrance.
When the stone door closed, the room beyond was empty and comfortably lit.
His token showed the first challenge, its reward, and the withdrawal command.
He drew his sword and tested the movement of his shoulders.
No one was watching for an affinity that did not belong on his record.
No one would examine the fight afterward.
Leon accepted the first stage with a grin.
All right.
Let’s earn something.

chapters.title: Chapter 674: The Number on the Wall
paragraphs: The first construct lost its sword before it completed its opening attack.
Leon caught the weapon on his own blade, turned it aside, and struck through the exposed center of its chest. The body broke into pale fragments before the stolen sword hit the floor.
A line appeared above the chamber entrance.
[Senior Course — Stage One: Cleared]
[First-clear contribution: 300]
He looked at the number, then at the place where the construct had stood.
I could get used to that.

The next stages required more attention without demanding much strength. One compressed the available fighting space. Another sent several opponents toward a pillar he had to protect. Their patterns were well made, but the force behind them remained far below what his body could withstand.
He cleared both without allowing an attack to land.
Stage Four reproduced a Peak Nascent Soul swordsman. Leon limited his output while testing the transition he had practiced that morning, giving the opponent time to pressure his Earth barrier.
The sword shifted toward the outside.
He released the unnecessary brace and answered with Lightning. The current crossed the opening cleanly, and the construct collapsed before its attack reached him.
There was no heat gathering in the branch afterward.
Leon checked the return once, pleased, then accepted the payment. Twelve hundred contribution waited in his account.
The Soul Transformation stages gave him more room to fight.
Stage Five spread a constraining field across the chamber. He broke its control with pressure of his own and reached the construct before it could establish the field again.

Stage Six used a more difficult arrangement: attacks from two directions, with the second timed to catch his answer to the first. Leon bent the path of the leading strike, forcing the rear opponent to defend itself, and finished both while they were recovering their positions.
He was enjoying the freedom. He could commit to a useful combination without considering whether someone outside would misunderstand the speed of the change or ask why he possessed it.
At Stage Seven, the benchmark rose to Early Void Immortal.

The construct carried a broad blade and used its pressure to deny a direct approach. Leon let Void Dominion spread through the unclaimed parts of the room, testing the boundary of its influence before crossing.
The blade descended where he had been.

He emerged beside the construct, armor covering his forearm, and drove an elbow into its flank. The impact opened a seam. His sword followed before the body could turn, and a brief holy strike through the exposed interior ended the exchange.
Mana still held his spatial route open as the Divinordial Heart supplied the blade through its separate channels.
Leon withdrew his sword and let both currents settle.
That would have earned him questions outside. Here, the chamber simply added five hundred contribution to his balance.
He took the short rest interval before continuing.
By Stage Eight, raw speed no longer decided the opening exchanges.

The Peak Void Immortal reproduction carried a spear and changed its reach by shifting the pressure surrounding the weapon. Leon turned aside the first thrust. The second shortened unexpectedly, trying to catch his wrist before he completed the parry.
He withdrew his hand and let the spear scrape across his armor.
Better.

He used Elemental Surge to strengthen a sequence of attacks rather than pouring everything into one blow. Ice obstructed the construct’s retreat, wind spoiled its attempt to clear the obstruction, and Lightning reached the opening beneath its raised arm.
The spear came back at him even as the strike landed.
Leon changed his footing, allowed the shaft to pass, and drove his holy-powered blade through the damaged region. The construct broke apart against the ice behind it.
Stage Nine reproduced Early Earth Immortal combat strength.

Its pressure reminded him of the more dangerous opponents he had faced in the Tower. He gave it the respect it deserved, watching how it controlled the space around its body before attempting a close attack.

The first shallow cut reached his upper arm when he misjudged the end of its defensive field. Life closed the wound while he circled. No audience saw the repair, and he did not have to conceal the current beneath another technique.

He fought more freely after that, combining short spatial changes with physical attacks until the construct committed too far to a turn. A concentrated strike broke its defense. The follow-up ended the stage.
Leon sat down when the rest interval began.
He had spent energy, but his breathing settled quickly. His balance now stood at three thousand eight hundred contribution.
Outside, two disciples stopped beside the results wall.
One had come to reserve a practice chamber. His companion had stayed because the new name on the senior-course list had continued climbing while they talked.
"Stage Nine," the first disciple said. "Isn’t that an Earth Immortal benchmark?"
"Early Earth Immortal," his companion replied.
They both looked at the cultivation entry beside Leon’s name.
"Peak Golden Core," the first said, quieter this time.
"He is the Palace Mistress’s disciple. You heard about the duel."
"I heard he survived Wei Zhaoran’s forbidden technique. This is different."
The hall elder approached to examine the updated result. The second disciple stepped out of her way, then hesitated.
"Elder, does the Hall measure what he uses?"
"Inside the chamber, it resolves the fight," she said. "Outside, we receive the result."
"Then nobody knows how he did it?"
"Leon knows."
She studied the wall a moment longer. By the time she returned to the steward’s desk, several more disciples had stopped to look.
Stage Ten took Leon longer than the preceding fights.

The Mid Earth Immortal reproduction used a heavy sword and a defensive field that resisted the easiest applications of his spatial control. He could still move around its protected region, but reaching its body required him to enter the weapon’s range.
He tested it with a sequence of quick attacks. The construct blocked the first two and stepped into the third, catching his forearm between its sword and his own.
Bone cracked beneath the armor.

Leon drove it back with a close elemental discharge and withdrew behind an ice barrier. Life repaired the arm while he kept the barrier moving between them. By the time the construct broke through, he could grip his sword again.
He remembered how the Gatekeeper in the Tower had resisted direct spatial interference. Trying the same failed approach with more power would waste strength here too.
Instead, he used the space beyond the defensive field to change where his attacks arrived.
The construct could protect its body. It could not make every direction equally convenient to defend.

He forced the sword low, crossed the opening with Raijin, and struck from a new angle before it could recover. Its counter caught his side, hard enough to jar his breath, but the holy blade reached the core first.
The chamber cleared around him.
[First-clear contribution: 1,000]
[Available contribution: 4,800]
Leon remained standing until the ache beneath his ribs eased. Then he sat and gave himself the full rest interval.
The next benchmark appeared when he requested it.
[Stage Eleven — Peak Earth Immortal Combat Reproduction]
[First-clear contribution: 2,400]
That would bring him to seven thousand two hundred. Enough for the marrow and preparation stock, with room for the medicine list as well.

He examined his condition carefully. The arm was whole. His reserves were reduced, but he had not exhausted either Heart. The next fight would be harder than the Lord-class enemies he had already defeated, and he would have to judge it by what it actually did.
I can withdraw. I don’t have to decide the whole fight from a line on a wall.
He stood and accepted.
Pressure settled across the chamber before the opponent appeared. A short experimental fold frayed as it crossed the center of the room, depositing him well short of where he intended.
The construct rose from the stone, three meters tall, its overlapping plates joined by pale channels. A long-hafted blade rested in its hands.
Leon let his armor cover him fully.
The construct stepped forward, and the floor beneath his boots trembled.
