chapters.title: Chapter 675: The Fifth Node
paragraphs: Leon met the first descending strike with his sword angled to carry it past his shoulder.
The weapons touched, and the force drove his boots through the surface of the floor.
He released the parry before it could pin him. A short spatial fold carried him toward the construct’s left side, where he drove a compressed frost lance beneath its raised arm.
The lance struck deeply enough to crack the plate.
Then the construct turned into the attack and brought the lower end of its weapon across his ribs.
His armor hardened before impact. He still felt something break.
Leon landed several paces away, coughing, and moved again before the blade reached him. It cut a groove through the stone where his head had been.
Fine. No trading blows until I know what I’m trading with.
Life gathered beneath his damaged ribs. He could feel the repair taking hold while he evaded the next attack, but he needed an opening to finish it without taking another hit.
He spread Void Dominion across the room to his right.

The construct followed, its next step slowing as its pressure encountered his control. Leon used the delay to draw a full breath and finish mending the ribs. Then he sent Lightning into the cracked plate.
Pale fragments scattered. The construct’s arm dipped, and he advanced behind a burst of fire.
Its blade came through the flames low enough to take his legs.
He jumped, folded sideways, and struck the wall feet first before pushing away.
The creature had barely moved from the place where he had first hurt it.
For the next several exchanges, Leon concentrated on making it turn.

Its battlefield control strengthened near its body. A fold that worked cleanly along the wall became unreliable beside its shoulder. He stopped trying to force passage through the strongest pressure and used the edges instead, crossing from one clear region to another whenever the weapon committed.
His sword opened the thigh plate. The construct answered with a rising cut that caught him across the upper arm.
He sealed the bleeding and kept moving.

Fire drove against its front while water struck the exposed joint from below. He froze the water in place and crossed behind the obstruction with Raijin, bringing the full force of his body into an attack against its back.
The impact staggered it.
Leon followed with holy energy along his sword, maintaining the elemental pressure through the Primordial Void Heart while the separate current entered the blade.
He reached something behind the armor. The construct jerked forward, and for an instant its pressure weakened.
Then the broken plates drew together around his sword.
He wrenched the weapon free before they could trap it and retreated beneath the sweep of the long blade.
By the time he reached the wall, the damage had closed.
Leon stared at the restored back.
"Oh, you’re going to be annoying."
He confirmed the recovery twice before committing another major attack.
Damage to a hip restored more slowly than damage near the head. The pale channels brightened before the outer plate reformed, and the flow always came from deeper in the body.
He began aiming for those channels.

The construct punished him for looking. A thrust drove through his outer defense and opened his thigh. Leon caught the haft beneath his arm before it could withdraw and turn the cut into something worse. His armor held against the dragging edge as he drove a concentrated elemental strike into its wrist.
The grip loosened.

He escaped through the gap, leaving blood on the stone, and raised an Earth barrier between them. The blade smashed through it almost immediately. Leon released the brace early and sent Lightning through the falling debris while he moved away.
Seraphine’s morning lesson bought him just enough time to get his leg working again.
She’s going to ask whether it helped.
He could already imagine her face when he answered.
By the time an hour had passed, he had located five dense knots inside the construct: one beneath each shoulder, one in the lower back, one behind the left hip, and one at the base of the skull.
Every major repair drew from them.
The knots were protected by thicker plating and the construct’s best defensive angles. There was no convenient exposed point waiting for him to notice it.
Leon took the left shoulder first.

He obscured his approach with Darkness, sent a bright flash across the construct’s opposite side, and entered beneath the blade when it turned to track him through its pressure. The deception only stole a fraction of a second. He spent it on a hardened spatial spear driven through the weakened shoulder plate.
The knot ruptured.
For several breaths, the shoulder hung uselessly.
Then the other four knots brightened, and the damaged one began forming again.
Leon stayed out of reach long enough to watch the whole process. The shoulder recovered in roughly fourteen seconds.
He glanced at the restored arm and swore.
Breaking one node changed the flow through the others. It did not end the recovery.

Over the following half hour, Leon tried interrupting the connections as well as the knots themselves. The construct rerouted the flow around the damage. When he destroyed two close together, the remaining nodes fed them in sequence.
He learned enough to plan a larger attempt, but the information was expensive.

A broken wrist slowed his sword hand until he created space to repair it. A shallow cut along his back remained open because healing it immediately would have distracted him from the weapon trying to split his head.

He had recovered from worse individual wounds. The repeated demand was beginning to weigh on him. Each major repair took concentration he wanted for the fight, and his body was growing less willing to answer instantly.
He could still stop. The token remained within reach beneath his armor.
Leon looked at the construct’s unmarked plates and felt a stubborn desire to leave something on them that stayed broken.
One proper attempt. Then I’ll know whether this is possible.

He forced the opponent toward the side of the chamber where his spatial control was strongest. Elemental Surge strengthened the ice closing around its forward foot. The construct broke the first restraint, stepped over the second, and raised its blade to strike him as he approached.
Leon used Raijin to pass the weapon.
His first attack entered the lower back. The node broke beneath a spatial spear, and he was already turning toward the left hip when the construct swung its elbow at him.
He ducked under it and ruptured the second knot through the joint.
The left shoulder came next. He reached it from below with his sword, holy energy driving through the damaged plating while mana maintained the restraint around the legs.
The construct tore one foot free.
Leon stayed close, took the scraping edge of its haft across his back, and struck the right shoulder before it could complete the turn.
Four nodes went dark.
Its pressure faltered so abruptly that he nearly overstepped. Leon caught himself and raised his sword toward the base of the skull.
The remaining node flared.

Energy rushed through the pale channels. The right shoulder, closest to the surviving knot, began restoring first. The construct recovered enough control of its arm to wrench the blade across its own body.
Leon tried to withdraw.
The haft caught him across the chest and threw him into the wall.
For a moment he could not draw breath.

His armor had held together, but the force beneath it left him on one knee with blood running over his tongue. The construct pulled its trapped foot free while pale light spread through its shoulders and down its back.
The hip node returned last.
Four broken knots, all restored by the fifth before he could stand.

Leon pressed a hand against his chest and began the repair. It took longer this time. He had to keep moving while broken ribs settled, raising a sloping barrier to turn the next strike instead of trying to meet it.
He stumbled behind the falling stone and finished drawing breath.
The head node had restored the nearest shoulder sooner than the full repair cycle. Fourteen seconds was an outside limit, not time he could safely spend.
He would have to break all five before the first useful restoration began.
The construct advanced with its blade level.
Leon straightened slowly. He knew where every node was now, and he knew what happened when he left one alive.
His hands were shaking. He tightened them around his sword and began looking for a way to reach the skull sooner.

Fourteen seconds was an outside limit, not time he could safely spend.
He would have to break all five before the first useful restoration began.
The construct advanced with its blade level.
Leon straightened slowly.
He knew where every node was now, and he knew what happened when he left one alive.
His hands were shaking.
He tightened them around his sword and began looking for a way to reach the skull sooner.

chapters.title: Chapter 676: Before It Can Recover
paragraphs: Leon spent the next few minutes avoiding a fight he had been trying very hard to win.
He gave ground along the wall, turned the blade with cheap angled defenses, and refused the openings that required another close exchange. The construct followed without tiring.
His chest settled as the repair completed. The relief was immediate, but the effort left him lightheaded for a step.
He could not keep paying that cost.
The fifth node was the problem. Reaching the shoulders forced him beneath the weapon, and reaching the skull afterward meant climbing past a defense that was already recovering.
Leon watched the construct turn its head to track a spatial probe.
Then I need it looking the wrong way before I get there.
He tried approaching the skull first. The construct rotated its body to keep the blade between them, exposing the lower back for a moment.
Leon took the opening with a small strike and withdrew.
On his second attempt, it kept its stance and thrust at him instead. He barely turned the point aside. The impact numbed his hand even through the armor.
It would not repeat a response simply because he wanted it to.
He would have to make the threat dangerous enough that protecting the skull became necessary.
The following exchanges left him with less room for mistakes.

He drove fire against the construct’s chest and used the glare to shift his approach. The opponent stepped through it, blade sweeping horizontally, and Leon folded beneath the cut into a region of space he had already claimed.
He reached the left hip. The construct dropped an elbow toward his head.
Leon abandoned the attack and caught the descending arm on an Earth brace. Stone burst against his shoulder. He released before the next impact and sent Lightning into the exposed wrist.
The hand spasmed open for an instant.
That was useful. It also hurt badly enough that he had to stop thinking about it until he escaped.
He changed sides, carried the momentum through a short burst of Raijin, and placed a holy cut across the lower back. The wound reached toward the node but did not break it.
The construct turned to protect the damaged region.
Leon watched the skull move with the shoulders and finally saw a sequence he might complete.

He tested parts of it over the next stretch of fighting. Every test used strength. Once, the blade caught his collarbone as he withdrew, and he had to spend an opening repairing damage instead of learning anything new.
His recovery still closed the injury quickly. Afterward, however, it took him several breaths to steady his grip.
I know. I’m trying to finish.
The thought was directed at his own body, which had become increasingly unhelpful about what he wanted.
Two hours had passed when he began preparing the final attempt.
The construct’s weight had opened long cracks in the floor. Leon used them to conceal two ice restraints, both positioned near places where he could still maintain reliable spatial control.
He let the enemy destroy the first.

The second stayed beneath an uneven shelf of stone, outside the path it had been taking. To bring it there, he would need to surrender the safer strip beside the wall and cross the center of its pressure.
Leon checked his remaining strength while retreating.

The Primordial Void Heart was still supplying his techniques, but repeated exertion had worn down his control. His holy attacks had spent a substantial part of the Divinordial Heart’s reserve. Neither had stopped working. The trouble was keeping everything coordinated while his arms grew heavy and another wound demanded attention.
He sealed a cut at his side and left the deeper ache alone.
If this attempt failed, he would withdraw. He disliked the decision enough to know he should have made it earlier.
The construct advanced.

Leon threatened the skull with a concentrated holy strike, strong enough that ignoring it would mean taking real damage. At the same time, a spatial attack approached the lower back from beyond the opponent’s protected field.
It turned to bring both threats within its defense.
He changed the angle, forcing another step.
The construct reached the uneven shelf.
Leon let the first attack fall short and drove the second into its raised weapon arm. The response was immediate: a sweeping counter aimed through his middle.
He moved with it. The haft clipped his side, but he had already committed to the retreat, and the impact carried him toward the clear space he needed.
His boots struck stone. He turned before the pain could interrupt him.
Ice locked around the construct’s feet as it followed.

Leon strengthened the restraint with Elemental Surge and drove wind against its upper body. Its pressure began breaking the ice immediately. He raised an Earth obstruction behind its rear foot, denying the simple backward step that would free the leading leg.
For a brief interval, it had to fight for its stance.
Leon crossed that interval with Raijin.
The lower-back node broke first, a spatial spear passing through plating he had weakened in the preceding exchanges.

He moved along its left side and drove his sword into the hip knot. The construct twisted toward him. He withdrew the blade and ducked beneath its elbow, using the movement to reach the left shoulder.
The third node ruptured against a concentrated strike.
Its weapon came down toward his back.

Leon folded away from the edge of the protected field rather than trying to pass through its center. He emerged high on the opposite side, shoulder striking the construct as he drove the fourth attack into the right shoulder knot.
The impact sent pain down his arm. He kept the hand closed long enough to feel the node break.
Four.
The skull brightened, preparing to restore the nearest damaged region.
Leon was already moving toward it.

He maintained the spatial pressure and elemental restraints through the Primordial Void Heart. The Divinordial Heart supplied his sword separately, holy energy gathering along the edge as he rose from beside the ruined shoulder.
The construct jerked its head away and tried to bring the haft between them.
Its arm no longer answered quickly enough.
Leon’s blade entered beneath the base of the skull and cut through the fifth node.
The restoration stopped before it reached the shoulder.
The construct was still moving.

Its weight tore one foot free, and the long blade dropped toward Leon as he landed. He threw himself inside the weapon’s reach, taking the shoulder against his armor instead of the edge across his neck.
For one frightening moment he could not lift his sword.
His arm had gone numb. The opponent’s chest filled his vision, cracked plates shifting as it tried to crush him against its body.
Leon caught the hilt with both hands.
Mana held the damaged layers apart. Holy energy remained in the blade.
He drove it through the chest and into the exposed core.
Something broke beneath the point.
The pressure vanished. Leon stumbled as the body collapsed around his sword, plates falling into a spreading heap of gray formation matter.
He landed on his knees beside it.
[Senior Course — Stage Eleven: Cleared]
[First-clear contribution: 2,400]
[Available contribution: 7,200]
Below the result, the chamber showed his stage duration.
Two hours and eleven minutes.
Leon tried to laugh and coughed instead. He wiped his mouth on a ruined sleeve, then sat back because his legs had made the decision without consulting him.
Done. It’s actually done.
He stayed there while the chamber withdrew the broken construct.
When he could concentrate properly, he repaired the remaining injuries. Skin closed. His shoulder settled. The pain diminished, leaving an exhaustion that healing did not remove.
Stage Twelve appeared as an available challenge.
Leon dismissed it without opening the description.
Seven thousand two hundred contribution. The marrow, the supplies, and enough left to bring something useful home.
He had what he wanted.
"End run," he said, pressing the token’s withdrawal control.
The results wall updated before the chamber opened.
The hall elder rose from beside the steward’s desk. Around her, disciples who had been discussing the previous record fell silent.
[Senior Course — Stage Eleven: Cleared]
[Run concluded]
[Safety status: Amber]
Then Leon walked out.
Dried blood covered the front of his robe. His armor had withdrawn, and he carried his sword low at his side because lifting it any higher seemed unnecessary.
The hall elder approached without asking him to explain the result.
"Do you need the medicine court?"
"Somewhere to sit first," Leon said.
She moved aside and indicated the bench beyond the entrance.
He thanked her, reached it, and sat down before noticing how many people were watching.
Under other circumstances, he would have enjoyed their expressions much more.

chapters.title: Chapter 677: Nine Measures
paragraphs: Ira reached him first.
She had been standing beyond the hall entrance when the door opened. Now she stopped in front of the bench and looked from his face to the blood on his robe.
"Is any of that still bleeding?"
"No." Leon lifted one hand. "I’ve closed everything."
Loriel arrived beside her and took the offered hand before he could lower it.
"May we use somewhere private?" she asked the steward.
He opened a screened consultation alcove off the public hall. Leon was grateful for the shorter distance even before he stood.
Inside, Seraphine closed the screen while Loriel examined him. Vyra set a cup of water within reach and waited until he drank before asking anything.
"How far?"
"Eleven."
Ira let out a breath.
"We saw it change. I thought the wall had made a mistake."
"You were there for the result?" Leon asked.
"We came after lunch," Seraphine said. "You’d already begun the last stage."
Her attention stayed on the ruined fabric beneath his collar. He looked down and realized how much blood had dried there.
"I know it looks bad."
"It looks as though you were hurt," she said. "Were you?"
"Yes."
She accepted the direct answer more easily than she would have accepted reassurance. Leon could see that in the way she stopped studying the robe and finally met his eyes.
"Badly?"
"A few times. The recovery worked."
Loriel’s fingers tightened around his wrist.
"And you kept asking it to work."
She finished the examination before explaining what she had found.
"There’s no open wound, and the bones have set properly. You don’t need me to close anything." Loriel released his hand. "You do need to stop spending yourself for a while."
"How long?"
"Give yourself a full day. Sleep, eat, and let your reserves recover without immediately using them again."
Leon leaned back against the bench.
He had expected that. Hearing it from her still made him think of the sealed marrow case he had not yet collected and all the work it might save him.
Loriel noticed his expression.
"Buying your supplies is fine," she added. "Starting another cultivation session is not."
"I wasn’t going to start one here."
"Good. Don’t start one at home either."
Ira sat beside him and touched an undamaged section of his sleeve.
"The last signal went amber," she said. "Then it stayed there."
"I was still fighting."
"We worked that part out." Her thumb moved once across the cloth. "There wasn’t much else to do."
Leon turned his hand and caught hers.
He had spent those minutes watching a blade, judging openings, deciding whether another repair would cost too much. He had not thought about the people outside watching a color refuse to change.
"I’m sorry you had to wait through it."
Ira looked down at their hands, then nodded.
Seraphine moved his cup closer when he reached for it. She did not tell him off. Somehow that made him want to explain the fight more carefully when they had time.
Ji arrived while he was replacing the worst of his clothing.
The hall elder admitted her to the alcove, then left them alone. Leon started to rise, but Ji motioned him back down.
"Stay there. I’ve already seen the result."
"Eleven," he said, unable to keep some satisfaction out of his voice.
"Yes." Her expression softened slightly. "You may look pleased. It was an extraordinary clear."
He had heard disciples whispering beyond the screen. This mattered more.
"Thank you, Master."
"I expected you to stop earlier. Apparently I underestimated what you could bring to a private trial." She glanced toward Loriel. "His condition?"
"The injuries are repaired. He needs roughly a day without serious exertion."
Ji nodded and returned her attention to Leon.
"Then take the day."
"I will."
"Did the Earth transition hold?"
That question brought back the shattered barrier and the Lightning strike that had bought him time to repair his leg.
"It did. Seraphine helped me get the timing right this morning."
"Good." Ji looked pleased with that answer too. "You can tell me more about the transition when you’re rested. The rest of the trial is yours to discuss or keep private."
Leon nodded. She had not asked about the techniques that took him through an Earth Immortal defense, or how he had stayed standing for more than two hours.
He found himself wanting to tell her more precisely because she had left the choice with him.
For now, he said, "I earned enough for the marrow."
"Then collect it before the vault clerks finish for the day." Ji stepped away from the screen. "And let someone else carry the case if you’re still shaking."
Leon looked at his hand. It had almost stopped.
The requisition clerk counted the allocation in front of him.
Nine pale cylinders rested in separate compartments within a fitted case. Each bore a thin inspection seal, and beneath them lay a slip identifying the batch and approved quantity.
"Five thousand four hundred contribution," the clerk said. "Please confirm."
Leon placed his token against the plate.
[Restricted requisition approved]
[Unaspected Spirit Marrow: Nine measures]
[Contribution remaining: 1,800]
The clerk let him examine one measure before closing the case.
It was heavier than he expected. Beneath the inspection seal, the condensed qi felt unusually even. He found none of the foreign rhythm he had spent so long removing from the cores.
Leon turned it between his fingers, careful not to disturb the seal.
Vyra watched his expression.
"Worth the price?"
"The material?" He looked up. "Yes."
"And the fight?"
He considered that separately.
"I’d like to be better prepared before I do it again."
"That sounds sensible." She held out her hand for the preparation list. "Which of these have you already checked?"
They purchased the array consumables and preparation stock next. Nine hundred contribution covered the intake fittings, replacement supplies, and materials he had selected from the schedule.

Loriel and Vyra chose two medicine-court items from the copied list for another six hundred. Both discussed the quantities before approving the purchase, leaving Leon with three hundred contribution unspent.
He liked that last number more than he expected.
There would be something waiting in the account when he next found a useful entry in a Palace ledger. For once, obtaining what he wanted had not emptied everything he possessed.
Ira carried the marrow case back to the residence.
Leon could have managed it. She picked it up before he reached for the handle, and after the afternoon he had given her, he decided against arguing.

The walk home was slow enough that he noticed things he had passed that morning without seeing: a repaired section of railing, laundry moving above a lower courtyard, two students trying to carry an overfilled basket between them without spilling its contents down the steps.
He would have offered to help on another day.
Today he watched one of them rescue a falling bundle with a desperate grab and quietly hoped they made it.
At home, they checked the purchases against the receipts. Leon placed the marrow in secure storage beside the supplies for his next session.

Three cores still held recoverable energy. The reservoir retained prepared supply. The new marrow would give him a much cleaner source to work with, but he would prepare it properly before admitting any of it to his cultivation cycle.
He closed the storage compartment without opening an inspection seal.
Seraphine watched him put the key away.
"Finished?"
"For today."
"Then come and sit down."
Leon followed her to the sitting room. Ira had already claimed one end of the couch and left enough room beside her for him.
He sat, accepted the fresh cup Vyra handed him, and listened while Loriel described what she intended to do with their medicine-court purchases.
For the first time since entering the Hall, he had no reason to watch the door.

chapters.title: Chapter 678: Their Turn
paragraphs: Leon fell asleep before dinner.

He had meant to close his eyes while Loriel finished describing the medicine-court supplies. When he opened them again, the room had darkened, a folded blanket covered his legs, and someone had moved the cup away from his elbow.
Ira sat beside him with a book resting unopened on her knee.
"How long?" he asked.
"A while."
"You could have woken me."
"I know." She set the book aside. "Are you hungry?"
He considered the question and discovered that he was.

He watched the last lamp through half-closed eyes.
"Was the waiting really that bad?" he asked.
Ira answered without lifting her head.
"I don’t like being unable to do anything."
"I know."
"Especially when you’re the one inside." She paused.
"I didn’t want somebody to open the chamber and spoil your fight.
I just wanted the signal to change."
Leon understood the distinction.
It would have bothered him too.
Seraphine’s fingers moved once against his chest.
"You’re allowed to be pleased with what you did," she said.
"We’re allowed to worry about what it cost."
He turned his face toward hers.
"That seems fair."
She kissed him again, briefly, then reached to extinguish the lamp.
In the dark, Ira shifted until her head rested comfortably against his shoulder.
"Tomorrow," she said, "we’re sleeping late."
Leon closed his eyes.
For once, he had no objection at all.
He woke to sunlight and the faint sound of movement elsewhere in the residence.
Seraphine was still asleep beside him.
Ira had pushed most of the blanket toward the foot of the bed during the night, despite her earlier complaint.
Leon considered reaching for the notes he had left in the sitting room.
The thought brought the marrow to mind: nine clean measures, sealed and waiting.
He wanted to open the case, inspect the material properly, and work out how much prepared energy each portion would supply.
He could do all of that after his rest.
For now, his shoulder felt comfortably heavy beneath Ira’s arm, and moving would probably wake Seraphine.
He settled back against the pillow instead.
A few minutes later, Ira stirred and opened one eye.
"Going somewhere?" she murmured.
"No."
She looked satisfied and went back to sleep.
Leon stayed where he was.
The next session could wait until tomorrow.

chapters.title: Chapter 680: A Lord Collects His Due
paragraphs: Leon sent the report that morning and set the communication plaque beside his tea.
Fourteen dead. The recorded cleanup. The Qiao courier seal. White Reed Crossing, six days away, with four days of travel needed to reach it.
He had included a copy of the surviving projection and a request for permission to follow the delivery. Now Ji had everything he could give her, which left him with the unpleasant task of waiting.

Their room occupied the upper floor of a respectable Moonfall inn. Seraphine had checked its wards before adding three layers of privacy protection. The sealed evidence cases lay beneath the bed, close enough for Leon to feel their contents without looking.

Everyone else had found something useful to do. Vyra was buying supplies with Ira. Seraphine was inspecting the neighboring rooflines, and Qingyue had gone to check the customs post at White Reed Crossing.
Loriel sat beside an open case of medicinal cuttings, replacing the merchant’s packing straw.
"You’re going to wear a hole in the table," she said.
Leon stopped tapping beside the plaque.
"I’m waiting."
"I noticed."
She lifted a cutting, examined its roots, and put it into fresh wrapping. Leon watched her work until his tea cooled.
The first notification arrived while he was pouring another cup.
[Cosmic System — Transfer Offered.]
[From: MoonWhoEatsHerself]
He stopped with the pot tilted.
A second notice appeared, then three more. By the time he set the pot down, eleven waited at the edge of his vision.
[From: LimbDealer]
[From: The Ninth Silence]
[From: Sablewright]
More followed.
The tribute.
Leon opened the pending transfers. Notifications kept arriving, pushing the earlier ones upward until he abandoned counting and checked the records instead.

He had lost track of the payment date. Between the basin expedition, the murdered workshop, and months of cultivation compressed into a brief stretch of outside time, checking his expected income had somehow slipped his mind.
That seemed a serious personal failure now.

Moon had sent the agreed half of her monthly earnings. LimbDealer had sent eighty percent, a figure Leon still found extraordinary considering he had only asked for fifty. Hundreds of other accounts offered their quarter-shares.
He accepted the transfers, keeping an eye on the accumulating amount.
[Monthly Tribute Received: 180,000,000 Causality]
For a moment, Leon simply stared.
Then he leaned back and smiled.
"Oh, that’s fucking lovely."
Loriel looked up.
Leon checked the total again. It remained exactly where it was.

One hundred and eighty million, collected while he had been struggling to establish the earliest layer of this world’s cultivation. Seven precious Void Immortal cores had become useless stones in the process, and somewhere beyond anything he could currently reach, beings vastly stronger than him had finished their accounts and set aside his share.
I should check my messages more often.
He put both hands behind his head.
Loriel lowered the cutting she was holding.
"That wasn’t your master."
"No."
"Good news?"
"Very."
She glanced at the silent communication plaque. "Then why do you look as though you’ve gotten away with something?"
Leon turned toward her.
There were several possible answers. None survived her expression.
He stood and checked Seraphine’s privacy layers, then added a spatial seal inside them. When he returned, Loriel had closed the case.
"Is something wrong?" she asked.
"Nothing new. But you have your own Cosmic System now, so you’ll understand what I’m talking about."
He sat beside her and explained the group.

Not every conversation or every strange name. Just enough for her to understand that some of its members stood far beyond anyone they had met in this world, and that the most powerful among them spoke to the others with the easy authority of people who expected obedience.
"And you speak to them?" Loriel asked.
"Occasionally. Under Elemental Paragon."
She recognized the name, of course. That made explaining the next part worse.
"Some of them spoke it aloud," Leon continued. "Something happened. A real phenomenon, strong enough to frighten them. I tested the name myself afterward. It wasn’t something I knew how to cause."
"What kind of phenomenon?"
"The kind that made them think I was a Lord of the Universe."
Loriel waited.
Leon rubbed the back of his neck.
"I didn’t correct them."
"You let them believe it?"
"I encouraged them."
"How?"
He considered softening the explanation, then decided she deserved the honest version.
"Two of them surrendered all the Causality they had as compensation for insulting me. I required half their future monthly earnings too. LimbDealer offered eighty percent instead."
Loriel’s mouth opened slightly.
"The others paid a quarter of their existing balances," Leon said. "And a quarter of what they earn each month."
"How many others?"
"Hundreds."
She stared at him.
"Hundreds?"
"Yes."
"Leon, you extorted hundreds of beings who could—"
"I know."
"And that was what just arrived?"
"A hundred and eighty million."
Loriel looked toward the empty air where his interface hovered, although she could see nothing there.
He let her absorb the number before adding the part he was least proud of.
"I also told the first two that nobody would touch them or their families. They had to remain alive to bear their punishment."
"You promised to protect them?"
"It sounded convincing at the time."
She pressed her lips together. Leon could see the laugh trying to escape, but then her attention returned to the spatial seal around the room.
"They don’t know anything about you," she said.
"They know the name. They know the phenomenon happened. Everything else is what they’ve decided those things mean."
"And if they learn the truth?"
Leon took her hand.
"You have to take this secret to your grave. If those beings find out what I really am, they’ll burn me alive."
Loriel’s fingers tightened around his.
He had meant the words plainly. There was no need to invent something more frightening than the truth.
"I won’t tell anyone," she said.
"Not even as a joke."
"I understand."
Her answer was immediate enough that he looked at her.
Loriel shifted closer.
"You trusted me with it," she said. "I’m not going to make you regret that."
Some of the tension left his shoulders.
For a little while, they sat together without speaking. Then Loriel glanced at him again.
"They thanked you, didn’t they?"
Leon sighed.
"They did."
She lowered her forehead against his shoulder. The laugh that escaped her was quiet and helpless.
He found himself smiling again.
It was a relief to have somebody beside him who understood how ridiculous it was.
When he opened DivineEchoElira’s group, he discovered that his absence had become a subject of discussion.
[Sablewright: He has not spoken in over a month. His attention must be elsewhere.]
[Vaunt of the Chained Choir: I heard there was a boundary dispute between two young universes. I cannot confirm it.]
[The Ninth Silence: Then why are you repeating it?]
[Vaunt of the Chained Choir: I said I could not confirm it.]
[The Ninth Silence: You could also have said nothing.]
Leon read the exchange aloud.
Loriel listened with her hand still resting in his.
"A dispute between universes?" she asked.
"Apparently."

He remembered sitting in Xyra’s accelerated zone, trying to understand why the Earth branch of his circulation kept lagging behind the other eight. He had dismantled the arrangement twice before admitting that the third version had the same problem.
I couldn’t get nine branches to behave inside one body.
"What will you tell them?" Loriel asked.
"As little as possible."
He considered several replies and deleted each before sending it.
Claiming to have settled anything would invite questions about where, how, and against whom. Denying the rumor might invite a different question, which he wanted even less.
Eventually, he settled on a short acknowledgment.
[Elemental Paragon: The offerings have been received. Continue as agreed.]
The group responded almost immediately.
[LimbDealer: Thank you, my Lord. I am grateful that my offering was acceptable.]
[Sablewright: We will not neglect our obligations.]
[Vaunt of the Chained Choir: Welcome back, Honored Paragon.]
Leon read the first few messages, then stopped.
"They sound relieved," Loriel said.
"They usually do."
She looked at him with an expression he could not quite name.
He knew what bothered her. These were real people, frightened of a punishment he had no ability to deliver. It was easier to enjoy the money before hearing how grateful they were to keep their lives.
He still enjoyed it.
That probably said something about him, but he could examine it after he stopped smiling.
A private message opened before he decided whether to leave the group.
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: Honored Paragon. Forgive the intrusion.]
Leon straightened.
[I would not ordinarily presume. But I have carried a difficulty for some time, and I have exhausted the people I can safely consult.]
[Two teachings from sources I have every reason to respect appear to require opposite actions. I cannot determine which applies, so I have refrained from acting.]
[This has delayed my preparations for eleven years.]
[May I explain?]
Leon read the messages to Loriel.
Her amusement faded.
"Can you answer something like that?" she asked.
"I don’t even know what she’s cultivating."
"Then perhaps—"
Loriel stopped.
He watched her reach the same problem he had.

Refusing was possible. A Lord owed nobody instruction. But he had already acknowledged the offerings, she had asked politely, and some reckless part of him wanted to know what a being like her considered difficult.
He could at least hear the question.
[Elemental Paragon: Proceed.]
Moon began replying.
Leon’s smile disappeared as the first explanation filled his vision.

chapters.title: Chapter 681: Wisdom He Never Intended
paragraphs: [MoonWhoEatsHerself: The first teaching comes from the Stillwater commentaries. It requires the boundary to be consolidated and closed before influence is extended beyond it. Otherwise, what passes through is lost, and each attempt worsens the instability.]
[My lineage’s transmission instructs me to release the boundary to complete the expansion. A held boundary cannot expand. The wording is explicit.]
[If I release it prematurely, I risk losing the preparation. If I continue holding it, I cannot complete the process.]
Leon read the explanation twice.

He understood boundaries. He had repaired spatial layers, maintained passages, and worked with the limits of his own dimensional world. What he did not understand was the particular structure Moon’s lineage cultivated—or what either author meant by closing and releasing it.
Those words could describe several different operations.
He read the messages aloud for Loriel.
"Do you recognize the teachings?" she asked.
"I’ve never heard of them."
"Could she explain the terms?"
"Probably. Then she’d wonder why I needed them explained."
Loriel drew her knees closer beneath her robe.
Leon looked back at the messages.

Moon had been cautious. Nothing in her account sounded foolish. She had valuable preparation to protect, two credible sources giving apparently contradictory instructions, and no confidence that acting would improve matters.
He knew that feeling rather well.
The difference was that she expected him to know the answer.
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: Neither source is one I can dismiss. I have compared the relevant passages repeatedly. Both describe the boundary I am preparing to extend.]
Leon considered asking for the complete texts, but that would only provide him with a larger quantity of things he did not understand.
Start with what she thinks they mean.
He composed a question.
[Elemental Paragon: Tell me why you believe they describe the same step.]
His finger moved against his knee as he sent it. There was no keyboard, no physical action required, yet he caught himself doing it anyway.
Loriel watched his face.
"What did you say?"
He told her.
"Do you think that’s the mistake?"
"I think I need her to explain more."
Moon’s reply appeared.
[Both address the boundary before its expansion. The first requires it to remain closed while influence is gathered and directed beyond it. The second requires its release.]
[My prepared influence must cross that boundary for the extension to become stable. Therefore, both requirements appear to govern the same operation.]
Leon read the answer aloud, more slowly this time.
There might be something in that distinction. Or he might simply be arranging unfamiliar words into an explanation he wanted to hear.
He did not trust himself to choose.
Moon sent another message before he could respond.
[The first passage does not actually say "before its expansion." That is my description.]
Loriel turned toward him.
A further message followed.
[It says "before influence is extended beyond it." I have treated those as equivalent.]
[I would like to verify the preceding section.]
Leon stayed quiet.
Several minutes passed. Outside, a cart rattled along the street, followed by an argument about who had left empty crates in the road.
He envied both participants. Their disagreement probably involved words whose meaning everybody understood.
Then Moon returned.
[The preceding section concerns establishing a boundary capable of retaining the gathered influence. The extension described there is a controlled test of whether that preparation holds.]

[The lineage transmission begins after that condition has been achieved. Its release is not the opening Stillwater warns against. The consolidated structure must remain intact while its fixed limit is relinquished.]
Leon frowned and read the messages again.
He could follow the distinction now, although he would not have trusted himself to perform either operation.

One text explained how to establish something capable of expansion. The other assumed the preparation was complete and described using it. Similar language had led Moon to compare instructions that belonged at different points.
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: They are consecutive.]
The next message took longer.
[I kept returning to the two commands because I believed that was where they disagreed. I should have returned to what each author required before giving them.]
Leon let out a breath.
Loriel touched his wrist.
"What happened?"
He explained as faithfully as he could.
"She thinks she was comparing preparation with the actual expansion. One of the words didn’t mean quite the same thing in both texts."
"Is she certain?"
As though answering her, Moon sent another message.
[I must examine my preparation against the complete Stillwater conditions. I have tested its stability, but not by the sequence described here.]
[There may still be deficiencies. At least I now know what I need to check.]
That sounded considerably better than an immediate attempt to break through.
Leon waited, unwilling to interrupt while she was finally making sense of her own problem.
[You did not choose a teaching for me.]
His stomach tightened.
[You asked why I had placed them in opposition. None of the people I consulted asked that. I showed them the same two passages, and we all continued arguing from my comparison.]
[Thank you for making me explain it.]
Leon leaned back.
Making you explain it was the only thing I could do.
He had spent the conversation trying to buy enough time to understand the question. She had used that time to find an answer.
He could be pleased about that without pretending he understood her cultivation.
After a moment, he sent the one piece of advice he trusted.
[Elemental Paragon: Verify the conditions before you act. Understanding the distinction does not establish that your preparation meets it.]
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: I will. Thank you, my Lord.]
Leon closed the private exchange.
"She’s going to check everything," he told Loriel. "Before trying anything."
"Good."
He rubbed his palms against his trousers and discovered they were damp.
"That could have gone badly."
"But it didn’t," Loriel said.
"This time."
She accepted that without arguing.
A new message appeared in the group.

[MoonWhoEatsHerself: Honored Paragon, thank you for your guidance. I will not share the details of our consultation. Your question showed me that I had been comparing two stages of a process as though they were competing instructions.]
[The Ninth Silence: An assumption carried into every rereading. Those are difficult to notice from inside your own reasoning.]
[Sablewright: Especially when everyone you ask accepts the comparison.]
[Vaunt of the Chained Choir: He could have given you the conclusion. Instead, he made you find where you had gone wrong.]
Leon read the exchange to Loriel.
Her mouth twitched.
"Don’t," he said.
"I haven’t said anything."
"You’re about to."
She smiled, then squeezed his arm.
"You did help her."
"I asked because I had nothing useful to tell her."
"And she found something useful while answering."
Leon looked back at Moon’s thanks.

He had expected the money to be the best part of opening the chat. He was still delighted about the money, but knowing she would not have to sit over the same two passages tomorrow felt unexpectedly good.
That did not make him qualified to guide her.
"I’m not answering the next one so quickly," he said.
Loriel glanced at him.
"Good."
The communication plaque chimed before he could decide whether she had agreed too readily.
Ji’s reply had arrived.
Leon rose and picked it up.
Evidence received and reviewed. Elder Ruan confirms the correspondence between the tool samples. Preserve the original recording.
You have permission to pursue the White Reed Crossing delivery under the existing terms of your assignment. Establish a daily reporting window before departure and report immediately upon contact.
The recording identifies a Qiao connection. It does not identify the Hollow Steward or authorize action against the clan as a whole. Keep Palace involvement concealed.
If the escort exceeds what your household can safely handle, observe and report. I will send what is needed.
Use your judgment, disciple.
He read the last sentence again.
After an afternoon pretending to possess wisdom beyond comprehension, receiving a sensible instruction from somebody who knew him was almost restful.
"Permission?" Loriel asked.
"Yes. We leave in the morning."
Only hours had passed since his report. The four-day route still left time to examine the crossing before the delivery, provided they did not waste tomorrow.
"Tell Vyra we have approval," Leon said. "I’ll go through the conditions with Seraphine when she returns. We need to speak to Qingyue before fixing the route."
Loriel began securing her case.
"And these?"
"Bring them."
"She needs different soil," Loriel said, checking one last cutting. "The merchant told me she preferred dry ground."
"She?"
"The plant."
"I understood that part."
Loriel gave him a brief smile and fastened the lid.
At the door, she looked back.
"I meant what I said."
Leon knew which conversation she meant.
"I know."
She left, and he began composing the acknowledgment to Ji.
A private notification opened beside it.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: You have been absent for some time. What kept you so occupied?]
Leon’s hand stopped above the plaque.
He knew that name.

She had questioned him before, politely enough that he could never decide how much suspicion lay beneath the interest. There had been no groveling, no frightened gratitude, and no assumption that he would dislike being asked.
She really was a Lord of the Universe.
Leon reread the message, hoping to find something in its tone that told him whether she had heard the rumor.
There was nothing. Just an ordinary question from someone who might understand every subject he could pretend to have been studying.
Ji’s authorization remained in his hand.
For one brief, tempting moment, he considered answering honestly.
I finally reached Early Qi Refinement.
He closed his eyes.
That would certainly give her something to think about.

Loriel drew her knees closer beneath her robe.
Leon looked back at the messages.
Moon had been cautious.
Nothing in her account sounded foolish.
She had valuable preparation to protect, two credible sources giving apparently contradictory instructions, and no confidence that acting would improve matters.
He knew that feeling rather well.
The difference was that she expected him to know the answer.
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: Neither source is one I can dismiss.
I have compared the relevant passages repeatedly.
Both describe the boundary I am preparing to extend.]
Leon considered asking for the complete texts, but that would only provide him with a larger quantity of things he did not understand.
Start with what she thinks they mean.
He composed a question.
[Elemental Paragon: Tell me why you believe they describe the same step.]
His finger moved against his knee as he sent it.
There was no keyboard, no physical action required, yet he caught himself doing it anyway.
Loriel watched his face.
"What did you say?"
He told her.
"Do you think that’s the mistake?"
"I think I need her to explain more."
Moon’s reply appeared.
[Both address the boundary before its expansion.
The first requires it to remain closed while influence is gathered and directed beyond it.
The second requires its release.]
[My prepared influence must cross that boundary for the extension to become stable.
Therefore, both requirements appear to govern the same operation.]
Leon read the answer aloud, more slowly this time.
There might be something in that distinction.
Or he might simply be arranging unfamiliar words into an explanation he wanted to hear.
He did not trust himself to choose.
Moon sent another message before he could respond.
[The first passage does not actually say "before its expansion." That is my description.]
Loriel turned toward him.
A further message followed.
[It says "before influence is extended beyond it." I have treated those as equivalent.]
[I would like to verify the preceding section.]
Leon stayed quiet.
Several minutes passed.
Outside, a cart rattled along the street, followed by an argument about who had left empty crates in the road.
He envied both participants.
Their disagreement probably involved words whose meaning everybody understood.
Then Moon returned.
[The preceding section concerns establishing a boundary capable of retaining the gathered influence.
The extension described there is a controlled test of whether that preparation holds.]
[The lineage transmission begins after that condition has been achieved.
Its release is not the opening Stillwater warns against.
The consolidated structure must remain intact while its fixed limit is relinquished.]
Leon frowned and read the messages again.
He could follow the distinction now, although he would not have trusted himself to perform either operation.
One text explained how to establish something capable of expansion.
The other assumed the preparation was complete and described using it.
Similar language had led Moon to compare instructions that belonged at different points.
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: They are consecutive.]
The next message took longer.
[I kept returning to the two commands because I believed that was where they disagreed.
I should have returned to what each author required before giving them.]
Leon let out a breath.
Loriel touched his wrist.
"What happened?"
He explained as faithfully as he could.
"She thinks she was comparing preparation with the actual expansion.
One of the words didn’t mean quite the same thing in both texts."
"Is she certain?"
As though answering her, Moon sent another message.
[I must examine my preparation against the complete Stillwater conditions.
I have tested its stability, but not by the sequence described here.]
[There may still be deficiencies.
At least I now know what I need to check.]
That sounded considerably better than an immediate attempt to break through.
Leon waited, unwilling to interrupt while she was finally making sense of her own problem.
[You did not choose a teaching for me.]
His stomach tightened.
[You asked why I had placed them in opposition.
None of the people I consulted asked that.
I showed them the same two passages, and we all continued arguing from my comparison.]
[Thank you for making me explain it.]
Leon leaned back.
Making you explain it was the only thing I could do.
He had spent the conversation trying to buy enough time to understand the question.
She had used that time to find an answer.
He could be pleased about that without pretending he understood her cultivation.
After a moment, he sent the one piece of advice he trusted.
[Elemental Paragon: Verify the conditions before you act.
Understanding the distinction does not establish that your preparation meets it.]
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: I will.
Thank you, my Lord.]
Leon closed the private exchange.
"She’s going to check everything," he told Loriel.
"Before trying anything."
"Good."
He rubbed his palms against his trousers and discovered they were damp.
"That could have gone badly."
"But it didn’t," Loriel said.
"This time."
She accepted that without arguing.
A new message appeared in the group.
[MoonWhoEatsHerself: Honored Paragon, thank you for your guidance.
I will not share the details of our consultation.
Your question showed me that I had been comparing two stages of a process as though they were competing instructions.]
[The Ninth Silence: An assumption carried into every rereading.
Those are difficult to notice from inside your own reasoning.]
[Sablewright: Especially when everyone you ask accepts the comparison.]
[Vaunt of the Chained Choir: He could have given you the conclusion.
Instead, he made you find where you had gone wrong.]
Leon read the exchange to Loriel.
Her mouth twitched.
"Don’t," he said.
"I haven’t said anything."
"You’re about to."
She smiled, then squeezed his arm.
"You did help her."
"I asked because I had nothing useful to tell her."
"And she found something useful while answering."
Leon looked back at Moon’s thanks.
He had expected the money to be the best part of opening the chat.
He was still delighted about the money, but knowing she would not have to sit over the same two passages tomorrow felt unexpectedly good.
That did not make him qualified to guide her.
"I’m not answering the next one so quickly," he said.
Loriel glanced at him.
"Good."
The communication plaque chimed before he could decide whether she had agreed too readily.
Ji’s reply had arrived.
Leon rose and picked it up.
Evidence received and reviewed.
Elder Ruan confirms the correspondence between the tool samples.
Preserve the original recording.
You have permission to pursue the White Reed Crossing delivery under the existing terms of your assignment.
Establish a daily reporting window before departure and report immediately upon contact.
The recording identifies a Qiao connection.
It does not identify the Hollow Steward or authorize action against the clan as a whole.
Keep Palace involvement concealed.
If the escort exceeds what your household can safely handle, observe and report.
I will send what is needed.
Use your judgment, disciple.
He read the last sentence again.
After an afternoon pretending to possess wisdom beyond comprehension, receiving a sensible instruction from somebody who knew him was almost restful.
"Permission?" Loriel asked.
"Yes.
We leave in the morning."
Only hours had passed since his report.
The four-day route still left time to examine the crossing before the delivery, provided they did not waste tomorrow.
"Tell Vyra we have approval," Leon said.
"I’ll go through the conditions with Seraphine when she returns.
We need to speak to Qingyue before fixing the route."
Loriel began securing her case.
"And these?"
"Bring them."
"She needs different soil," Loriel said, checking one last cutting.
"The merchant told me she preferred dry ground."
"She?"
"The plant."
"I understood that part."
Loriel gave him a brief smile and fastened the lid.
At the door, she looked back.
"I meant what I said."
Leon knew which conversation she meant.
"I know."
She left, and he began composing the acknowledgment to Ji.
A private notification opened beside it.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: You have been absent for some time.
What kept you so occupied?]
Leon’s hand stopped above the plaque.
He knew that name.
She had questioned him before, politely enough that he could never decide how much suspicion lay beneath the interest.
There had been no groveling, no frightened gratitude, and no assumption that he would dislike being asked.
She really was a Lord of the Universe.
Leon reread the message, hoping to find something in its tone that told him whether she had heard the rumor.
There was nothing.
Just an ordinary question from someone who might understand every subject he could pretend to have been studying.
Ji’s authorization remained in his hand.
For one brief, tempting moment, he considered answering honestly.
I finally reached Early Qi Refinement.
He closed his eyes.
That would certainly give her something to think about.

chapters.title: Chapter 682: The Art of Sounding Certain
paragraphs: Ji’s communication plaque lay beside Leon’s elbow, its seal dark now that he had finished reading her instructions.
The message in front of his eyes remained.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: You have been absent for some time. What kept you so occupied?]
For a moment, he wanted to tell her.

Seven months of his own time, seven preserved Void Immortal cores, and more failed adjustments than he cared to remember—all to establish Early Qi Refinement. He was proud of it. He had earned the right to be proud of it, and discussing the work with someone who actually understood cultivation would have been a pleasure.
Unfortunately, this particular person believed he was a Lord of the Universe.
She might congratulate me. Right before asking what the fuck I’ve been doing with everyone’s money.
Leon pulled his chair closer to the table.
He could tell her about the method. He needed to leave out the part where its creator had only recently managed to cultivate with it.
[Elemental Paragon: I have been developing a cultivation method that accommodates different affinities while preserving their individual properties. It has kept me occupied.]
He read the message once more before sending it.
Accurate. Restrained. Nothing he would have to defend with a demonstration.
Her response arrived while he was reaching for his cup.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: Why preserve them? Finding the principle they share would simplify the structure considerably.]
Leon lowered the cup.

That was a reasonable question. He had considered the same approach while working through his early designs, and he had reasons for rejecting it. His body, existing abilities, and plans for the Scripture all favored keeping the affinities distinct.
None of those reasons sounded especially impressive at the scale on which she lived.
He began typing anyway.
[Elemental Paragon: Because I have not decided that what they share is the only part worth keeping.]
That sounded better than he had expected.
Encouraged, he continued.

[A common principle is an efficient foundation. But if I build everything around it, the method will favor the properties that fit that foundation. I would rather retain the differences until I know what I want to do with them.]
He should have stopped there.
[What fire does is not necessarily what fire and water have in common. Reducing both to the same explanation may be elegant, but elegance was not the purpose of the exercise.]
Leon stared at the last sentence.
The exercise.
Seven months sitting in Xyra’s accelerated field, correcting the same stubborn branch until he wanted to bite something, and he had called it an exercise.
The Lord took a little longer to answer.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: That depends on the reduction. A sufficiently complete principle need not discard anything.]
Of course it does. Of course there’s a better version.
Another message followed.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: But preserving the distinctions gives you room to develop their interactions separately. Is that what interests you?]
Leon’s fingers hovered above the table.
It did interest him. It simply had not been the grand intention behind every decision he had made.
[Elemental Paragon: Among other things. I would prefer the method to leave me more than one direction of development.]
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: An expensive preference.]
He looked at the message and almost smiled.
[Elemental Paragon: I have noticed.]
For the first time since opening the conversation, he sent a reply without worrying about it.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: How many affinities are you retaining?]
[Elemental Paragon: Nine, currently.]
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: Separately regulated, then brought through a common circulation?]
Leon sat a little straighter.
[Elemental Paragon: Through a neutral section, yes. The branches remain distinct.]
He had offered only a broad description. She had not seen the Scripture, his body, or the Primordial Void Heart supplying the circulation, and he intended to keep it that way.
Still, her next question landed uncomfortably close.
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: And are you matching their flow?]
Leon glanced down at his own chest.
[Elemental Paragon: For the present structure. It gave me a consistent starting condition.]
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: Reasonable. It becomes less useful if you carry that condition into every level of output.]
He forgot about his tea.

[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: Different affinities respond differently to pressure and to one another. Identical flow can produce unequal strain. I would compare what happens where the currents meet before deciding how closely their rates need to match.]
Leon read the message twice.
He understood every word. That made the realization more irritating.

He had spent so long making the nine branches behave consistently that consistency had become the first thing he demanded of every later design. When a branch departed from the pattern, he corrected it.
During some of his tests, the Earth branch had repeatedly settled slightly below his intended rate. He had treated that as a fault to eliminate.
It might still be a fault.
But he had never allowed it to remain long enough to discover whether the rest of the circulation became more stable around it.
I kept asking why it wouldn’t match.
He leaned forward, elbows on the table.

There were reasons for the matched flow. He had needed a reliable baseline while establishing the Scripture’s first native circulation, and the method worked. That did not mean the same proportions would serve him equally well when he increased the output.
His mind began assembling tests before he could stop it.
Change one branch. Keep the others fixed. Measure the strain where it returned to the neutral route. Then repeat at a slightly different volume.
The neutral section complicated everything. A comfortable rate inside one branch might create a dangerous imbalance when it rejoined the others.
He had questions about that. Quite a few.
Asking all of them would make it painfully clear how new this was to him.
[Elemental Paragon: I have retained the matched flow as a reference. I have not yet established how far the individual rates can depart from it without affecting the common route.]
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: Then it should make an interesting comparison. A stable interaction tells you more than matching measurements alone.]
Leon let himself sit with that for a few breaths.

She had not solved the Scripture. She could not have, from the little he had told her. She had pointed at an assumption he now wanted to examine, which was useful enough that he felt an absurd urge to thank her properly.
Instead, he wrote:
[Elemental Paragon: I will compare the responses before making any changes permanent.]
[Lord of Illusion and Mystery: Let me know if you find something unusual.]
Leon’s brief relief faltered.
Right. There’s a later conversation now.
[Elemental Paragon: If the results warrant it.]
She sent nothing further.
He waited anyway, until waiting began to feel ridiculous, then closed the interface.

The room was quiet. Somewhere below, an inn worker was arguing with a guest about a missing basin. Leon listened to them for a moment, grateful that neither person expected him to understand the foundations of existence.
Then he found paper.
He recorded her observation first, as closely as he remembered it, followed by the questions he had been unable to ask. Beneath those, he sketched the neutral route and its nine branches.
His pen paused over Earth.
You had better turn out to be doing something useful. I’ve spent far too long correcting you.
He ran one ordinary circulation while seated at the table. Mana moved through the established route without difficulty, supplied by his Primordial Void Heart. He changed nothing.

The experiment would need privacy, careful measurements, and time inside his dimensional world. Xyra could provide the time easily enough. What Leon could not do was disappear into the work and forget the people waiting for him outside.
White Reed Crossing came first.
He folded the notes and put them away before he could persuade himself that one tiny adjustment would hardly count as an experiment.
Only then did he pick up his tea.
It had gone cold.
Leon drank it anyway, still pleased enough with what he had learned that he barely noticed.

chapters.title: Chapter 683: What the Registry Didn’t Say
paragraphs: Loriel returned with the others less than an hour later.
She looked at Leon first, then at the folded paper beneath his hand. Whatever she read in his expression made her relax a little, but she asked no questions in front of Qingyue.
Vyra spread a supply list across the table.
"We can leave at first light, Young Master. The route takes four days at the pace we discussed."

"Good." Leon moved his notes aside and placed Ji’s plaque where everyone could see it. "Daily reports once we leave. An immediate update when we make contact with the delivery. We preserve the evidence and keep the Palace’s involvement private."
Seraphine read the authorization before passing it to Vyra.
"And if we find something that needs more people?" she asked.
"We tell my master what we’ve found. She’ll arrange support."
Vyra checked that part herself, then nodded.

Qingyue had brought news of the road and the crossing’s customs office. The officer in charge had held the position for six years, and the freight rules had apparently changed very little during that time.
"That helps," she said. "We can ask ordinary questions without looking as though we’ve arrived to inspect the place."

They settled the remaining arrangements over supper. By the time Leon went to bed, their evidence was packed securely and Vyra had made sure the resource-buying cover included actual resources worth buying.
They left Moonfall the next morning.
An hour beyond the gate, Ira brought her horse alongside Leon’s.
"You’ve been distracted since last night, Young Master."
"I had an idea."
She looked at him with immediate suspicion. "What kind?"
"Something I want to test when we have a quiet room and time to spare."
"Can it wait until then?"
Leon glanced at her.
Ira’s expression remained perfectly serious.
"Yes," he said.
"Good." She eased her horse back toward Loriel. "I wanted to hear you say it."

The road grew busier with freight as they traveled east. By the second day, grain wagons and covered cultivation-goods carts outnumbered passengers. At the waystations, almost every conversation eventually became an argument about tolls.
Qingyue pointed out the markings on a pair of wagons ahead.
"Bonded transit. Those are going straight onto a barge."
Leon studied the painted seal. "The owner’s mark?"

"The customs bond. The owner’s is underneath." She indicated a smaller character near the axle. "We’ll need to distinguish goods passing through from goods being held. Otherwise we could spend the whole visit watching wagons that leave an hour later."
It was the sort of detail Leon would have had to ask someone about. Qingyue knew it without slowing down.
On the third evening, they stopped at a merchants’ rest house with a crowded yard and a kitchen that smelled promising. Vyra secured a table while Seraphine checked the rooms.
By the time the food arrived, Qingyue was hungry enough to stop thinking about freight.
For a little while.
Ira took a piece of fish from Leon’s plate while answering Loriel’s question about the road.
She did it without asking. Leon merely shifted his cup out of the way so her sleeve would not catch it.
Qingyue noticed, then tried not to notice.
It was a small thing. People who traveled together grew comfortable with one another. She had shared food with companions herself.

A few minutes later, Seraphine leaned past Leon to reach the water jug. On the way back, she straightened the folded edge of his collar with two fingers. He continued explaining something to Vyra, apparently unaware that she had done it.
Loriel sat close beside him. When the server squeezed past their table, she moved nearer rather than drawing away, and remained there after the woman had gone.
Qingyue lowered her eyes to her bowl.
Oh.
The possibility settled into place with embarrassing ease.
He was probably sleeping with them.

Not necessarily all four. She could not establish that by watching people eat, and she had no intention of asking. But the easy familiarity suggested something that continued well beyond their public duties.
She had not thought he was like that.

Which was foolish, perhaps. Leon was extraordinarily handsome, and his talent had drawn the Palace Mistress’s personal attention. Of course women would be attracted to him. Nothing about that required an explanation.
It was the four attendants together that bothered her slightly.
With everything you have going for you, surely you could spend a little more time cultivating.
She took another bite and immediately remembered how little she knew about his days.

He could have spent every private hour working for all she knew. She had seen enough of his ability during the trouble at her family’s estate to know it had not appeared merely because he had a pleasing face.
Still, the thought persisted.
Four beautiful women attending to him, traveling with him, looking entirely at ease reaching into his space.
Leon asked her whether the western landing handled medicinal goods.
Qingyue looked up a fraction too late.
"Some," she said. "Mostly the packaged varieties. Fresh plants usually go through the smaller yards where they can be kept out of the sun."
He thanked her and returned to the discussion.
She watched him for another moment.
It isn’t my business.
That was true. Whatever happened in his rooms concerned him and the women involved. None of them looked unhappy with the arrangement.
Qingyue concentrated on her supper.
Leon caught her giving him an odd look the following morning.
He checked his sleeve in case he had spilled breakfast on it.
Nothing.
The second time, he met her eyes. Qingyue turned toward an approaching cart and remarked on its axle width as though that had been her interest all along.
Leon considered asking, then decided against it.
She was answering questions and helping with the route. Whatever else occupied her could remain hers until she chose to say it.
They reached White Reed Crossing on the fourth day.

A broad river ran beyond the customs house, brown-green beneath the afternoon light. The ford lay upstream, where carts waited their turn through the shallows. Downstream, three timber landings served the barges, with fenced holding yards stretching behind them.
Porters shouted over one another. Someone was trying to persuade a mule onto a loading ramp. The mule appeared to have a better understanding of the ramp’s condition than its owner.
Leon watched a plank bend beneath one hoof.
"I wouldn’t," he murmured.
The mule backed away.
Once they had rooms, Vyra checked the delivery date against their arrival.
"The handover is the evening after tomorrow, Young Master. We have this afternoon and tomorrow to locate it."
They began with the freight offices.

Qingyue identified the yards that accepted consignments held for named collectors. Vyra then visited one of the landing clerks to inquire about storage for a possible cultivation-goods purchase. The inquiry was genuine enough; if the terms were favorable, she intended to use them.
Leon accompanied her for the first conversation, then left her to it when the clerk began discussing insurance exclusions.
He understood every word. He simply suspected Vyra would get more out of the man without him standing there looking increasingly bored.
She returned with a rate card and two useful names.

"Only two yards regularly accept that arrangement," she said. "The eastern yard’s available space has been taken by a bonded tea shipment. The western one reserved its inner shed eleven days ago, paid through the end of the month."
"For what?" Leon asked.
"The clerk wasn’t told. He complained that they’re paying to keep most of it empty."
Seraphine spent the remaining daylight near the western yard.
Her report was brief.

"Four outer guards, Young Master. They rotate around the inner fence. The yard workers handle the front compound, but the foreman calls one of the guards whenever he needs anything beyond the second gate."
"Could it be valuable freight?" Qingyue asked.
"Easily," Seraphine replied. "It’s worth watching. That’s all we know yet."
Leon looked at the small sketch she had made of the yard.
A reserved shed, guards separate from the ordinary workers, and a collector expected soon.
Enough to follow.
He set his finger beside the river-facing wall.
"Then we find somewhere with a view of this side."
