The route takes four days at the pace we discussed."
"Good." Leon moved his notes aside and placed Ji’s plaque where everyone could see it.
"Daily reports once we leave.
An immediate update when we make contact with the delivery.
We preserve the evidence and keep the Palace’s involvement private."
Seraphine read the authorization before passing it to Vyra.
"And if we find something that needs more people?" she asked.
"We tell my master what we’ve found.
She’ll arrange support."
Vyra checked that part herself, then nodded.
Qingyue had brought news of the road and the crossing’s customs office.
The officer in charge had held the position for six years, and the freight rules had apparently changed very little during that time.
"That helps," she said.
"We can ask ordinary questions without looking as though we’ve arrived to inspect the place."
They settled the remaining arrangements over supper.
By the time Leon went to bed, their evidence was packed securely and Vyra had made sure the resource-buying cover included actual resources worth buying.
They left Moonfall the next morning.
An hour beyond the gate, Ira brought her horse alongside Leon’s.
"You’ve been distracted since last night, Young Master."
"I had an idea."
She looked at him with immediate suspicion.
"What kind?"
"Something I want to test when we have a quiet room and time to spare."
"Can it wait until then?"
Leon glanced at her.
Ira’s expression remained perfectly serious.
"Yes," he said.
"Good." She eased her horse back toward Loriel.
"I wanted to hear you say it."
The road grew busier with freight as they traveled east.
By the second day, grain wagons and covered cultivation-goods carts outnumbered passengers.
At the waystations, almost every conversation eventually became an argument about tolls.
Qingyue pointed out the markings on a pair of wagons ahead.
"Bonded transit.
Those are going straight onto a barge."
Leon studied the painted seal.
"The owner’s mark?"
"The customs bond.
The owner’s is underneath." She indicated a smaller character near the axle.
"We’ll need to distinguish goods passing through from goods being held.
Otherwise we could spend the whole visit watching wagons that leave an hour later."
It was the sort of detail Leon would have had to ask someone about.
Qingyue knew it without slowing down.
On the third evening, they stopped at a merchants’ rest house with a crowded yard and a kitchen that smelled promising.
Vyra secured a table while Seraphine checked the rooms.
By the time the food arrived, Qingyue was hungry enough to stop thinking about freight.
For a little while.
Ira took a piece of fish from Leon’s plate while answering Loriel’s question about the road.
She did it without asking.
Leon merely shifted his cup out of the way so her sleeve would not catch it.
Qingyue noticed, then tried not to notice.
It was a small thing.
People who traveled together grew comfortable with one another.
She had shared food with companions herself.
A few minutes later, Seraphine leaned past Leon to reach the water jug.
On the way back, she straightened the folded edge of his collar with two fingers.
He continued explaining something to Vyra, apparently unaware that she had done it.
Loriel sat close beside him.
When the server squeezed past their table, she moved nearer rather than drawing away, and remained there after the woman had gone.
Qingyue lowered her eyes to her bowl.
Oh.
The possibility settled into place with embarrassing ease.
He was probably sleeping with them.
Not necessarily all four.
She could not establish that by watching people eat, and she had no intention of asking.
But the easy familiarity suggested something that continued well beyond their public duties.
She had not thought he was like that.
Which was foolish, perhaps.
Leon was extraordinarily handsome, and his talent had drawn the Palace Mistress’s personal attention.
Of course women would be attracted to him.
Nothing about that required an explanation.
It was the four attendants together that bothered her slightly.
With everything you have going for you, surely you could spend a little more time cultivating.
She took another bite and immediately remembered how little she knew about his days.
He could have spent every private hour working for all she knew.
She had seen enough of his ability during the trouble at her family’s estate to know it had not appeared merely because he had a pleasing face.
Still, the thought persisted.
Four beautiful women attending to him, traveling with him, looking entirely at ease reaching into his space.
Leon asked her whether the western landing handled medicinal goods.
Qingyue looked up a fraction too late.
"Some," she said.
"Mostly the packaged varieties.
Fresh plants usually go through the smaller yards where they can be kept out of the sun."
He thanked her and returned to the discussion.
She watched him for another moment.
It isn’t my business.
That was true.
Whatever happened in his rooms concerned him and the women involved.
None of them looked unhappy with the arrangement.
Qingyue concentrated on her supper.
Leon caught her giving him an odd look the following morning.
He checked his sleeve in case he had spilled breakfast on it.
Nothing.
The second time, he met her eyes.
Qingyue turned toward an approaching cart and remarked on its axle width as though that had been her interest all along.
Leon considered asking, then decided against it.
She was answering questions and helping with the route.
Whatever else occupied her could remain hers until she chose to say it.
They reached White Reed Crossing on the fourth day.
A broad river ran beyond the customs house, brown-green beneath the afternoon light.
The ford lay upstream, where carts waited their turn through the shallows.
Downstream, three timber landings served the barges, with fenced holding yards stretching behind them.
Porters shouted over one another.
Someone was trying to persuade a mule onto a loading ramp.
The mule appeared to have a better understanding of the ramp’s condition than its owner.
Leon watched a plank bend beneath one hoof.
"I wouldn’t," he murmured.
The mule backed away.
Once they had rooms, Vyra checked the delivery date against their arrival.
"The handover is the evening after tomorrow, Young Master.
We have this afternoon and tomorrow to locate it."
They began with the freight offices.
Qingyue identified the yards that accepted consignments held for named collectors.
Vyra then visited one of the landing clerks to inquire about storage for a possible cultivation-goods purchase.
The inquiry was genuine enough; if the terms were favorable, she intended to use them.
Leon accompanied her for the first conversation, then left her to it when the clerk began discussing insurance exclusions.
He understood every word.
He simply suspected Vyra would get more out of the man without him standing there looking increasingly bored.
She returned with a rate card and two useful names.
"Only two yards regularly accept that arrangement," she said.
"The eastern yard’s available space has been taken by a bonded tea shipment.
The western one reserved its inner shed eleven days ago, paid through the end of the month."
"For what?" Leon asked.
"The clerk wasn’t told.
He complained that they’re paying to keep most of it empty."
Seraphine spent the remaining daylight near the western yard.
Her report was brief.
"Four outer guards, Young Master.
They rotate around the inner fence.
The yard workers handle the front compound, but the foreman calls one of the guards whenever he needs anything beyond the second gate."
"Could it be valuable freight?" Qingyue asked.
"Easily," Seraphine replied.
"It’s worth watching.
That’s all we know yet."
Leon looked at the small sketch she had made of the yard.
A reserved shed, guards separate from the ordinary workers, and a collector expected soon.
Enough to follow.
He set his finger beside the river-facing wall.
"Then we find somewhere with a view of this side."

chapters.title: Chapter 684: The Man in the Shipment
paragraphs: They watched the western yard through the following day.

There was little to reward the attention. Porters brought sacks into the front compound, argued about their count, and carried several out again. The foreman ate his midday meal beneath an awning. Beyond the second gate, the four guards changed positions at regular intervals.
Nobody opened the inner shed.
Leon took his turn observing in the afternoon, then returned to the rooms before dusk to compare what they had seen.
"The night crew stays in the front yard," Qingyue said. "They unload late carts, but the river deliveries stop once the landing lamps are put out."
Vyra had confirmed the same arrangement through the freight office. Neither had needed to mention the western shed.
Seraphine pointed to a stack of timber on her sketch.
"From here we can see over the inner fence. The loading awning blocks the view from the road."
Leon nodded. "We’ll take it after dark."

Ira and Loriel would remain near the public landing, close enough to respond without gathering six unfamiliar people around one fence. Vyra and Qingyue would keep the rooms, the evidence, and their route back clear.
Before leaving, Leon checked Ji’s reporting plaque. Their daily update had gone through. Any discovery worth acting on would receive a separate report.
The covered wagon arrived well after sunset.
Leon lay beside Seraphine beneath the edge of a tarpaulin, watching through a gap between stacked beams. They had a clear view of the second gate and most of the ground before the shed.
The wagon bore no house mark.
Its driver waited while one of the guards inspected a token. Then the gate opened, and he brought it inside.

The four outer guards left their usual positions to receive it. Two stayed near the wheels while the other two watched the approaches. A fifth guard emerged from the shed with a middle-aged man carrying a small, dark case.
The man looked like a clerk. Plain sleeves, tidy hair, no visible weapon.
He checked the case’s clasp while the wagon stopped.
Two escorts climbed down from the rear.
Between them, they brought out a prisoner.
Leon shifted closer to the gap.

The captive appeared to be around fifty. He wore a stained inner robe, and his feet dragged briefly before he found his balance. The escorts held him under the arms, supporting enough of his weight that Leon could not tell whether he was injured, exhausted, or both.
His eyes moved around the yard.
Conscious, then. Aware of his surroundings.
Bindings circled his lower forearms, holding them together in front of him. They were narrow and dark, with a faint pattern Leon could not distinguish at this distance.
His hands remained free.
One escort adjusted his grip as they lowered the captive from the wagon, taking care not to catch the man’s fingers against the wooden side.
Leon felt his attention sharpen.
They need those intact.
The clerk stepped closer.
"Can he reproduce the seam-cutting?" he asked.
One of the escorts nodded. "And the depth work. He trained the two at the Moonfall shop."
Leon glanced at Seraphine.
She was watching the men below, her expression still.
"He’ll need a proper bench," the escort continued. "And tools."
"They’re being arranged," the clerk said. "I want him working by the end of the week. We’ve already lost enough time replacing the Moonfall staff."
The prisoner said something too quietly for Leon to catch.
The escort answered, "Inside."
No shout. He simply tightened his grip and turned the man toward the shed.
The fifth guard opened the door. Both escorts took the captive through while the clerk remained outside, speaking to the driver.
A few minutes later, the escorts returned without their prisoner. One accepted a receipt from the clerk. They climbed onto the wagon, and the driver took them back through the gate.
Leon counted them out.
Driver and two escorts departing. Four guards resuming their positions around the compound. The fifth staying inside with the captive.
The clerk checked his case again, then entered the shed.
Seraphine waited until the wheels had faded beyond the yard.
"Replacement staff," she said softly.
Leon kept looking at the door.
Fourteen people had died in the Moonfall workshop. The men here spoke about replacing them as though a broken furnace had interrupted production.

The reserved shed had been arranged well before Leon arrived. Whether this particular prisoner had already been in their hands or had been redirected afterward, the organization had been preparing another supply route.
They had not needed to know anyone was investigating them.
That made the room full of bodies in Moonfall worse somehow.
Leon drew his attention back to the yard.
"We have five guards remaining," he murmured. "Four outside, one with the prisoner. The clerk is inside too."
Seraphine nodded. "The escorts have gone."
"I couldn’t read the bindings from here."
"Neither could I."
That was the first problem. Not the guards.

Leon could remove ordinary restraints easily. He could also kill everyone in the yard before most of them understood they were under attack. Neither fact told him what those bands might do when disturbed.
The man wearing them would bear the consequences of a careless guess.
"The case may hold a control," Seraphine said.
"Possibly." Leon watched the lit window. "He kept checking it, but it could be payment or documents. We need to see whether he uses it around the prisoner."
"And whether the fifth guard has anything similar."
"Exactly."

Below them, one of the outer guards paused to speak with a porter through the fence. The porter pointed toward a stack of empty crates. After a short exchange, the guard moved them aside and returned to his route.
Ordinary workers still had reasons to come close.
Leon waited until the porter had left.
"Have Ira check the river side of the shed," he said. "Doors, windows, anything we can use to bring him out. No entry yet."
"Loriel?"
"She stays near the landing until we know his condition. Once we move, I want her ready to receive him."
Seraphine studied the gap between the shed and the outer fence.
"We can bring him through there if it’s clear."
"Check where the night workers can see it. I don’t want a frightened carter raising an alarm before we’ve left the compound."
She nodded and began easing backward beneath the tarpaulin.
Leon caught her sleeve lightly before she went.
"Tell Vyra what we heard. I’ll send the contact report."
Seraphine touched his wrist in acknowledgment, then slipped down from the timber.
Leon waited until she was clear before taking out Ji’s plaque. Sheltered beneath the covering, he kept its light screened while recording the essentials.

They had located a captive formation master. The receiving agent had explicitly connected his work to the murdered workshop. The final handover remained scheduled for tomorrow night. Leon intended to extract him once they had identified his restraints and secured a route out.
He sent the report and put the plaque away.
There was no need to ask his master to repeat the authority she had already given him. There was every reason to tell her what he planned.
A shadow crossed the shed’s window.
Leon could not tell whether it belonged to the clerk, the guard, or the prisoner. He watched until it disappeared.
Until tonight, the delivery had been a useful piece of evidence: something to follow, intercept, and trace back to the people who supplied the formation-breaking tools.
Now he had seen the man expected to make them.

He wondered whether the captive knew what had happened to his former students in Moonfall. Whether the guards had told him, or whether he still believed he could finish whatever work they demanded and go home.
Leon shifted carefully, finding a more comfortable position between the beams.
Tomorrow night is their deadline.
He intended to move before it.
For now, he watched the doors.

chapters.title: Chapter 685: Enough of Other People’s Business
paragraphs: The clerk finally opened his case four hours after the wagon left.

Leon shifted beneath the tarpaulin, easing his weight off a beam that had been pressing into his ribs. Through the shed’s lit window, he could see the man set the case on a bench and turn something inside it.
Across the room, the captive straightened.
His hands stopped trembling. He looked down at them, flexed his fingers, then reached for the tools the clerk placed in front of him.
"There," Leon murmured.
Seraphine was already studying the change.
"The suppression weakened when he adjusted it," she said. "I can follow the connection now."

So could Leon. With the controller active and the captive circulating again, the restraint’s structure was much easier to distinguish. The bands pressed against his channels, limiting how much energy he could move. The case regulated that pressure through a thin spiritual tether.
Leon traced it carefully before checking the bands themselves.
No concealed attack. No secondary formation waiting to activate if the connection broke.
All that watching for a man with a dial.
Still, he preferred the wasted hours to discovering something unpleasant after he had cut it.
"Ordinary suppression," he said. "Sever the tether and it releases. We take the case intact."
Seraphine nodded. "Ira found a clear route behind the shed. The night workers are leaving for their meal."
"Then let’s stop lying on this wood."

They passed the instructions through the group and waited for Qingyue’s signal from the public yard. She had positioned herself where she could see the workers’ path and intercept anyone wandering back early with an innocent request for directions.
When the last porter disappeared up the bank, Leon moved.
He crossed the distance into the shed and caught the clerk’s wrist before the man realized someone stood beside him. His other hand covered the open case.
The clerk tried to turn.
Leon put him facedown on the bench.
"Keep still."
The man drew breath to shout. Leon sealed the sound within a small fold of space and removed the communication token from his belt.
Behind him, the guard reached for his weapon.
Seraphine entered through the side door, caught the draw with the flat of her blade, and drove him to the floor. By the time his cheek struck the boards, his sword was beyond reach.
Outside, Ira dropped the two guards at the gate before either got a weapon clear. The remaining pair turned toward the noise and found Vyra between them and the shed.
A narrow line of flame closed their route to the river.
One tried to force his way past her. She struck him down without disturbing the fence behind him. His companion hesitated just long enough for Ira to reach him.
It took roughly nine seconds.
Leon listened for an alarm and heard only the clerk’s boots scraping against the floor.
"Done outside," Vyra reported from the doorway.
He nodded and looked toward the captive.
The older man had not left his stool. His forearms rested on the bench, his fingers curled around an engraving tool he seemed to have forgotten he was holding.
"Whose men are you?" he asked.
"Jade Moon Palace," Leon said. "We’re taking you out of here."
The captive’s gaze moved to Seraphine, then back to him.
"To another workshop?"
"To give an account of what happened to you."
"That’s all?"
Leon secured the clerk before answering.
"That’s what I need from you. Whether you accept the Palace’s protection afterward is something you can discuss with them."
The man studied him without looking reassured.
Fair enough. Leon doubted he would have believed it either.
Loriel entered and approached the stool.
"May I check your circulation before we release the restraint?"
After a moment, the captive put down the engraving tool.
She took his wrist, examined him, and glanced at Seraphine.
"Slowly. He’s been suppressed for some time."
With Leon holding the controller, they eased the pressure down before Seraphine severed the tether. She then released the bands and set them beside the case.
The captive rubbed one bare forearm.
He tried to stand.
Loriel caught his shoulder and guided him back onto the stool.
"Not yet. Your channels are bruised, and you haven’t been eating properly."
"I can walk."
"I saw you come out of the wagon," she said. "Sit for a few minutes. Nobody here needs you to prove it."
He looked as though he wanted to argue, then lowered his eyes to his hands.
"They took me from my house," he said.
Loriel’s voice softened. "You can tell us once you’ve had something to drink."
Leon left them to it.

Vyra found the collection schedule in a locked drawer, along with the consignment manifest and correspondence concerning the Moonfall workshop. Seraphine secured the controller. Ira brought the outer guards inside, their cultivation sealed, while Qingyue confirmed that nobody in the public yard had noticed the seizure.
Six prisoners, one witness, and enough paperwork to keep a Palace recorder occupied.
Leon questioned the clerk in a corner of the shed.
The man initially insisted that he handled legitimate freight. Leon placed the suppression case beside him and asked whether bound craftsmen were listed under household goods or livestock.
The clerk abandoned that explanation.

He supplied the collector’s description, the expected arrival time, and the phrases used to acknowledge delivery. He admitted that the captive was intended to replace the Moonfall craftsmen. When asked about their deaths, he said the order had come from above and that he had not been consulted.
He sounded more frightened of being blamed for the delay than troubled by the murders.
Leon kept questioning him until the answers began repeating.
The clerk claimed never to have met the Hollow Steward. Perhaps that was true. Perhaps he had one last piece of information he hoped to bargain with.
Palace interrogators could decide.

"He books the freight and pays the holding fees, Young Master," Vyra said after checking his identification against the records. "The correspondence supports that much. I’ll separate his statements from what we can verify."
"Good. Keep the originals together."
Leon stepped outside long enough to clear his head.
The river smelled of wet timber and fish. Farther up the bank, someone laughed at the tea stall.
Tomorrow’s collector would lead to another contact. There might be a storehouse, a buyer, or an office somewhere with more names waiting in a drawer.
He could follow them.
He could also spend that time doing something he actually wanted.

The Lord’s observation had been bothering him throughout the journey. He had caught himself sketching branch ratios beside Vyra’s supply figures that morning, and she had pushed his hand off the page before he ruined her arithmetic.
I’ve done enough to hand this over.
The captive was safe. They had records, prisoners, and a scheduled meeting the Palace could exploit. Leon had no reason to make the entire organization his personal responsibility.
He sent Ji a concise report.

The formation master had been recovered alive, with no additional injuries during extraction. Six prisoners were secured: the shipping agent and five guards. The controller, manifest, correspondence, and collection schedule were intact.
He included the collector’s description and the agreed arrival time the following evening.
Then he added his request.
I would like to transfer the prisoners and the remaining operation to your investigators. We have secured the witness and the supply records. Please advise where to hand them over.
Ji replied before the hour ended.
Agreed. You have given us enough to continue.

Elder Shan’s detachment is already on the northern trade road. I have ordered them to divert. They will reach you tomorrow afternoon, before the scheduled collection. Hold the prisoners and preserve the appearance of ordinary business until then.
Shan will take responsibility for the collector and subsequent arrests. Submit your full account when you return.
Leon read the message, then went inside.

Loriel had found broth among the kitchen supplies. The captive held the bowl himself, although she watched closely whenever his injured arm shifted. Vyra was organizing the records by date. Ira had discovered a bottle of wine and was examining its seal.
"Tomorrow afternoon," Leon told them. "Elder Shan takes over before the collection."
Vyra reached for a clean sheet. "I’ll prepare the inventory."
"And after the handover?" Seraphine asked.
Leon tucked Ji’s plaque into his sleeve.
"Afterward, I’m going to work on my Scripture."
Ira put the bottle down.
"You sound pleased."
He was. The papers in his room had been waiting long enough.

The night workers are leaving for their meal."
"Then let’s stop lying on this wood."
They passed the instructions through the group and waited for Qingyue’s signal from the public yard.
She had positioned herself where she could see the workers’ path and intercept anyone wandering back early with an innocent request for directions.
When the last porter disappeared up the bank, Leon moved.
He crossed the distance into the shed and caught the clerk’s wrist before the man realized someone stood beside him.
His other hand covered the open case.
The clerk tried to turn.
Leon put him facedown on the bench.
"Keep still."
The man drew breath to shout.
Leon sealed the sound within a small fold of space and removed the communication token from his belt.
Behind him, the guard reached for his weapon.
Seraphine entered through the side door, caught the draw with the flat of her blade, and drove him to the floor.
By the time his cheek struck the boards, his sword was beyond reach.
Outside, Ira dropped the two guards at the gate before either got a weapon clear.
The remaining pair turned toward the noise and found Vyra between them and the shed.
A narrow line of flame closed their route to the river.
One tried to force his way past her.
She struck him down without disturbing the fence behind him.
His companion hesitated just long enough for Ira to reach him.
It took roughly nine seconds.
Leon listened for an alarm and heard only the clerk’s boots scraping against the floor.
"Done outside," Vyra reported from the doorway.
He nodded and looked toward the captive.
The older man had not left his stool.
His forearms rested on the bench, his fingers curled around an engraving tool he seemed to have forgotten he was holding.
"Whose men are you?" he asked.
"Jade Moon Palace," Leon said.
"We’re taking you out of here."
The captive’s gaze moved to Seraphine, then back to him.
"To another workshop?"
"To give an account of what happened to you."
"That’s all?"
Leon secured the clerk before answering.
"That’s what I need from you.
Whether you accept the Palace’s protection afterward is something you can discuss with them."
The man studied him without looking reassured.
Fair enough.
Leon doubted he would have believed it either.
Loriel entered and approached the stool.
"May I check your circulation before we release the restraint?"
After a moment, the captive put down the engraving tool.
She took his wrist, examined him, and glanced at Seraphine.
"Slowly.
He’s been suppressed for some time."
With Leon holding the controller, they eased the pressure down before Seraphine severed the tether.
She then released the bands and set them beside the case.
The captive rubbed one bare forearm.
He tried to stand.
Loriel caught his shoulder and guided him back onto the stool.
"Not yet.
Your channels are bruised, and you haven’t been eating properly."
"I can walk."
"I saw you come out of the wagon," she said.
"Sit for a few minutes.
Nobody here needs you to prove it."
He looked as though he wanted to argue, then lowered his eyes to his hands.
"They took me from my house," he said.
Loriel’s voice softened.
"You can tell us once you’ve had something to drink."
Leon left them to it.
Vyra found the collection schedule in a locked drawer, along with the consignment manifest and correspondence concerning the Moonfall workshop.
Seraphine secured the controller.
Ira brought the outer guards inside, their cultivation sealed, while Qingyue confirmed that nobody in the public yard had noticed the seizure.
Six prisoners, one witness, and enough paperwork to keep a Palace recorder occupied.
Leon questioned the clerk in a corner of the shed.
The man initially insisted that he handled legitimate freight.
Leon placed the suppression case beside him and asked whether bound craftsmen were listed under household goods or livestock.
The clerk abandoned that explanation.
He supplied the collector’s description, the expected arrival time, and the phrases used to acknowledge delivery.
He admitted that the captive was intended to replace the Moonfall craftsmen.
When asked about their deaths, he said the order had come from above and that he had not been consulted.
He sounded more frightened of being blamed for the delay than troubled by the murders.
Leon kept questioning him until the answers began repeating.
The clerk claimed never to have met the Hollow Steward.
Perhaps that was true.
Perhaps he had one last piece of information he hoped to bargain with.
Palace interrogators could decide.
"He books the freight and pays the holding fees, Young Master," Vyra said after checking his identification against the records.
"The correspondence supports that much.
I’ll separate his statements from what we can verify."
"Good.
Keep the originals together."
Leon stepped outside long enough to clear his head.
The river smelled of wet timber and fish.
Farther up the bank, someone laughed at the tea stall.
Tomorrow’s collector would lead to another contact.
There might be a storehouse, a buyer, or an office somewhere with more names waiting in a drawer.
He could follow them.
He could also spend that time doing something he actually wanted.
The Lord’s observation had been bothering him throughout the journey.
He had caught himself sketching branch ratios beside Vyra’s supply figures that morning, and she had pushed his hand off the page before he ruined her arithmetic.
I’ve done enough to hand this over.
The captive was safe.
They had records, prisoners, and a scheduled meeting the Palace could exploit.
Leon had no reason to make the entire organization his personal responsibility.
He sent Ji a concise report.
The formation master had been recovered alive, with no additional injuries during extraction.
Six prisoners were secured: the shipping agent and five guards.
The controller, manifest, correspondence, and collection schedule were intact.
He included the collector’s description and the agreed arrival time the following evening.
Then he added his request.
I would like to transfer the prisoners and the remaining operation to your investigators.
We have secured the witness and the supply records.
Please advise where to hand them over.
Ji replied before the hour ended.
Agreed.
You have given us enough to continue.
Elder Shan’s detachment is already on the northern trade road.
I have ordered them to divert.
They will reach you tomorrow afternoon, before the scheduled collection.
Hold the prisoners and preserve the appearance of ordinary business until then.
Shan will take responsibility for the collector and subsequent arrests.
Submit your full account when you return.
Leon read the message, then went inside.
Loriel had found broth among the kitchen supplies.
The captive held the bowl himself, although she watched closely whenever his injured arm shifted.
Vyra was organizing the records by date.
Ira had discovered a bottle of wine and was examining its seal.
"Tomorrow afternoon," Leon told them.
"Elder Shan takes over before the collection."
Vyra reached for a clean sheet.
"I’ll prepare the inventory."
"And after the handover?" Seraphine asked.
Leon tucked Ji’s plaque into his sleeve.
"Afterward, I’m going to work on my Scripture."
Ira put the bottle down.
"You sound pleased."
He was.
The papers in his room had been waiting long enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 686: A Fortune Worth Spending
paragraphs: Elder Shan reached the crossing shortly after midday.

His people arrived in small groups from the road and the river, dressed as travelers and freight workers. By the time he entered the shed, two had already taken over the approaches without attracting the foreman’s attention.
Leon verified his authority token and handed him Ji’s instructions.
The transfer took an hour.

Vyra walked a recorder through the documents while Seraphine explained the restraint and surrendered the controller. The clerk and five guards were moved into secure custody. Shan’s people took responsibility for maintaining the yard’s appearance until the evening collection.
"You have his identification phrases?" the elder asked.
"Recorded alongside his description of the collector," Leon replied. "We haven’t independently verified either."
"We will."
Shan closed the case containing the evidence.
"The Palace Mistress has released you from the assignment. My people can handle tonight."
Leon had expected at least a few more questions.
"That’s everything?"
"Unless you’ve forgotten another prisoner."
"Six was enough."
"Then go."
Before they left, the formation master approached Leon beside the waiting transport. Loriel had explained the available protection, and he had agreed to travel with the Palace escort.
"I didn’t thank you," he said.
"You were busy deciding whether we were worse than the last people."
The man gave a tired, reluctant smile.
"I still don’t understand why you came."
"We were investigating the tools made at the Moonfall workshop. The trail brought us here."
"And you found me."
Leon nodded.
For a moment, the man looked down at the support Loriel had wrapped around his forearm.
"Thank you," he said again, more firmly.
"You’re welcome."
Leon watched him climb into the transport, then joined the others on the western road.
Four days later, they reached Moonfall.
Qingyue parted from them inside the eastern gate, where the road divided toward the merchant districts.
"The investigation will continue?" she asked.
"Shan has the witness and the records. His team was assigned to intercept the collector after we left."
"But you’re finished."
"With this assignment, yes."
Qingyue adjusted the strap of her bag.
Leon could understand why she wanted more. It had been her family’s estate, her relatives endangered by the tools that started all this.
"They have people who can trace payments and question prisoners," he said. "I’ve given them something useful to work with. I’m not going to spend the rest of the year following it myself."
She studied him, then nodded.
"No. I suppose you have your own work."
"I do."
"Then thank you for helping with ours."
There was no accusation in it. Leon appreciated that.
They said their farewells, and his household found rooms for the night.
After the doors were secured and the privacy wards checked, Leon sat down and opened the Cosmic System’s purchasing interface.

The tribute installment had arrived shortly before they left for White Reed. One hundred and eighty million Causality, and he had spent the journey thinking about a stubborn Earth branch instead of deciding what he could buy for it.
Now he had time to look properly.
Finished cultivation methods appeared among the first results.
He examined several out of curiosity, then changed the search. They might be worth studying later, but he wanted resources for the Scripture he had already built.
Time was covered. Xyra could give him a thousand subjective days for one outside without difficulty.
Energy was what he needed: a reserve he could draw from in controlled quantities while comparing different circulation rates.
He worked through the listings until one made him stop.
[Primordial Condensate — Void-Compatible Cultivation Reserve]
[Refined, unaffiliated energy. Stored without a previous cultivator’s imprint. Suitable for controlled absorption through void-natured refining structures.]
[One measure: one sealed reservoir containing one hundred equal portions.]
[Price: 11,000,000 Causality per measure.]
Leon opened the detailed specification.

The stated energy content mattered more than the name. Comparing it with the quantities he had processed from his preserved cores, he estimated that each reservoir held enough for numerous low-output trials. How long it lasted during serious cultivation would depend on what the Scripture demanded.
The packaging allowed him to draw a fraction of a portion and reseal the rest. He would not have to expose an entire reserve whenever he wanted to repeat one measurement.
He checked the compatibility conditions again.

His Primordial Void Heart could refine it. The reserve would supply energy; his own affinities and the Scripture would still have to shape and circulate it. Nothing in the listing promised improved comprehension or a completed method.
That suited him.
He selected ten measures, looked at the total, and paused.
One hundred and ten million was a considerable purchase even after the tribute. He reviewed the specifications once more, then confirmed it.
[Purchase confirmed.]
[Primordial Condensate: Ten measures.]
[110,000,000 Causality deducted.]
Ten sealed reservoirs appeared, each small enough to fit in his palm.
Leon picked one up and laughed.
A moment later, Loriel knocked at the connecting door.
"Come in."
She entered, glanced at the containers, and looked at his face.
"What did you buy?"
"Cultivation fuel."
"That is apparently very exciting fuel."
He read her the description, including the portion controls. When he told her the price and quantity, she sat on the edge of the bed.
"All ten?"
"All ten."
Loriel took the reservoir he offered her, careful to leave its seal untouched.
"How long will they last?"
"I’ll know after I test the intake. At low output, long enough that I can repeat a failed comparison without immediately calculating whether it was worth the expense."
She looked up.
"That’s what you’re pleased about?"

"Partly." Leon leaned back in his chair. "I spent seven months of my own time establishing that first circulation. I want to find out what it can do when I stop forcing every branch into the same pattern."
"And you want to start tonight."
He smiled.
Loriel handed the reservoir back.
"I thought so. I’ll tell the others you’re going inside."
Once the household knew his plans and the room was secured, Leon opened a passage into his dimensional world.
Xyra was on the mansion steps.
"You brought supplies," she said, looking at the reservoirs.
"And something to test."

He gave her his written notes from the conversation with the Lord. They contained the observation about differing flow rates and the questions he had recorded afterward, with nothing identifying the speaker.
Xyra read them while he arranged the containers.
"You want the eastern flat?"
"Yes. A thousand to one, if you don’t mind."
She nodded, and the accelerated zone settled into place without any visible effort.
Leon grinned at her.
"I missed this."
"You were welcome to come back."
"I know."
That was part of what had finally made him stop following the investigation.
On the flat, he prepared the intake array and opened a fresh record book. He left nine reservoirs sealed and connected the tenth without drawing from it yet.
First came the unchanged circulation.

Mana from his Primordial Void Heart followed the established route. Leon measured the branch rates, their return timing, and the strain where they rejoined the neutral section. He recorded the correction needed to keep Earth matched to the others.
The method remained stable.
That mattered. Whatever happened next, he had a working arrangement to return to.

He then admitted a minute quantity of condensate through the intake and allowed his Heart to refine it. The energy entered cleanly, but he still waited through another complete cycle before proceeding.
No unexpected reaction.
Leon wrote that down too.
He was still at Early Qi Refinement in this world’s cultivation system. The reserve beside him did not change that. Neither did the excitement making him want to skip ahead to a larger test.
He settled his hands on his knees.
One change. See what it actually does.
Holding the other eight branches at their recorded rates, he eased the correction on Earth by a fraction.
Then he watched its return to the neutral route.

chapters.title: Chapter 687: Nine Different Answers
paragraphs: The Earth branch settled into a slower rhythm, and Leon’s first thought was that he should have tried this months ago.

A small, constant effort eased. He had been correcting that branch for so long that he barely noticed himself doing it anymore. Now the current moved without his interference, steady enough that he allowed it another complete cycle.
That’s better.
Then it returned to the neutral route.
Water wavered at the junction.
Leon followed the disturbance through the next cycle. Earth’s slower return had changed how the two currents met, and Water now needed the attention he had just stopped giving Earth.
"Oh, fuck off."
He reduced the input and restored his previous settings. The circulation steadied before the disturbance could become anything more than an uncomfortable pressure beneath his ribs.
For a moment, he sat looking at the unopened reservoirs.
Then he reached for his record book.
Less correction in Earth. More correction in Water. No overall improvement yet.
He underlined the last word.

The Lord’s observation had produced something real. Earth had run more comfortably when he let it depart from the matched rate. He simply had eight other branches that also needed to be comfortable with the arrangement.
Leon reviewed the two cycles again in his memory.
He had been measuring how much energy moved through each branch and how quickly it traveled. What he had neglected was the condition of that current when it returned, and what it encountered there.
The common route had worked under the old proportions. Changing Earth meant changing the meeting.
Fine. At least I know where to look.
He began again at a lower input.
For the first week, he changed only Earth’s rate. He repeated each trial with slightly different intake volumes, watching the return junction instead of concentrating entirely on the branch itself.
The results refused to give him one convenient answer.

A rate that reduced strain at low output caused Water to drift when he increased the supply. Another arrangement steadied both currents but forced him to compensate where Wind rejoined farther along the route.
He could make any individual section feel excellent if he ignored what it did to the rest.
That was becoming a deeply irritating talent.

By the end of the first month, his notes had changed. The columns of branch measurements remained, but beside them were sketches of the junctions and short descriptions of what happened as the currents met.
Earth returned more gently at one setting. Water needed a little more separation at another. Lightning tolerated a narrow range of pressure before its arrival began disturbing the neighboring flow.
He stopped treating each result as a setting to copy and began looking for the relationships behind it.
During the second month, he found a combination that held for most of an afternoon.
Leon kept it running while he ate.
He had a bowl balanced on his knee and was reaching for another mouthful when a familiar pressure developed near the lower junction.
He stopped chewing.
You waited until I was happy.

The problem took him two days to isolate. He had allowed the intake to rise gradually without adjusting the returning currents. The balance had been stable at the earlier volume. He had asked it to accommodate more and assumed it would behave the same way.
That mistake went into the record book in unusually large writing.
Xyra found him studying it later.
"You could move the food away from the diagrams," she said.
Leon looked down at a spot of sauce beside the Water branch.
"I know what that mark means."
"Does it mean Water needs more salt?"
He laughed despite himself and moved the bowl.
Xyra sat on the low wall beside the flat. Maintaining the accelerated zone required no visible attention from her, and she looked far more interested in the food than in the array.
Leon passed her a clean bowl.
For a while, they ate without discussing cultivation.
Then she glanced at the latest diagram.
"You keep placing Space after the other returns."
"It’s disruptive. I wanted the others settled before it joins them."
"Does that help?"
"Sometimes."
"And the rest of the time?"
"It disturbs everything I’ve just settled."
Xyra considered that while turning her spoon between her fingers.
"When I change how places meet, I have to consider what already crosses between them. I can’t arrange everything else first and expect the change to fit."
Leon looked at the diagram again.
Her experience was not the same as circulating energy through a body. It did, however, make him notice how consistently he had treated Space as an addition to an otherwise completed arrangement.
"I should compare it earlier in the cycle," he said.
"You should eat before you start."
He finished the bowl.
The first variation failed. The second was worse. But the disturbance shifted to a different junction, and following it taught him something he had missed in the previous arrangement.
He kept working.
By the beginning of the third month, he had a circulation he genuinely liked.

The branches ran at different rates. Their returns were offset where necessary, with enough room in the neutral route for the currents to settle without one affinity dominating the next. He still watched the input carefully, but maintaining the arrangement required noticeably less attention.
Leon tested it through a long seated session.
Then he stood to fetch water.
The circulation drifted.
He stopped halfway to the cistern, followed the change, and felt three of the returning currents beginning to crowd one another.
Restoring the old baseline was easy.
Admitting why he had needed to restore it was less pleasant.
He filled his cup and stood there drinking.
Nearly three months, and it works best when I do absolutely nothing else.

His body could walk without troubling him. He could shape ice, release lightning, or fold a short distance through space with practiced ease. The weakness belonged to the new arrangement: it depended too heavily on the attention he gave it while sitting still.
He had made a comfortable cultivation pattern. He had yet to make one he could reliably carry into the rest of his life.
After that, he moved the tests off the mat.
He walked the flat while circulating. He turned abruptly, accelerated, slowed, and held conversations with Xyra while allowing his attention to follow what she was saying.

Drawing on one affinity changed the demands on the others. A brief lightning technique pulled the balance away from the proportions he had established at rest. Correcting too sharply then troubled the common route.
Leon practiced letting the circulation recover without forcing every current back at once.
Some arrangements were slightly less efficient on paper and far more dependable in use. He learned to prefer them.
He also learned when to stop.

After one particularly stubborn session, he spent an hour on the grass with his notes closed, listening to Xyra describe a change she wanted to make near the mansion. When he returned to the array, he found a mistake in his own measurements that he had been staring past all morning.
Near the end of the third month, the revised circulation held through a complete movement test.

Leon crossed the flat, shaped frost along his forearm, dispersed it, and released a narrow thread of lightning toward a marked stone. He folded four paces sideways, checked the returning currents, and continued walking.
The junctions remained comfortable.
He repeated the sequence at a different pace.
Then again, drawing less energy into the ice and more into the lightning.
By the time he stopped, he was grinning.
He sat down to record the results and realized that he had already begun thinking about the next cultivation session. He had not needed to keep dragging his attention back to Earth.
The improvement was modest enough to describe in a few lines. Living with it felt much better than those lines suggested.
Leon checked the remaining energy in the reservoir, set the intake for a sustained session, and put the movement notes aside.
He wanted to see how far this could take him.

He stopped treating each result as a setting to copy and began looking for the relationships behind it.
During the second month, he found a combination that held for most of an afternoon.
Leon kept it running while he ate.
He had a bowl balanced on his knee and was reaching for another mouthful when a familiar pressure developed near the lower junction.
He stopped chewing.
You waited until I was happy.
The problem took him two days to isolate.
He had allowed the intake to rise gradually without adjusting the returning currents.
The balance had been stable at the earlier volume.
He had asked it to accommodate more and assumed it would behave the same way.
That mistake went into the record book in unusually large writing.
Xyra found him studying it later.
"You could move the food away from the diagrams," she said.
Leon looked down at a spot of sauce beside the Water branch.
"I know what that mark means."
"Does it mean Water needs more salt?"
He laughed despite himself and moved the bowl.
Xyra sat on the low wall beside the flat.
Maintaining the accelerated zone required no visible attention from her, and she looked far more interested in the food than in the array.
Leon passed her a clean bowl.
For a while, they ate without discussing cultivation.
Then she glanced at the latest diagram.
"You keep placing Space after the other returns."
"It’s disruptive.
I wanted the others settled before it joins them."
"Does that help?"
"Sometimes."
"And the rest of the time?"
"It disturbs everything I’ve just settled."
Xyra considered that while turning her spoon between her fingers.
"When I change how places meet, I have to consider what already crosses between them.
I can’t arrange everything else first and expect the change to fit."
Leon looked at the diagram again.
Her experience was not the same as circulating energy through a body.
It did, however, make him notice how consistently he had treated Space as an addition to an otherwise completed arrangement.
"I should compare it earlier in the cycle," he said.
"You should eat before you start."
He finished the bowl.
The first variation failed.
The second was worse.
But the disturbance shifted to a different junction, and following it taught him something he had missed in the previous arrangement.
He kept working.
By the beginning of the third month, he had a circulation he genuinely liked.
The branches ran at different rates.
Their returns were offset where necessary, with enough room in the neutral route for the currents to settle without one affinity dominating the next.
He still watched the input carefully, but maintaining the arrangement required noticeably less attention.
Leon tested it through a long seated session.
Then he stood to fetch water.
The circulation drifted.
He stopped halfway to the cistern, followed the change, and felt three of the returning currents beginning to crowd one another.
Restoring the old baseline was easy.
Admitting why he had needed to restore it was less pleasant.
He filled his cup and stood there drinking.
Nearly three months, and it works best when I do absolutely nothing else.
His body could walk without troubling him.
He could shape ice, release lightning, or fold a short distance through space with practiced ease.
The weakness belonged to the new arrangement: it depended too heavily on the attention he gave it while sitting still.
He had made a comfortable cultivation pattern.
He had yet to make one he could reliably carry into the rest of his life.
After that, he moved the tests off the mat.
He walked the flat while circulating.
He turned abruptly, accelerated, slowed, and held conversations with Xyra while allowing his attention to follow what she was saying.
Drawing on one affinity changed the demands on the others.
A brief lightning technique pulled the balance away from the proportions he had established at rest.
Correcting too sharply then troubled the common route.
Leon practiced letting the circulation recover without forcing every current back at once.
Some arrangements were slightly less efficient on paper and far more dependable in use.
He learned to prefer them.
He also learned when to stop.
After one particularly stubborn session, he spent an hour on the grass with his notes closed, listening to Xyra describe a change she wanted to make near the mansion.
When he returned to the array, he found a mistake in his own measurements that he had been staring past all morning.
Near the end of the third month, the revised circulation held through a complete movement test.
Leon crossed the flat, shaped frost along his forearm, dispersed it, and released a narrow thread of lightning toward a marked stone.
He folded four paces sideways, checked the returning currents, and continued walking.
The junctions remained comfortable.
He repeated the sequence at a different pace.
Then again, drawing less energy into the ice and more into the lightning.
By the time he stopped, he was grinning.
He sat down to record the results and realized that he had already begun thinking about the next cultivation session.
He had not needed to keep dragging his attention back to Earth.
The improvement was modest enough to describe in a few lines.
Living with it felt much better than those lines suggested.
Leon checked the remaining energy in the reservoir, set the intake for a sustained session, and put the movement notes aside.
He wanted to see how far this could take him.

chapters.title: Chapter 688: Six Months Before Dawn
paragraphs: Mid Qi Refinement came nine days after Leon began sustained cultivation with the revised circulation.
He felt the change developing well before it settled.

The energy he refined remained within the native structure more readily. Successive cycles strengthened what the previous ones had established, and the small corrections he still made no longer consumed most of his concentration.

His Primordial Void Heart supplied the mana. The Scripture carried it through the nine affinity branches and back through the neutral route, while the condensate provided the reserve needed to continue.
Leon ate, rested, checked his results, and returned to the mat.
On the ninth day, the structure held a greater volume without reverting when he reduced the intake.
[Cultivation: Mid Qi Refinement]
He opened his eyes and smiled at the empty flat.
Then he tested it.
Two junctions needed adjustment under the increased flow. He lowered the output, compared their responses, and corrected the imbalance before continuing.
The work occupied an afternoon.
That pleased him almost as much as the breakthrough. He understood why the corrections helped now. He was no longer trying combinations and hoping the next one happened to feel better.
The fourth month ended with three reservoirs empty.
Leon kept the containers beside the array so he could see exactly what he had spent. Research had consumed a substantial amount, and the cultivation sessions were drawing more as his capacity grew.
He considered the four unopened reservoirs at the far end of the row, then turned his attention back to the one currently connected.
There was no point saving fuel by refusing to use it for the purpose he had bought it.
Late Qi Refinement took most of the fifth month.

As the volume rose, the returning currents pressed harder against the margins he had left between them. He spent several days refining the transition through the common route, then checked the result while moving.
The first test passed. The second revealed a tendency to overcorrect after a sudden draw on Lightning.
He fixed that before increasing the intake again.

Eventually, he began recognizing the changes before he needed to consult the figures. He could feel a current arriving too sharply or a junction taking longer to settle. The numbers remained useful, but they confirmed what his body was teaching him.
[Cultivation: Late Qi Refinement]
Leon read the notification with a cup in his hand.
He had been waiting for it. Even so, he set the cup down, checked the circulation, and read it again.
One more.
By the end of that month, four reservoirs stood empty.
The sixth month demanded more patience.

He had designed the Scripture’s first stage to carry the whole of Qi Refinement. Reaching its upper limit forced him to verify that the common route could support the volume the branches were now returning.
The neutral section needed to accommodate that growth while remaining neutral.
Several easy adjustments favored one affinity enough to make the others less stable later in the cycle. Leon rejected them, even when the immediate improvement was tempting.
He remembered Ji examining his early work, asking what would happen when he built more upon it.
He wanted to have a better answer thanI hoped that part would stop mattering.
The fifth reservoir emptied during the work.
He opened the sixth.

The final change arrived quietly while he was circulating at a familiar, steady input. The refined energy settled throughout the native structure, and the next cycle passed without the small loss of stability he had been correcting.
Leon maintained it.
He lowered the intake, then increased it gradually. The circulation held.
[Cultivation: Peak Qi Refinement]
He sat with the message in front of him.
His old strength remained where it had always been. He had not suddenly become powerful because a new cultivation framework had finally reached its first realm’s peak.
But the Scripture had worked.
He had taken an idea, built a route for it, corrected what failed, and cultivated through an entire native realm using something of his own making.
I made that.
Leon laughed under his breath.
He wished the others were there to hear it, then reminded himself that he could go and tell them as soon as he finished checking.

The remaining days went into consolidation and practical tests. He used the rest of the sixth reservoir, maintaining the new cultivation while moving and employing familiar abilities at controlled output.
The result remained stable.
At the end of six subjective months, six reservoirs were empty and four were still sealed.
Foundation Establishment would require the next stage of the Scripture. He had notes and questions concerning it, but he left those closed.
He had earned breakfast first.
A little over four hours had passed outside.
Leon returned through the passage into his secured room in Moonfall. The sky beyond the shutters was still dark.
For a moment, he stood beside the same chair he had left earlier that night.
His notes had filled another book. He had worn through a brush, revised the circulation repeatedly, and spent weeks thinking about individual junctions.
Outside, the inn had barely finished sleeping.
He washed, changed, and found Ira awake in the adjoining room.
She looked up from the windowsill.
"Well?"
"Peak Qi Refinement."
Ira’s feet came off the sill.
"Already?"
"Six months for me."
She considered that, then stood and gave him a quick, firm hug.
"Sit down. I’m getting the others."

They ate in private before dawn, with the shutters closed and the wards active. Someone in the kitchen had begun preparing congee, and Vyra had persuaded them to send up a pot along with fish, pickled vegetables, and tea.
Leon discovered that he was hungry enough to stop talking halfway through his explanation.
Seraphine pushed the fish closer.
"Eat. You can tell us afterward."
He did, then described the Earth branch, the changed returns, and the embarrassing walk to the cistern.
Ira laughed at that part.
"You should have called me. I’d have made you stand up much earlier."
"You’d have thrown something."
"Probably."
Seraphine was more interested in the testing.
"I’ve noticed a hesitation when I bring the newer circulation into one of my sword sequences," she said. "Only during the transition. It settles when I repeat the form slowly."
"That might be worth comparing at different output," Leon replied. "It may have nothing to do with what I found, but I can show you how I recorded it."
"I’d like that."
Vyra asked how much condensate remained.
"Four reservoirs," he said. "Six used, including the research."
She nodded. "Then you have something left when you begin the next stage."
"And time to decide how to use it," Leon said.
That led them into their own preparations.

Seraphine wanted to study materials that would support lightning and light together through Golden Core condensation. She had no intention of selecting something merely because it strengthened one affinity impressively.
Ira’s concern was endurance under heat.
"I can supply the flame," she said. "What I need is a structure that will hold up when I use it properly."
"So look at what tolerates the intensity," Vyra said, "before buying something that adds more."
Ira pointed her spoon at her. "Yes. That."
Vyra wanted to examine resources suited to sustained external control. A material praised for one explosive release might offer little to someone holding and adjusting flame over a wide area.
Loriel listened while turning her cup.

"I want living material I can cultivate," she said when Leon asked. "Something compatible with my path that survives in conditions I can maintain. A rare herb is useful, but I’d rather establish a reliable source than keep searching for replacements."
"That sounds like more work," Ira said.
"It is."
Loriel smiled as though that was part of the appeal.
Leon listened to them compare possibilities. None had a complete answer yet, and none sounded content to let the next breakthrough happen merely because a manual listed the steps.
He wanted to help them find what suited them.
For now, they had somewhere to return to, libraries to consult, and a garden Loriel was already asking after.
"We’ll leave for the Palace today," Leon said.
Vyra reached for the teapot.
"After breakfast."
He held out his cup.
"After breakfast."

chapters.title: Chapter 689: A Share Worth Waiting For
paragraphs: By the time they reached Jade Moon Palace, Leon had finished his report and read it twice for anything he had forgotten.
Vyra’s supply accounting required no such revision.
Han Suwen accepted both at the residence gate, glanced through the expenditure list, and paused over the final figures.
"Everything is accounted for?"
"Everything drawn from the household allowance," Vyra said. "The unused materials are listed on the reverse."
Han Suwen turned the page.
Leon watched her expression settle into something close to approval.
"I’ll have the balance credited back to the account."
"Thank you."
Loriel was already looking past them toward the inner garden. Ira had put down her bags long enough to stretch, then picked them up again after catching Vyra’s eye.
The ordinary familiarity of the residence pleased Leon more than he had expected.
He spent the afternoon putting his cultivation records in order and leaving the more private ones behind his own wards.
Ji saw him the following morning.
She read the White Reed account while he drank the tea that had been set out for him.
"Elder Shan took the collector that evening," she said at last. "The records have given my investigators several useful directions. They will continue from there."
Leon set down his cup.
"Did the formation master reach safety?"
"He is under Palace protection. His account is being checked against the correspondence."
"Good."
Ji placed the report on the table.
"You handed over a living witness, six prisoners, and intact records. That was a useful conclusion to the assignment."
"Thank you, Master."
"Now. You mentioned changes to your circulation in the note you sent with this."
Leon took out the three sheets he had prepared.
He had removed the dates and the records of his energy supply. What remained showed the old branch relationships, the revised arrangement, and the responses he had measured at different outputs.
Ji drew the first sheet toward her.
Leon explained the Earth adjustment and how the resulting strain had appeared elsewhere.

"I had been treating the matched rates as something the method needed permanently," he said. "They were useful while I established the structure. After that, I kept correcting departures from the pattern without testing whether some were preferable."
"And you found they were."
"Some of them. Only after adjusting how the returning currents interacted."
Ji compared the figures.

"Unequal circulation is familiar," she said. "Keeping nine affinities stable through one neutral route is where your difficulty lies. You cannot borrow the proportions from a method built for two or three and expect them to hold."
"I tried enough combinations to become convinced of that."
Her eyes lifted toward him.
Leon told her about getting up for water.
A faint amusement entered her gaze.
"And until then you had tested it seated?"
"I had tested changes in output. I hadn’t adequately tested divided attention."
"Those are different demands."
"Yes. I’m aware."
"I imagine you are."
He let her enjoy that for a moment.
Ji returned to the records.
"And now?"
"It holds through movement and the changes I’ve tested. I left more tolerance in several junctions instead of choosing the arrangement with the lowest cost at rest."
"That was sensible."
She asked about two transitions, and Leon answered from his notes. When the discussion reached a point he had not tested, he said so.
Ji marked the place lightly.
"Compare a sustained draw with repeated short releases when you next have the opportunity. The same average consumption can place different demands on the return."
Leon made a note.

She had not seen his private training records or examined the new native cultivation beneath his older foundation. He intended to keep the conversation on the method, and she allowed it to remain there.
"May I retain these?" she asked.
"These copies, yes."
Ji placed them beside his report.
"Then we can discuss what you should prepare for next."
She unrolled a chart of Ashen Rain Basin.
The entrance complex was marked beneath the western survey region. Around it, the Palace’s survey notes had become considerably more detailed since Leon’s visit.

"Ruan is maintaining the seal and observing the realm’s formation," Ji said. "The original estimate was three to six months. We do not yet have enough consistent measurements to replace it with a reliable opening date."
Leon leaned closer to the chart.
"So we have time."
"Time to prepare. Not a reason to assume the earliest estimate is a promise."
"Understood."
"When the Grotto-Heaven opens, we intend to send an expedition. Your role in finding and securing the entrance will be reflected in your allocation."
That had his full attention.
Ji noticed.
"You may ask directly, Leon."
"What does the allocation give me?"
"A personal share of the distributable gains, with priority when choosing suitable resources to fill that share."
He considered the wording.
"Before the ordinary distribution?"
"Yes. Once the finds have been assessed, you make your selections before the remainder is assigned."
"And those selections count against my share."
"They do. Priority determines when you choose. It does not give you a second allocation."
"Vyra will want that written down."
"It will be."
Leon smiled.
Ji continued before he could ask the next question.
"If a single discovery exceeds the value of your allocation, it requires a separate agreement. You do not acquire an unlimited claim by pointing first."
"I was about to ask."
"I know."
She tapped the entrance marked on the chart.

"The Palace also retains responsibility for the realm’s infrastructure. Anything necessary to preserve its stability or access is outside ordinary distribution. We will establish those boundaries before entry."
That was reasonable. Leon had spent enough time repairing the entrance to understand why letting excited cultivators dismantle important structures would be a problem.
"Can I select materials for my household?"
"Within your allocation, yes. Their needs are yours to consider. Their own contributions can also be recorded through the normal process."
He thought of the breakfast conversation in Moonfall.
Seraphine would want the compatibility reports. Vyra would want to know how valuation was handled. Loriel would probably ask whether living specimens could be preserved until she examined them.
Ira would ask what could withstand her fire.
Ji watched his attention move across the chart.
"Before you make a list of treasures," she said, "remember that we have not seen the interior."
"What can Ruan tell?"

"The forming realm shows strong storm and spatial-temporal characteristics. Combined with the basin’s existing deposits, that gives us reasons to expect useful materials. It does not establish their quality, quantity, or accessibility."
"So no catalogue."

"No catalogue," Ji agreed. "There may be resources suited to you. There may also be things the Palace values highly that you have little use for. Your priority allows you to choose intelligently once we know the difference."
Leon liked that considerably more than being promised an unnamed treasure.
He asked a few practical questions about assessments and the recording of finds. Ji answered what had been decided and identified what still needed to be settled.
By the time he left, he understood what he had earned and where its limits lay.
On the path back to his peak, he found himself thinking about Foundation Establishment.

The first stage of the Scripture now had a complete cultivation history behind it. He knew how it behaved throughout Qi Refinement. The next stage would ask different things of the vessel and the energy it held, and four reservoirs would not relieve him of the need to understand those changes.
He wanted materials worth studying. He wanted options suited to his own path, and enough freedom to reject impressive things that did not fit.
The others wanted much the same.
Below him, the residence came into view. Loriel was in the garden with one of the workers, examining a tray of seedlings. From the western courtyard came the sound of Ira striking a practice target.
Leon slowed at the gate.
There was work waiting, but he had chosen this work.
He went inside to find Vyra and tell her about their share.
