"Understood."
"When the Grotto-Heaven opens, we intend to send an expedition.
Your role in finding and securing the entrance will be reflected in your allocation."
That had his full attention.
Ji noticed.
"You may ask directly, Leon."
"What does the allocation give me?"
"A personal share of the distributable gains, with priority when choosing suitable resources to fill that share."
He considered the wording.
"Before the ordinary distribution?"
"Yes.
Once the finds have been assessed, you make your selections before the remainder is assigned."
"And those selections count against my share."
"They do.
Priority determines when you choose.
It does not give you a second allocation."
"Vyra will want that written down."
"It will be."
Leon smiled.
Ji continued before he could ask the next question.
"If a single discovery exceeds the value of your allocation, it requires a separate agreement.
You do not acquire an unlimited claim by pointing first."
"I was about to ask."
"I know."
She tapped the entrance marked on the chart.
"The Palace also retains responsibility for the realm’s infrastructure.
Anything necessary to preserve its stability or access is outside ordinary distribution.
We will establish those boundaries before entry."
That was reasonable.
Leon had spent enough time repairing the entrance to understand why letting excited cultivators dismantle important structures would be a problem.
"Can I select materials for my household?"
"Within your allocation, yes.
Their needs are yours to consider.
Their own contributions can also be recorded through the normal process."
He thought of the breakfast conversation in Moonfall.
Seraphine would want the compatibility reports.
Vyra would want to know how valuation was handled.
Loriel would probably ask whether living specimens could be preserved until she examined them.
Ira would ask what could withstand her fire.
Ji watched his attention move across the chart.
"Before you make a list of treasures," she said, "remember that we have not seen the interior."
"What can Ruan tell?"
"The forming realm shows strong storm and spatial-temporal characteristics.
Combined with the basin’s existing deposits, that gives us reasons to expect useful materials.
It does not establish their quality, quantity, or accessibility."
"So no catalogue."
"No catalogue," Ji agreed.
"There may be resources suited to you.
There may also be things the Palace values highly that you have little use for.
Your priority allows you to choose intelligently once we know the difference."
Leon liked that considerably more than being promised an unnamed treasure.
He asked a few practical questions about assessments and the recording of finds.
Ji answered what had been decided and identified what still needed to be settled.
By the time he left, he understood what he had earned and where its limits lay.
On the path back to his peak, he found himself thinking about Foundation Establishment.
The first stage of the Scripture now had a complete cultivation history behind it.
He knew how it behaved throughout Qi Refinement.
The next stage would ask different things of the vessel and the energy it held, and four reservoirs would not relieve him of the need to understand those changes.
He wanted materials worth studying.
He wanted options suited to his own path, and enough freedom to reject impressive things that did not fit.
The others wanted much the same.
Below him, the residence came into view.
Loriel was in the garden with one of the workers, examining a tray of seedlings.
From the western courtyard came the sound of Ira striking a practice target.
Leon slowed at the gate.
There was work waiting, but he had chosen this work.
He went inside to find Vyra and tell her about their share.

chapters.title: Chapter 690: Room for What Comes Next
paragraphs: Vyra had a slate waiting when Leon returned from Ji’s peak.
He looked at it, then at the tea cooling beside her elbow.
"You’ve been here a while."
"Long enough to wonder whether you remembered to ask what happens when something you want exceeds your share."
"I did."
"Good. Sit down."
Seraphine occupied the window seat, with Ira stretched across the other end and Loriel reading at the table. Leon took the empty chair and explained the agreement.

His discovery earned him a personal allocation from the expedition’s distributable gains, with priority selection within that allocation. He could choose resources for his household. Anything exceeding his share required a separate agreement, while the realm’s access mechanisms and structural resources remained with the Palace.
Vyra wrote three short lines.
"That will do."
"You sound surprised."
"I prefer hearing the terms before being pleased about them."
Ira lifted her head. "Can you be pleased now?"
"A little," Vyra allowed.
Seraphine had been listening without interrupting. Now she closed the book resting against her knee.
"I’d rather begin looking before the realm opens."
"For your Core materials?" Leon asked.
She nodded. "Lightning and light occurring together naturally. The Palace records mention several possibilities. I want to examine them before deciding what suits me."
"Then find out what’s available. After my next session, we’ll go."
"All of us?" Ira asked.
"If there’s something worth going for."
Seraphine was already marking her page. Leon watched her get up, pleased by how quickly a vague future promise had become something she could use.
He had work of his own to begin.

That night, he entered the dimensional world from his sealed cultivation chamber. Xyra prepared the accelerated region around the eastern flat, where his notes and the four remaining condensate reservoirs waited.
"One thousand to one?" she asked.
"Yes."
"It’s ready."

She said it while examining the fruit he had brought her. Leon accepted the reminder that something capable of giving him months before morning required less of her attention than choosing what to eat.
He settled beside his books.

The Palace’s Foundation Establishment texts were thorough. They explained how to temper expanded meridians, stabilize the Qi Sea, and begin forming the structure that later cultivation would develop. Their authors had anticipated mistakes Leon would otherwise have made himself.
He had copied several warnings into his notes.
What the manuals could not provide was a foundation designed for affinities its creator did not yet possess.

Most methods committed to a particular path. Their structure supported known demands, and that commitment made them dependable. Even the texts covering several affinities worked toward an arrangement suited to those affinities.
Leon understood the appeal. He could probably finish something tailored to his current nine much sooner.
Then he would spend the next addition regretting it.
I didn’t call it the Formless Myriad Scripture because nine sounded impressive.
He turned back to his own circulation diagram. The neutral centre remained sound. Around it, his branches operated at different rates and accommodated the changes he had tested during Qi Refinement.
Those allowances had limits. He knew them well enough to avoid them, which had begun to feel suspiciously like solving the problem.
The Lord’s advice returned while he was examining a junction he had adjusted dozens of times.
Balance need not mean equal flow.
He had used it to stop forcing unlike affinities through matching schedules. Now he wondered why the schedule needed to remain fixed at all.
During a fight, his demands changed constantly. A foundation intended to accept future affinities would have to tolerate changes greater than those.
He remembered composing an impressive explanation for a woman who could probably have dismantled it with a single question.
Instead, she had given him something useful.
Leon laughed before he could stop himself.
Xyra glanced over from the low wall. "What?"
"Remembering advice I should have understood sooner."
"How much sooner?"
He looked at the diagrams covering the ground.
"Don’t ask."
The first month went into an arrangement he could test without committing it to a permanent foundation.

He used his established circulation to support short experimental cycles, feeding them carefully measured condensate. The native Qi Sea remained under observation throughout. Whenever a trial became unstable, he returned to the reliable pattern he already knew.
His first serious attempt worked while every affinity stayed within its familiar range.
Leon increased Lightning and Space together, reduced Earth and Water, and kept the overall input unchanged.
Pressure gathered at the return junction.
He compensated almost automatically. The pressure eased.
Then he realized what his hands, breathing, and attention had all stopped doing.
I’m holding it together again.
He restored the previous distribution and noted the result. Nothing had torn. There was no need to spend a week recovering from a lesson he could learn by stopping promptly.
The design depended too heavily on the resting branches continuing to accept a particular share of the circulation. Changing two demands unsettled the others.
For eleven days, he tried adding unused capacity to the trial arrangement. Spare routes seemed sensible. Eventually, another affinity would need somewhere to circulate.
The extra routes did nothing to solve the present problem.
Leon stared at the latest result, irritated enough to want to blame the diagram.
There was plenty of room. The energy still arrived where the arrangement could not accommodate it.
He crossed out three pages and kept the fourth, which showed exactly why it had failed.

Through the second month, he began changing where neutral energy waited before entering an affinity branch. Rather than requiring every branch to accept its usual supply, he allowed the intake to respond to demand while keeping the shared reserve unaffiliated.
Lightning could draw more without demanding that Water carry lightning through its own route. Water could ease without leaving a return junction dependent on energy that would no longer arrive.

The adjustments required more than widening passages. Some responded too late; others continued feeding a branch after its demand had fallen. Leon spent days finding tolerances that did not require his constant intervention.
Meals interrupted the work. Sleep helped more than he liked admitting.
Once, he woke with his cheek pressed against a page and discovered that the line he had spent the previous evening studying was a crease in the paper.
He ate properly after that.
Near the end of the second month, he repeated the first test.
Lightning and Space increased. Earth and Water eased.
The reserve supplied the change, and the returning currents settled without pushing the junction beyond its tolerance.
Leon waited.
He reached for his cup. Took a drink. Put it down on the correct page this time.
Eleven minutes passed before he restored the original distribution.
Nothing needed rebuilding.
He wanted to stand up and declare it solved. Instead, he tried a different combination, found a delay in Fire’s return, and spent the afternoon correcting it.
By evening he had completed twelve trials. Two failed, both safely, and both gave him something specific to examine.
He walked over to Xyra with an appetite he had ignored for hours.
"Is there anything left to eat?"
She moved the fruit bowl toward him.
Leon took one and sat on the wall. For once, he let the notes remain where they were. He had a promising result, an explanation for it, and months in which to find out whether he was wrong.
That was enough to enjoy dinner.

chapters.title: Chapter 691: A Foundation of His Own
paragraphs: The second reservoir opened on the first morning of the third month.
Leon set the empty vessel beside his notes and connected the new one to the regulating array. He had learned enough from the first to resent its loss less than he expected.
Now he needed to find out how badly his promising arrangement could misbehave.

He began with input volume. Slow increases produced no difficulty, but a sharp increase left energy waiting at three junctions. Widening them relieved the pressure and made the next reduction troublesome instead.
For a week, every improvement seemed to arrive carrying another problem.
Leon eventually found himself looking at two diagrams that differed by a single adjustment. One handled increased intake. The other recovered cleanly when he reduced it.
He placed them beside each other and stopped trying to make either do both.
The junction needed room to accommodate the change, with a controlled return to its resting state afterward. Fixing it at either extreme was what kept producing trouble.

Once that worked, he concentrated demand in individual affinities. Fire drew heavily for an hour. Ice followed after the circulation settled. Darkness required a different allowance, and he was glad he had tested it before congratulating himself.

The reserve remained neutral until energy entered the branch that needed it. That distinction mattered. Letting one affinity’s excess spill into another would have defeated the purpose of the entire design.
By the fourth month, he could vary several demands together without watching every junction.
Then Ji’s suggestion ruined a very pleasant morning.
He had copied it beneath the measurements he had shown her: compare sustained draw with short bursts at a similar average demand.
Leon ran a steady Lightning cycle first.
It behaved beautifully.
He repeated the same average demand through abrupt pulses. The first pulse tightened the lower junction. The second arrived before it had fully recovered.
He stopped before the third.
"Oh, come on."
Xyra looked over from where she was sitting in the shade.
"Bad?"
"Annoyingly reasonable."
The system responded quickly enough once demand changed. It did not respond before the change arrived. Each sudden draw briefly concentrated strain where the continuous test had spread it out.
Ji had identified the distinction without needing his private routes or knowing what realm he was actually cultivating.
Leon added the result beneath her suggestion.
Ask better questions next time she looks at your work.

He spent three weeks distributing a small neutral reserve nearer the branch entrances and adjusting how quickly it replenished. Holding that energy ready reduced efficiency slightly, but it allowed a sudden demand to be met before the rest of the circulation caught up.
He tested the change until he stopped expecting it to fail.
Only then did he begin moving.
Walking was straightforward. Talking while walking exposed a hesitation he had missed. Using frost, then Lightning, then a short spatial fold required adjustments to two return routes.
His familiar abilities remained familiar. What needed attention was the new circulation running beneath their changing demands.
Leon eventually carried out an entire sequence while discussing dinner with Xyra.
"You’ve asked me that already," she said.
"Have I?"
"Twice."
He checked the circulation. It had held through the spatial fold, the lightning discharge, and his own apparently terrible conversation.
"Then tell me something else."
Xyra threw a fruit at him.
He caught it, laughed, and recorded the successful test after he finished eating.
The breakthrough began in the fifth month.

Leon examined his meridians again before drawing from the third reservoir. His former foundation remained undisturbed; the work concerned the native cultivation structure he had been building alongside it.
The strength he already possessed made some preparations easier. It could not decide how his new Qi Sea should stabilize.

He tempered the expanded routes gradually, allowing each adjustment to settle before proceeding. Nine days passed in measured cycles, meals beside the array, and sleep whenever continued attention became less useful than rest.
The Qi Sea took longer to satisfy him.
When he pressed too quickly, one affinity began influencing where the energy settled. Leon eased the process, corrected the distribution, and started again from the last stable point.
He wanted the underlying structure neutral. Accepting a bias now because he could compensate for it would leave him correcting the same compromise in every later realm.
On the sixteenth day, the Qi Sea held its shape when he relaxed his active guidance.
Leon waited through another complete circulation.
The first foundation structure remained beneath it, supporting the settled energy without relying on a single affinity’s pattern.
[Native Cultivation: Early Foundation Establishment]
He read the notification twice.
Then he opened his eyes and looked around the empty flat, wishing someone had happened to be watching.
That would have been a good moment to have an audience.
He was smiling anyway.

There was nothing complete about the whole Foundation realm. His platform still required development, and the fuller integration described in the later stages lay ahead. The new structure did, however, remain steady when he examined it, relaxed, and examined it again.
He had made it work.
Leon sat there longer than necessary, enjoying the result before he allowed himself to list everything that still needed testing.
The System had confirmed his realm. It had offered no verdict on future affinities. He would have to prove that part when he had something genuinely new to integrate.
The remainder of the fifth month went into settling the breakthrough. During the sixth, he repeated the movement and demand tests under the new conditions.
Two tolerances needed widening. A return route became more efficient than expected, which pleased him until he discovered it had altered the timing farther along.
He corrected that too.
By the end of six subjective months, three reservoirs stood empty beside the array. The fourth remained sealed.
Leon cleaned the equipment, put his notes in order, and thanked Xyra.
"Finished?" she asked.
"With this part."
"Good. You’ve been walking past the same view for months without looking at it."
He looked across the dimensional world before leaving. She was right. He gave himself a few minutes beside her, with nothing circulating except what now ran comfortably on its own.
Four and a half outside hours after entering, he stepped back into the sealed chamber on his personal peak.
Ira waited in the adjoining inner sitting room. Loriel had fallen asleep in a chair with a book resting against her chest.
"You were quick," Ira said quietly.
"Six months."
She studied him, then put down the knife she had been cleaning.
"You did it?"
"Early Foundation."
Her grin arrived immediately. She stood and caught his wrist, giving him a quick, pleased squeeze.
"Good. Seraphine found something, and she’s been trying very hard to let you finish."
"What something?"
"A crystal. She has drawings."
"That sounds dangerous."
"There are several drawings," Ira whispered, glancing at Loriel.
Leon laughed softly. He took the book before it slid from Loriel’s lap and laid it on the table.
For him, it had been months since he saw them. He wanted to wake everyone, tell them what had worked, and hear whatever small things had happened during their evening.
Instead, he sat beside Ira.
"Tell me about the crystal."
She leaned back against the chair and began with the part about its guardian.

chapters.title: Chapter 692: Something Worth the Journey
paragraphs: Seraphine brought three drawings to breakfast.
Ira looked across the table at Leon, who kept his expression straight with some effort.

"Dawnspar," Seraphine said, placing the first sheet in front of him. "Lightning and light formed together in the same mineral structure. There are recorded growths on the sea stacks off the northern point."
The drawing showed a pale crystal with violet branches running through a golden centre.
"The Palace has samples?" Leon asked.
"Two prepared pieces in the mineral vault. I examined both yesterday."
"And?"

"Good materials. Either could be useful with the right supporting resources." Seraphine moved the second drawing beside the first. "But these are individual specimens. The relationship between their affinities changes as they grow. What suits another cultivator’s method may not suit mine."
Leon studied the small notes beside each illustration.
"You couldn’t tell from the pieces?"
"I could tell enough to know I want to compare them with active growths. These were harvested decades ago. Their structure has settled."
"So we go and let you choose."
Seraphine looked up. "You don’t want to hear the alternatives?"
"I’ll read them on the way."

He liked having the Palace’s resources available. He also liked being able to choose something better suited to the people who mattered to him. A few days spent helping Seraphine prepare properly seemed an excellent use of his time.
Across the table, Vyra drew the third sheet toward herself.
"Does it explain transport?"
"The next page," Seraphine said.
"There are more pages?" Ira asked.
Seraphine handed her the account of the guardian.
Ira settled down to read.

The northern point lay three days away by Palace transport, followed by a morning’s journey in a smaller boat. They arranged the necessary permissions and left with records of the known growths, preservation instructions, and three carrying cases.
Vyra checked the cases herself before accepting them. Their linings could maintain an isolated specimen’s charge, but only if adjusted to the material placed inside.
Loriel read the harvesting notes and added stone-cutting tools to their supplies.
"I thought she was taking a crystal," Ira said.
"It grows into rock," Loriel replied. "We may need to bring some."
"How much?"
"I’ll tell you when I see it."
Leon approved of that answer. He was becoming suspicious of anyone who could promise an exact result without examining what they were working with.

For most of the journey, Seraphine alternated between the records and her own technique notes. She borrowed clean paper from Vyra, returned with questions for Loriel, and once asked Leon to demonstrate a small separation of light from lightning so she could compare how their residual energies faded.
He did it twice before admitting he did not know what she was looking for.
"That’s all right," she said. "I do."
Her pleasure when the second demonstration confirmed something made him glad he had asked.
On the second evening, he found her on a sheltered section of deck. The crew worked at the opposite end of the vessel, beyond the quiet ward he set around their seats.
"Have you decided what the perfect one looks like?" he asked.
"I’ve decided what I want it to do. Apparently the appearance can be misleading."
"An inconvenient habit in expensive things."
Seraphine smiled and put her notebook aside.
He sat close enough for their shoulders to touch. For a while she watched the red light spread across the water.

"I could spend months studying the vault pieces," she said. "I’d understand them very well by the end. But I’d still wonder whether I chose them because they were suitable or because they were there."
"And now?"
"Now I get to find out."
She leaned against him. Leon rested his hand over hers and let the conversation lapse.
He had missed this during seclusion: being beside someone without needing to explain what he was thinking.
The boatman who carried them out the following morning was an older Palace disciple with a weathered face and an impressive dislike of the local birds.
"Leave food uncovered and they’ll take it from your hand, Senior Brother."
"I’ll keep that in mind."
Ira closed the paper around her breakfast.
The sea stacks rose from grey water in a group of eleven. Dark rock stood above white surf, its upper ledges scattered with pale mineral growths. Gulls wheeled over the outermost stack.
The boatman pointed toward a sheltered inlet beneath a lower rock.
"I’ll wait there. Signal when you’re ready."
"Middle stack, Young Master," Seraphine said. "The largest recorded growths are on its upper ledges."
They ascended together, leaving the boat well below and out of earshot.
Salt had collected in the hollows of the stone. Dawnspar clusters grew from narrow cracks, some no longer than Leon’s finger, others reaching his waist.
Ira stopped beside the largest.
"That one looks promising."
Seraphine examined it before shaking her head.
"Strong lightning aspect. Stable, too. It might suit someone who uses light mainly to guide lightning."
"But not you?"
"Not what I’m building."

She moved slowly along the ledge, holding her hand near each likely specimen and introducing a trace of her own energy. Leon could perceive the responses, but their significance became clear only when she explained what pleased or disappointed her.
One crystal answered quickly to lightning and sluggishly to light. Another held both well but resisted the rapid transitions her sword method required.
Seraphine spent nearly an hour comparing them.
At a smaller cluster near the seaward edge, she stopped.
"This one."
Leon crouched beside her.
The formation was roughly the size of two fists. Fine violet lines surrounded a warm golden interior. When Seraphine alternated the faint traces of her affinities, the response followed cleanly.
She repeated the test more slowly.
The pleasure in her expression was easy to recognize.
"Better than the vault pieces?" he asked.
"For me," she said. "Yes."
Stone scraped behind them.
A huge heron had landed at the inland end of the ledge, forty paces away. Blue-white light ran along its feathers. A ridge of pale crystal protruded between its folded wings.
Ira lowered her pack.
"No trouble," she said quietly.
Loriel was looking at the bird’s back. "The records mentioned crystal deposits on mature ones. It feeds on loose discharge around the growths."
The heron spread one wing.
Lightning snapped from its feathers into a nearby cluster. Violet flared through the mineral, briefly overwhelming the gold.
Seraphine’s hand tightened around Leon’s sleeve.
"Keep it away from this end."
He looked from the larger crystal to the specimen beside them. Its response was still steady.
"How much interference can yours take?"
"I don’t want to find out while harvesting it."
The heron lowered its head and opened its beak. Its attention moved between Ira and the group crouching near the growths.
Leon rose without releasing more energy than he needed.
They could kill it easily enough. That would not help if its first discharge spoiled what Seraphine had spent the morning choosing.
"Which ground do you want clear?" he asked her.
Seraphine looked along the ledge, judging the distances. She laid her notebook beside the chosen cluster and weighted its corner with a stone before answering.
"Everything between us and that split in the rock. Ira can have the other side."

chapters.title: Chapter 693: Leave That One Intact
paragraphs: Ira moved before the heron finished opening its wings.
She ran along the inland side of the ledge, passed its lowered beak, and struck the rock beside its feet with a narrow thrust of flame.
The bird lunged after her.

Ira let it follow, keeping her retreat along the bare stone beyond Seraphine’s chosen boundary. Its beak punched through the place where her shoulder had been. She caught the shaft of her lance against its neck and turned its next strike farther inland.
Lightning burst from its feathers.
Vyra’s Crownfire rose between the bird and the crystal beds. The discharge struck the low curtain and scattered within it, contained before it could reach the nearest growth.
Leon stepped beside Seraphine and bent the space above and around their section of ledge. An arc striking the boundary would turn away rather than cross it.
He left the working area open around the three of them.
"Stray discharge won’t reach us," he said. "The rock is still connected underneath."
Seraphine nodded. "That’s what I’m examining."
At the other end of the ledge, the heron tried to take flight.
Ira caught it as its feet left the stone. Her lance pierced the outer muscle beneath one wing, avoiding the joint, and she drove it down onto the bare inland shelf.
Vyra narrowed the Crownfire around it before another discharge could spread.
The bird struck once with its beak. Ira pressed her weapon lower, holding the wing extended until its struggling stopped.
Less than half a minute had passed.
"Keep it there," Seraphine called.
Ira glanced back. "Take your time."
Leon returned his attention to the crystal.
Seraphine knelt at its base while Loriel brushed loose salt and grit from the crack. Fine mineral threads extended beneath the visible cluster, penetrating the stone.
"How deep?" Leon asked.
Seraphine followed the threads with her perception.
"A hand’s depth below the main growth. A little farther on this side."
She indicated the seaward edge. Beneath it, an old fracture ran diagonally toward the drop.
Loriel leaned over to examine the exposed face.
"The weather’s been working underneath it. You can see where pieces have already fallen."
"Can we take a larger block?" Leon asked.
"Only if we lift half the ledge," Seraphine replied. "There are thinner threads extending beyond the main root. I’ll have to separate those cleanly."
She set her fingers against the rock and closed her eyes.
Leon waited. Behind them, the heron scraped a claw across stone. Vyra spoke quietly to Ira, and the scraping stopped.
Seraphine opened her eyes again.
"I have the line."
She drew her sword and placed its edge beside the crack. A fine pulse of lightning entered the stone, following the boundary she had chosen.
The first cut went cleanly.
At the second, a violet line brightened inside the crystal.
Loriel lifted a hand. "Its response changed."
"I felt it."
Seraphine withdrew the blade and introduced a trace of light through her fingertips. She paused, measured the response, and added less the second time.
The violet line settled.
Leon watched without interrupting. She had spent the morning learning the specimen’s behaviour, and now she was using that knowledge while cutting it free.
"How close?" he asked.
"Back within the response I measured. The structure’s intact." Seraphine checked it again. "I’m restoring what was there. If the inner growth splits, adding light won’t put it back together."
"Good."
She adjusted the energy along her blade before making the next cut.
This time the crystal barely stirred.
The heron gave a harsh cry from the inland shelf and struck the rock with its free foot. Ira shifted her stance and forced the leg down.
A tremor travelled through the ledge.
Beneath Seraphine’s hand, the old fracture opened.
Leon caught the supporting slab with a spatial hold before it dropped, but a thin thread beneath the cluster had already pulled taut.
Seraphine stopped moving.
"Hold it exactly there."
"I have it."
Loriel shifted closer, watching the crystal while Seraphine lowered her face toward the opening.
The thread lay below the last cut. If the stone moved again, it would tear through the denser growth she wanted to preserve.
Leon could lift the whole section. He could also crush it without effort. Neither would help her now.
"Can you reach?" he asked.
"Yes. Give me a moment."
She changed her grip on the sword and slid the point into the narrow gap.
The gold at the crystal’s centre flickered. Loriel reported the change in a low voice, and Seraphine answered with another measured trace of light.
Her blade advanced.
Leon felt the supporting stone become lighter as the last connection parted.
"Free," Seraphine said.
She lifted the block with both hands.
He shifted the three of them and the specimen to a broad patch of bare rock farther along the ledge. The unsupported seaward slab broke away behind them and fell into the surf.
Seraphine looked down at what she held.
Loriel’s fingers hovered near the violet lines.
"Still steady."
Only then did Seraphine let out the breath she had been holding.
Vyra kept the heron restrained while Leon brought over a carrying case. Seraphine set the block into its cradle, and Loriel helped adjust the lining to preserve the response they had recorded.
They checked it twice before closing the lid.
At the inland shelf, Ira looked toward Leon.
"Finished?"
"With the crystal."
She glanced down at the bird beneath her lance.
Loriel was already approaching. "We can leave it alive."
"It has strong opinions about that," Ira said.

"The records describe these birds feeding on excess charge and shedding it back into the beds. We don’t know how much the growths depend on them." Loriel studied the wound. "And that wing is repairable."
Leon looked across the untouched clusters. They might want another specimen someday. Killing the creature would earn them less than keeping a productive site intact.
"Treat it," he said. "We’ll release it once we’re aboard."
Ira withdrew her lance when Loriel was ready. Vyra maintained the restraint while the torn muscle closed.
By the time they descended, the heron could fold both wings. Leon held it in place until the boat had pulled away from the stack, then released his grip.
It rose to its feet and watched them leave.
The boatman took one look at its spread wings and put more strength into his oar.
Seraphine kept the case against her knees throughout the crossing.
Later, alone in the transport’s passenger cabin, Leon sat beside her.
"The adjustment during the cut," he said. "You knew how much light it needed."
"Only because I tested it first."
"That was good work."
She ran her thumb along the case’s clasp.
"I thought I’d be more relieved," she admitted. "Mostly I want to open it again."
"Will that hurt it?"
"No."
"Then open it."
She did, checking the gold and violet within the cradle before smiling.
Leon leaned closer to look with her. After a moment, Seraphine rested her shoulder against his.
She began telling him how the specimen differed from the vault pieces. This time he understood enough to follow, and when he asked a question, she turned the case so he could see the answer.

chapters.title: Chapter 694: What Waits Beyond the Gate
paragraphs: For two days after their return, Seraphine occupied the small preparation chamber beside the inner garden.
Leon found her there on the second evening, sitting before the dawnspar with a sheet of observations balanced on her knee.

The crystal rested in a preservation array assembled by Vyra from the Palace’s instructions. Loriel had helped establish the conditions around the stone, and Seraphine had set the final energy balance herself.
"How is it?" Leon asked.
"Exactly how I brought it back."
"That sounds less exciting than you look."
"I’ve checked it after resting, after sword practice, and after a full circulation." She tapped her notes. "It still responds the way I need."
He crouched beside her to examine the gold within the violet branches.
"What remains?"
"A stabilizer suitable for condensation, and trials with the materials together. I need to know how they behave under compression."
"So no surprise breakthrough tomorrow?"
Seraphine looked at him. "You’re asking me that?"
"An entirely reasonable question."
She smiled and moved the sheet so he could read it.

The dawnspar would support the interaction at the centre of her future Core. She had made progress, and she understood what to examine next. Leon liked that more than a promise that one fortunate trip had settled everything.
Outside, Ira was arguing with Vyra about whether a heat-testing chamber’s damaged floor counted as part of the test.
Loriel passed the open door carrying two small pots.
"Was it?" Leon asked her.
"I wasn’t there."
"A very careful answer."
"She asked whether the floor was reinforced before she started," Loriel said, and continued toward the garden.
Seraphine laughed under her breath.
Leon stayed with her until she finished the next set of observations. When she finally put the sheet aside, he persuaded her to come and eat before Ira’s explanation grew any longer.
He reviewed his own part in the expedition the following morning.

The spatial hold beneath the breaking slab had demanded sustained control, followed by the sudden movement of three people and a block of stone. His native circulation had accommodated both without pulling his attention from the work.
He recorded that result beside the earlier trials.
One field test added evidence. It did not tell him how the method would behave under every pressure he might eventually face.

The sealed reservoir stood beside his desk. Leon checked its storage seal and left it untouched. Further advancement would have its turn; he wanted the new foundation settled before deciding how best to use what remained.
Ji summoned him on the fourth day.
He arrived to find a map spread across her table, with a report placed beside it. The outline of Ashen Rain Basin was familiar. New marks surrounded the entrance complex they had repaired.
"Your household returned with what it wanted?" Ji asked.
"A suitable dawnspar specimen for Seraphine."
"Han Suwen’s report mentioned that you left the guardian alive."
"It contributes to the crystal beds. We may want to harvest there again."
Ji nodded. "Sensible."
She moved the report toward him.
"Ruan has something you’ll find interesting."
Leon sat down.

Since the Palace secured the basin, Ruan had been measuring the energy reaching the repaired nexus from the forming realm. The work required no entry beyond the threshold, and Ji made clear that none had taken place.
"Storm activity, spatial fluctuations, and temporal irregularities," she said. "Those were expected. There are also traces she believes may indicate heat-rich regions and living growth."
"Believes?"
"The readings pass through an entrance complex with its own effects. She is careful about attributing everything she detects to the interior."
Leon looked at the first page. Several observations were repeated across successive measurements, with uncertain results marked separately.
"What changed?"
"She has enough repetitions to compare the relationships. Look here."
Ji indicated two lines that rose together.
One represented a surge associated with storm energy. The other recorded a spatial response. The same sequence appeared farther down the page, then again on the next.
"They arrive together?" Leon asked.
"Within the resolution of her measurements. More interestingly, the interference is much lower than her models predicted."
He leaned forward.
"How much lower?"
"Consistently enough that she checked the instruments and repeated the measurements through another part of the nexus."
"And obtained the same result."
"Close enough to justify further study," Ji said. "That is what she has established. The explanation remains open."
Leon turned the page.

Ruan had listed several possibilities. An arrangement within the realm might allow these energies to coexist with relatively little disturbance. The entrance itself might be separating or regulating what reached her instruments. The effect might belong to one narrow region rather than the entire Grotto-Heaven.
He appreciated the alternatives, though he knew which one he wanted to be true.

For months, he had worked on a circulation that adjusted when unlike affinities changed their demands. Here was evidence that might let him observe a related problem in an environment far larger than his own body.

paragraphs: The evenveil jade was beautiful, and Seraphine did not want it.

Leon had watched her test it for most of an hour in the medicine court. The pale green disc sat beside the dawnspar, with a thread of her spiritual energy running through both. Across the bench, the court’s specialist studied a formation plate whose reading had scarcely wavered.

"An excellent result, Senior Brother Leon," the woman said. "Evenveil is one of our most reliable stabilizers for dual-affinity condensation." She turned the plate toward Seraphine. "How does the return feel?"
"Slow."
The specialist checked the reading again. "Show me."

Seraphine withdrew her energy and fed it through faster, beginning with lightning before cutting sharply into light. The return remained smooth, but Leon felt the small hesitation before it answered her.
"There," Seraphine said. "If I commit to a lightning strike and need light in the follow-through, that’s a delay I have to account for."
"You could compensate."
"I could. I’d rather see whether I need to."
The specialist considered her for a moment, then reached for the catalogue.
Leon leaned back, smiling into his tea. He had expected to spend the morning listening to prices. Watching Seraphine make someone reconsider a faultless reading was considerably more interesting.
They tested five more candidates over the next two days. The Palace had all of them in stock, along with several the specialist dismissed after seeing Seraphine’s requirements.

Vyra arranged the requisition through the household’s contribution account, leaving Leon little to do except accompany Seraphine and occasionally offer an opinion. She asked for it twice. Both times, she listened carefully and chose something else.
He liked that more than he expected.
The second stabilizer had the same hesitation as the evenveil. The third favored light slightly, a difference Seraphine noticed before the formation plate settled.
"Perhaps one part in forty," she said. "It isn’t much, but I’d have to keep correcting it. Does the bias increase under compression?"
The specialist brought out its testing record. It did.
They put it aside.

The fourth responded quickly until Seraphine reversed the sequence, when it tried to settle her energy back into its previous pattern. The fifth was excellent at maintaining a steady release. Leon suggested it might be worth keeping for comparison, and Seraphine agreed, though she doubted she would choose it.
"For someone holding a defensive technique, perhaps," she said. "I change direction too often."
The sixth was tracewire silver, an unimpressive coil of gray metal with a brighter seam running through it.
Seraphine’s first test produced a less even reading than the jade. On her second, she changed the order of her affinities twice. The return followed her both times.
Leon set down his cup.
"Better?" he asked.
"Much." She repeated the transition, then deliberately slowed it. "It isn’t trying to choose a pace for me."
The specialist watched another cycle before speaking.
"Its stability margin is narrower. You’ll have to establish the timing yourself before condensation."
"That’s work I can do," Seraphine said.
"Then do it at several densities. A good result here isn’t permission to skip the difficult part."
Seraphine nodded, already looking toward the testing array. "May I try a higher compression?"
They stayed until the specialist lit the lamps.

When Seraphine paused to rest, the woman brought her water and asked which test had felt most natural. They compared the result with the fifth candidate instead of simply discarding its records. Leon watched Seraphine point out the difference, pleased that the conversation had become a discussion between two people who took her requirements seriously.
By then, Seraphine had a page of measurements, a provisional preparation schedule, and the silver wrapped in a cloth she checked twice before placing it beside the dawnspar’s case.
At the door, a clerk offered Leon the remaining test instructions.
"Give those to her," he said. "She’s the one doing the work."
Seraphine accepted them with a small bow. "Thank you, Young Master."

She maintained the proper distance on the walk home, though once, when the road bent out of sight of the court, Leon caught her looking down at the case with a smile she had apparently forgotten to hide.
That evening, Seraphine found him in the protected inner residence with a book open across his knees.
"I’d like tonight," she said.
Leon looked up. "Tonight?"

"With you. Before I begin." She folded her arms, then seemed to think better of it and let them fall. "Ira’s at the western platform. Vyra has finished with the accounts, and Loriel knows not to come looking for us."
He closed the book, keeping a finger between its pages out of habit. Seraphine glanced at his hand.
"Were you planning to finish that?"
"Not anymore."
That earned him the smile he had seen on the road.

She crossed to his chair and took the book from him, placing it on the table before settling beside him. For a while she said nothing. Her shoulder pressed against his, and he rested his hand over hers.
"I thought I’d be nervous," she admitted.
"About seclusion?"
"About choosing everything myself. The crystal, the stabilizer, how I want the Core to work." She rubbed a thumb over his knuckles. "Mostly, I keep wanting to start."
Leon knew that feeling well enough. He also knew what happened when it persuaded him to ignore food, sleep, and anyone knocking on his door.
"Then why wait until tomorrow?" he asked.
Seraphine turned toward him. "Because I’d like tonight."
"Right. I deserved that."
She laughed softly and leaned in to kiss him.

He had meant to tell her that he was pleased she had disagreed with him at the medicine court. With her hand against his cheek, it suddenly seemed a strange thing to bring up. He kissed her back instead, drawing her closer until she stopped smiling long enough to complain that the chair was too narrow.
"You chose it," Leon said.
"I’m choosing somewhere else."
She stood and held out her hand. He let her lead him into the adjoining room, leaving the book where she had put it.

chapters.title: Chapter 698: The Core She Wants
paragraphs: Seraphine’s sword reached the target, and the light arrived late.
She stopped with the blade against the practice post. A narrow scorch marked the place where lightning had struck; the following cut had bitten a finger’s width away from it.
Against a stationary post, both attacks had landed. Against something moving, the second could have missed altogether.
"Again," she muttered.
She released the partial compression in her circulation. The next attempt left a single clean mark.
Six weeks into her preparation, she could reproduce the problem whenever she wanted. Solving it had proved less accommodating.

The eastern flat inside the dimensional world gave her plenty of room to work. Xyra had established the accelerated boundary with no more effort than Leon might spend opening a door. Beyond the practice ground stood a small shelter, a table for her records, and a bench that Ira had claimed on her first visit.
Seraphine set her sword down and recorded the density of the trial.

The tracewire silver was doing what she had chosen it for. It supported compression without imposing a fixed pace. Her own circulation, however, grew less willing to change direction as she drew it tighter.
Straight thrusts remained fast. The Eighth Form did not.

That movement began with lightning, then followed the same attack with light as she turned her wrist. She liked it because an opponent could commit to avoiding the first strike and still be caught by the second. Under compression, the transition gave them longer to recover.
She tried it once more, then caught herself reaching for the testing array again.
Eat first. Loriel will ask.
A covered dish waited in the shelter. Ira had left a note beneath it assuring her that she had only taken one dumpling.
There were three empty places in the dish.
Seraphine ate the rest while reading yesterday’s measurements.
The household visited without crowding her. Loriel checked her circulation regularly and had already persuaded her to take two days off when a junction became tender under repeated compression.
Seraphine had resented the interruption until she returned to find she could distinguish changes she had stopped noticing while tired.
Vyra helped arrange her records so that failed trials were as easy to find as successful ones.
"Write why you rejected it," she said, tapping a blank column. "Otherwise you’ll try the same thing again and be annoyed with yourself."
Seraphine had already done that twice. She filled in the column.

Ira brought food and news of her own preparations. One afternoon she spent so long complaining about an uncooperative mineral that Seraphine laughed until her stomach hurt. It was a pleasant change from thinking about the same fraction of a second.
When Leon visited, she showed him the marks on the practice post.
He asked her to repeat the movement slowly, then watched the corresponding return through the testing plate.
"They’re arriving together here," he said, indicating the narrowest junction.
"They always have."

"And there’s less room under compression." He moved his finger away. "I ran into something similar with the Scripture. Changing when the branches returned helped more than forcing them through faster."
Seraphine studied the plate. "You staggered them."
"Some of them. The arrangement changed with demand." He glanced at her notes. "Yours won’t need to work like mine, but you could test whether the timing is part of the problem."

She wanted to reach for the array immediately. Instead, she asked him to stay while she repeated the original trial. If she was going to change the return, she wanted to be certain what it was doing first.
Over the following weeks, Seraphine tested light returning ahead of lightning, then behind it, then at different intervals as compression increased.
The first improvement was small enough that she distrusted it. She repeated the trial after resting, changed her starting stance, and tried the same timing through a different sword form.
It held.

By the end of the second month, she had a range of workable intervals and a clear understanding of what happened when she chose badly. Too little separation crowded the return. Too much left her feeding the next movement unevenly.

One trial carried the first cut perfectly and weakened the second. Another worked when she began from rest but failed after a retreating step. She kept those records beside the successes, marking the circumstances rather than blaming her footwork and moving on. In a fight, she would not always have the stance she wanted. The circulation had to answer from the one she actually had.
She could feel the difference in her wrist before the testing plate displayed it.

That pleased her more than the clean readings. Her swordsmanship had begun long before she learned this world’s circulation, and she had no intention of treating those years of experience as something to discard.

Much of her fighting had been shaped by protecting someone behind her. She knew how to leave room to retreat, how to turn an attack aside without committing her whole body, how to notice a threat that was not aimed at her.
The Eighth Form was a movement she enjoyed for its own sake.
She remembered the satisfaction of first making its second cut land where she wanted. Even alone on the practice ground, she had smiled afterward.
I’m keeping that.
Her next trial was clean. So was the one after it.
She spent several more days testing at low output, where it was easier to overlook an uneven return. Only when those results matched did she prepare for condensation.
Early in the third month, Seraphine sat inside the array with her sword resting within reach.
There was nothing it could help her cut. She had put it there anyway.
Loriel finished checking the circulation and withdrew. Leon waited near the shelter, far enough away to leave her space. When Seraphine looked toward him, he raised a hand.
She returned the gesture, closed her eyes, and began.

Her Qi Sea drew inward under steady pressure. She guided the prepared dawnspar energy through her lightning and light circulation while the refined tracewire supported the compression. Beneath the gathering energy, her foundation platform contracted toward the forming Core Embryo.
She followed the sequence she had rehearsed, adjusting the return intervals as density increased.
For a time, every change matched her records.
Then crystallization began.

The return tightened more quickly than it had in any partial trial. Light cleared the junction, but lightning reached it before the previous flow had fully passed. Seraphine felt the familiar hesitation through the movement she was holding in her mind.
She steadied the compression without letting it reverse.

Her next breath came carefully. The Core could finish at the present timing; the circulation remained sound. But the delay would be built into the result, and correcting it afterward would be far harder.
She knew which adjustment had worked in her trials. What she did not yet know was how far the interval would need to widen at the final density.
A little at a time. You know what an uneven return feels like.
Seraphine moved the light forward by the smallest amount she could control.
The first crystalline layer trembled around the change. She held the embryo steady, waited for the return, and felt the path begin to clear.
Now she had to bring the lightning through without losing it.

Her wrist had already begun turning. Light carried the follow-through into the space he now occupied, and the flat of her blade tapped his ribs before he completed his recovery at the pace they had agreed.

"There it is."
Seraphine could not stop smiling. "Again."
"You’re allowed to enjoy the first one."
"I am. I’d enjoy a second."
He changed his timing, and she discovered how much work remained. Leon won the next exchanges comfortably, though twice she forced him to alter the response he had begun.

By the time they stopped, her forearms ached and her notes had acquired three new corrections. The additional output changed the pressure along her blade; the grip she used in the Third Form needed adjusting before it became a bad habit.
She sat beside him on the wall and flexed her fingers.
"I thought I’d finish one thing," she said. "Now I want to change half my forms."
"Do you mind?" Leon asked.
"Ask me after I’ve had a bath."

She looked down at the blade across her knees. During the preparations, she had imagined the successful transition so often that she had worried the real thing might feel ordinary. It had felt better. Leon nudged her shoulder, and she realized she was smiling at her sword while he waited patiently beside her.
"Thank you for the targets," she said.
The others had brought their own preparation work into the dimensional world during her seclusion and continued it after returning.
Ira had selected a dense fire-aligned mineral from the Palace’s unworked stock. Its resistance to sudden heating had frustrated the craftsmen who tested it, which interested her considerably.
"I want to hold more inside without releasing it every time I move," she told Leon. "This might help. If I can persuade it to accept the heat first."

Vyra had ordered components suited to sustained external control. The formation hall had supplied several established arrangements; she was comparing how they behaved when a flame’s shape and pressure kept changing.
"The standard tests hold one pattern," she explained. "Mine needs to keep working while I alter it."
Loriel maintained two trial plantings in the garden, testing possible supports for her life-force circulation. She showed the others her observations but was not yet willing to choose between them.
All three remained at Peak Foundation Establishment, with work of their own to finish.
That evening, Leon took the last sealed condensate reservoir from storage and set it beside his Scripture notes.
Seraphine paused at the door. "Your turn?"
"That’s the idea."
She glanced at the cylinder, then at the pages. "Leave room for corrections."
Leon opened to a fresh sheet and broke the final seal.

sentences.text: The lightning returned cleanly, and Seraphine almost relaxed too soon.
As the Core Embryo compressed further, the interval narrowed again.
She caught the change, eased the light forward, and waited through another complete circulation before touching the lightning’s return.
Light was the easier flow for her to regulate finely.
She used it to establish the interval, then brought the lightning into place behind it.
Nothing had to be forced through the junction alongside anything else.
The next cycle passed without hesitation.
She repeated it, feeling for the unevenness that had spoiled her early trials.
On the following cycle, she imagined the turn of her wrist through the Eighth Form.
Both responses came when she wanted them.
Seraphine allowed crystallization to continue, making smaller adjustments as the Core settled.
The last of her foundation contracted into a violet-veined crystal, and she maintained the complete circulation until its shape held without her constant attention.
Only then did she open her eyes.
Her sword lay beside her knee.
She reached for it, stopped with her fingers above the hilt, and laughed under her breath.
Not yet.
You can wait until you can stand properly.
Across the flat, Loriel had already risen from her chair.
Consolidation occupied the rest of the third month.
Drawing energy from the new Core felt different from drawing it from her Qi Sea.
Seraphine kept anticipating the old response, adjusting too early, then having to correct herself.
She slept badly for a while.
During one check, Loriel found that she had continued holding unnecessary tension at a lower junction even after ending a cycle.
"Rest it for the afternoon," Loriel said.
"You’re making it work when it doesn’t need to."
"Can I practice without circulating?"
"You can sit with me and eat something."
Seraphine went with her.
By evening the discomfort had eased, which made arguing about it seem rather pointless.
The most troublesome adjustment appeared at low output.
Her staggered return worked beautifully during a demanding sword movement, then drifted when she let the flow settle.
It took several days to recognize that she was preserving an interval meant for a much heavier load.
Once she stopped overcorrecting, ordinary circulation became comfortable.
At the end of the third month, she completed her checks, set the records aside, and sat for a while enjoying the simple fact that nothing required fixing that morning.
[Native Cultivation: Early Golden Core]
Ira arrived with lunch and slowed when she saw her expression.
"Finished?" she asked.
Seraphine nodded.
Ira put the tray down with unusual care, then hugged her hard enough to make her laugh.
"Finally.
I was running out of things to complain about."
"No, you weren’t."
"I was saving the good ones." Ira released her and went to call the others.
Vyra arrived first, looked over the completed record, and smiled before drawing Seraphine into a brief embrace.
Loriel wanted one final check and then, satisfied, squeezed her hand.
Leon came across the flat while Ira was redistributing the lunch.
"The Eighth Form?" he asked.
Seraphine had been waiting for someone to ask that.
"Faster," she said.
"Only a little, but I can feel it."
His expression brightened.
"When do I get to see?"
"As soon as Loriel stops looking at me like that."
"After lunch," Loriel said.
"You can describe it after lunch."
They returned through the passage into Leon’s sealed inner chamber with the completed notes and the empty preparation cases.
A little over two outside hours had passed since Seraphine entered seclusion.
Three days later, she met him in a protected practice yard on his peak.
Leon stood inside the marked exercise circle, turning a practice blade in his hand.
"Same distance each time?" he asked.
"To begin with.
Then change the angle."
"And the short folds?"
Seraphine considered the circle.
"Keep them within the markers.
I want to test the transition, not spend the afternoon chasing you."
He grinned.
"Fair."
At first he gave her straightforward openings, withdrawing as she committed.
Her lightning cut met his blade; light followed along the changing angle before he could close that opening at the exercise’s chosen pace.
He increased the pressure and made her repeat it from the other side.
Seraphine missed twice, corrected her footing, and tried again.
When Leon began using short folds, she watched where his feet settled after each return.
He had limited himself to the circle, but he varied the direction enough that she could not simply memorize it.
She drove a lightning cut toward his shoulder.
He vanished from its path and reappeared near the left marker.

chapters.title: Chapter 700: The Palace’s Choice
paragraphs: The higher flow lasted half a cycle before Leon shut it down.

He sat on the eastern flat inside his dimensional world, watching the reservoir’s measured feed diminish. Nothing had torn. He had stopped as soon as pressure began collecting at the neutral center, but his irritation arrived with the same speed as if something had gone wrong.
It worked perfectly at the old volume. Naturally.
His foundation could accommodate the additional energy. The circulation could not yet redistribute the supply quickly enough when demand changed.
He ran a slower trial and followed the delay.

The nine affinity branches already operated at different rates, drawing on the neutral reserve as needed. Their supply routes, however, still responded on the same schedule. Under a sudden increase, the busiest route finished receiving its share too late.
He had improved what each branch did with its energy and left the distribution behind.
Leon reached for his notes.

The Lord of Illusion and Mystery had made unequal flow sound almost embarrassingly obvious. He wondered whether she would find it amusing that he was still discovering places where he had failed to apply it.
Fortunately, he had no reason to tell her.
The work took a fortnight of subjective time.

Leon widened the supply paths used most heavily during his ordinary techniques and adjusted when the neutral reserve fed them. The elemental circulations remained distinct; he was changing how their needs were met, not pouring fire into water and hoping they would get along.
His first successful test was seated. He enjoyed it for perhaps a minute before getting up to find out what movement would ruin.

He walked with ice gathering along his forearm, released it, and called lightning while folding a few paces sideways. The demand rose sharply. Supply reached the active branches before pressure could build at the center.
On the next trial, he held a rock within a pocket of space and moved the pocket with him. That worked too.
Then he concealed the fold, increasing the demands of Darkness and Space together, and found a route he had left too narrow.
"Of course it’s you," he muttered, marking the junction.
Widening everything would have been easy and wasteful. It would also have taught him very little about whether the foundation could adjust when an unfamiliar demand appeared.
He corrected the restriction and repeated the earlier trials, varying the order so he could not unconsciously prepare the next response.
The arrangement held.

Only then did he settle into sustained cultivation, gradually increasing his working volume until his circulation maintained it without constant correction. The reservoir fed the process in measured portions. By the time his foundation stabilized at the new capacity, most of what remained had been drawn into the array.
[Native Cultivation: Mid Foundation Establishment]
Leon opened his eyes and stretched his legs before standing.

He had the beginnings of a foundation that could change its response. Someday it would need to do that for an affinity he did not yet possess. For now, keeping the present nine working under a heavier load was satisfying enough.
The last portions went into consolidation. When he finished, he turned the empty cylinder in his hand and checked the seal out of sheer reluctance to put it down.
Ten reservoirs purchased. Ten consumed.
Worth it. Expensive as hell, but worth it.
He set the cylinder aside and began recording what the next stage would require.

Xyra passed the shelter while he was writing and asked whether he wanted the training zone left ready. Leon nearly said yes out of habit, then looked at the empty reservoir. He thanked her and gathered his notes. He wanted to tell the others before deciding what to attempt next.
Outside, the remaining weeks passed toward the Grotto-Heaven’s original three-month assessment mark.

Leon left the accelerated training for specific work. He spent ordinary days testing his circulation in the practice yards, reading, and discovering how many small tasks appeared when five people actually lived in a residence.

Loriel recruited him to hold a tree upright while she checked its roots. Ira returned from the medicine court carrying a second opinion about her mineral and arguing aloud with both opinions. Vyra persuaded the formation hall to modify a testing schedule after showing exactly where its standard measurements missed her requirements.
Seraphine changed her grip for the Third Form, then found the adjustment affected the Seventh. Leon heard about both over dinner and was called outside afterward to provide a moving target.

He liked these evenings. Nobody needed him to be impressive at the table, though Ira remained very interested in whether she could beat his newly improved native circulation without using her full strength.
He told her to finish her own preparations first.
One afternoon, he checked the date of the previous Cosmic tribute installment against the local calendar. The next expected payment remained some weeks away.

The higher beings followed their own cycles. He had expected those cycles to differ from the clock here, and his working estimate was roughly three local months between receipts. The Grotto-Heaven’s opening did not change that calculation.
He closed the interface without posting anything.
Asking a basic question in that company could become a much more expensive mistake than buying another reservoir.
Recognition within the Palace reached him in small, unmistakable ways.

A formation specialist requested his account of the repaired entrance. Two disciples under consideration for the expedition sought his opinion about carrying supplies through shifting terrain. Han Suwen included him in correspondence that would previously have gone directly to an elder.
The people involved knew what he had found. Beyond that circle, the account remained a survey team recovered from a broken formation field.
Ji summoned him a fortnight before the expected opening.

"Your allocation remains as agreed," she said. "Priority selection within your personal share. Structural and access resources remain with the Palace. Your household’s separate contributions receive their own credit."
Leon nodded. "Understood."
"And if something exceeds that allocation, ask before treating it as yours."
"I can manage that."
She gave him a look that suggested she would remember the answer.

They discussed supplies and collection procedures. Leon asked about preserving living specimens, then about recording the energy conditions around them. If the realm offered both useful materials and a chance to study how different energies coexisted, he wanted to bring back more than a bag of stones.
Ji approved the recording equipment.
"One more thing," she said as he rose. "If you must choose between a load and the people carrying it, leave the load."
"I will."
"Even if you chose it first."
Leon smiled. "Especially if someone else can help me retrieve it later."
"That is an answer I believe."
Three days later, a new packet from Ruan brought him back to Ji’s study.
The preliminary tests concerned the inner threshold. No one had entered the true realm, but its admission array had begun responding to the signatures Ruan presented.
Ji placed the readings before him.
"The lower signatures are accepted for passage," she said. "Those above Golden Core are refused. Concealing the higher signatures hasn’t changed the response."
Leon read the measurements twice.
"Would that keep the elders outside?"
"If the opening confirms it, yes." Ji gathered the pages. "Ruan is checking the boundary again. We may need a very different expedition."
Her gaze settled on him, and Leon began to understand why she had called him personally.
